<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
    Let $({{\mathrm D}},{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}})$ be complete, let $\tau_o>0$ be such that
    $\tau_o^{-1}+\kappa > 2\eta_+$ and suppose that
    \begin{itemize}
            \item ${\mathsf b}$ is $\eta$ interaction dissipative and nonnegative on the diagonal 
        according to 
        \eqref{introeq:disseta}-\eqref{introeq:diagonal}; 
        \item for every $\tau\in (0,\tau_o)$,
	every $\bar x,x\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	the functions $y \mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$, given by
    \begin{align*}
        {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)=\frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,y) - \frac{1}{2\tau} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x) + {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}\,,
    \end{align*}
    are barycentrically $(\tau^{-1}+\kappa)$ convexlike with respect to some
    continuous barycentric system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$;
        \item $x \mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ satisfies a suitable (conditional) upper semicontinuity. 
    \end{itemize}
     Then for any initial condition $x_0\in{{\mathrm D}}$, there exists a solution $(X_\tau^n)_{n\ge 0}$ to (VMS), which satisfies the discrete EVI \eqref{introeq:bEVI}.
     There exists a continuous curve ${\mathsf x} : [0,+\infty) \to {{\mathrm D}}$ with ${\mathsf x}(0)=x_0$ that satisfies the EVI
     \begin{align*}
         \frac12\frac{{\mathrm d}} {{\mathrm d} t} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)+\frac{\kappa}{2} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)\le {{{\mathsf b}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}\quad\text{$t\in (0,+\infty)$,}\quad 
	\text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}}\,.
     \end{align*}
     Any continuous curves ${\mathsf x},{\mathsf y}$ which satisfy the EVI above also satisfy the contraction estimate
     \begin{align*}
         {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf y}(t)) \le e^{\lambda(t-s)} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(s),{\mathsf y}(s))\,, \quad \text{for all }0\le s\le t\,.
     \end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order}
    A set of energy functionals $(F^{(i)})$ are $(\eta,\kappa)$-monotone, 
    with rate $\lambda = \eta-\kappa$, if
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\kappa$ convexity: $y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$ is barycentrically $\kappa$-convexlike with respect to a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$.
        \item $\eta$ dissipativity: ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)} + {{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)} \le \eta {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)$.
    \end{itemize}
    Equivalently, each $F^{(i)}(\cdot,x^{(-i)})$ is barycentrically $\kappa$-convexlike and for every $x, y \in {{\mathrm D}}$, 
        \begin{align*}
    \sum_{i=1}^N 
   F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-  F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) + F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) \le \eta \,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)  \,.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:barycentric maps}
    A $J$-barycentric map in ${{\mathrm D}}\subset{{\mathrm X}}$ is
a map
$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}:\bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}\to {{\mathrm D}}$.
We set $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{i}:=\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\mathsf e}_J^i)$.


A system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$ of $J$-barycentric maps 
in ${{\mathrm D}}$ is a collection
of $J$-barycentric maps $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}$
such that the evaluation map
\begin{equation}
	\mathsf E 
	:{\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}\to {{\mathrm D}}^J,
	\quad
	\mathsf E[\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}]:=\big(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{1},
	\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{2},\cdots 
	\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{J}\big)
	\quad\text{is surjective,}
\end{equation}
i.e.~for every collection of $J$ points in ${{\mathrm D}}$, denoted ${\boldsymbol x}\in {{\mathrm D}}^J$,
there exists $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$ 
such that $x_j=\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j}=\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\mathsf e}_J^j)$, $j=1,\cdots,J$.


A system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ of barycentric maps
is the union of
$J$-systems ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$, for every $J\in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:convexlike}
	Let $\varphi:
     {{\mathrm D}}\to 2.30$,
    ${{\mathrm D}}\subset {{\mathrm X}}$.
	\begin{enumerate}[\rm (1)]
		\item 
	We say 
	that $\varphi$ is \textbf{$\kappa$-convexlike} 
	with respect to 
	a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2$ of 2-barycentric maps
    in ${{\mathrm D}}$ 
	if 
	for every 
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ and
	${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{2}$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:B2-convex}
		\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}))\le 
		\alpha_1\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{1})+\alpha_2\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{2})
		-\frac\kappa2\alpha_1\alpha_2
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{1},\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{2}).
	\end{equation}
	\item We say that $\varphi$ is \textbf{barycentrically $\kappa$-convexlike}
	with respect to a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$
	of barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$
	if for every integer $J\in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}$, 
	every $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$, and
	every ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:convex}
		\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}))\le 
	\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha_j\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j})-
	\frac \kappa 4\sum_{j,k=1}^J
	\alpha_j\alpha_k{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j},\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{k})
	\end{equation} 
\item We say that $\varphi$ is \textbf{barycentrically quasi-convexlike}
	with respect to a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$
	of barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$
	if for every integer $J\in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}$, 
	every $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$, and
	every ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:quasi-convex}
		\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}))\le 
		\max \Big\{\varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j}):
	j\in \{1,\cdots,J\},
	\alpha_j>0\Big\}
	\end{equation} 
	\item
     
	A collection $(\varphi_a)_{a\in A}$ of functions
is \textbf{jointly} $\kappa$-convexlike (resp.~barycentrically $\kappa$ convexlike, 
barycentrically quasi-convexlike)
if every function
$\varphi_a$ is $\kappa$-convexlike 
(resp.~barycentrically $\kappa$-convexlike,
barycentrically quasi-convexlike)
with respect to a common system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$
of $2$-barycentric maps
 (resp.~a 
common system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ of barycentric maps)
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:radial-convexity}
    A bifunction ${\mathsf a}$ is $\xi$ {\em radially convex} if for every $x,y\in{{\mathrm D}}$ there is a family
	$(z_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ in ${{\mathrm D}}$, with $z_0=x$ and $z_1=y$, such that
    \begin{equation}
		\label{eq:radial-convex}
		{\mathsf a}(z_t,x)\le (1-t)\,{\mathsf a}(x,x)+t\,{\mathsf a}(y,x)
		-\frac\xi2\, t(1-t)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y),\qquad t\in[0,1],
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:convex1} 
	In a geodesic metric space ${{\mathrm X}}$
	there is a natural system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$ of $2$-barycentric maps given by all the minimal, constant speed geodesic paths
    associated with 
	${\mathsf x}:[0,1]\to{{\mathrm X}}$
	satisfying \eqref{eq:geodesic}.
    We just set
    $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((1-t),t):={\mathsf x}_t$.
    
	A function $\varphi$ is geodesically $\kappa$-convex if
	it is $\kappa$-convexlike 
	with respect to a subsystem ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2\subset {\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:interp_vector_space}
	In a vector space $V$ 
	we can  use 
	the canonical convex combinations
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol v};{\boldsymbol \alpha})=
	\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha_jv_j$
	parametrized by the points ${\boldsymbol v}
	=(v_1,\cdots,v_J)\in V^J$.
	Notice that 
	the family of shifted norms
	$\varphi_w(x):=\|x-w\|_{V}$, $w\in V$, 
	is jointly convex.
	If the corresponding squared family 
	$\psi_z(x):=\frac 12 \|x-z\|^2_{V}$ with $z\in V$ 
	is jointly $1$-convex then $V$ is a Hilbert space. See \cite{jordan_inner_1935} for how the parallelogram law ensures that a Banach space is induced by an inner product, $\<x,y>=\frac{1}{4}(\norm{x+y}^2 - \norm{x-y}^2)$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:NPC}
     A geodesic space $({{\mathrm X}},{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}})$ is a nonpositively curved (NPC) space in the sense of Alexandrov if 
     the collection of functionals
     $x\mapsto 
     \frac 12{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,z)$, $z\in {{\mathrm X}}$, 
     is jointly $1$-convex 
     with respect to the 
     geodesic system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$
     (see Example~\ref{ex:convex1}).
     
     Equivalently, 
     for every 
     $z,x_0,x_1\in {{\mathrm X}}$ 
     there exists a geodesic ${\mathsf x}$ 
     joining $x_0$ to $x_1$ such that 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:cn}
        {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),z) \le (1-t){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,z) + t{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_1,z) - t(1-t) {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x_1),
        \quad t\in [0,1].
    \end{align}
See \cite{bridson_metric_1999,Laokul_2020} for more details. 
	It is worth noticing 
    that in a NPC space 
	for every ${\boldsymbol x}=
    (x_1,\cdots,x_J)\in {{\mathrm X}}^J$ 
	we can define
	\begin{displaymath}
		\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol x};{\boldsymbol \alpha}):=
		\mathop{\rm argmin}\limits_{x\in {{\mathrm X}}}
		\sum_{j=1}^J \alpha_j{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,x_j);
	\end{displaymath}
	The unique minimizer defines a 
	$J$-barycentric map 
	and the collections ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}$ 
    of all these maps
	is a barycentric system.
	The family
	$x\mapsto \frac 12{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,z)$, $z\in {{\mathrm X}}$,
	is jointly $1$-convex 
    with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}$ 
    for every choice of $z\in {{\mathrm X}}$.

    Similarly, if $\varphi:{{\mathrm X}}\to (-\infty,+\infty]$
    is geodesically $\kappa$-convex 
    with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$ 
    then it is barycentrically
    $\kappa$-convex with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathscr{X}=\mathscr P_p({{\mathrm X}}),$ $p\ge 1,$ 
	${{\mathrm X}}$ being a complete and separable metric space. We endow $\mathscr{X}$ with the $p$-Wasserstein metric $\mathscr W_p$. As for the first example,
	we can consider the collection 
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$ of maps parametrized by 
	${\boldsymbol \mu}=(\mu_1,\cdots,\mu_J)\in \mathscr{X}^J$:
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \mu};{\boldsymbol \alpha})=\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha_j \mu_j$.
	The family $\mu\mapsto \mathscr W_p(\mu,\nu)$, 
     $\nu\in \mathscr{X}$, is
	jointly convex.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
Let us suppose that 
	${{\mathrm X}}$ is a separable Banach space, with 
	 $\mathscr{X}=\mathscr P_p({{\mathrm X}}),$
	 we can consider a reference standard Borel probability space
	 $(\Omega,\mathfrak B,\mathbb{P})$ with an atomless Borel probability measure $\mathbb{P}.$
	We introduce the collection 
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$ of maps parametrized by 
	${\boldsymbol X}=(X_1,\cdots,X_J)\in (L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{P},{{\mathrm X}}))^J$:
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol X};{\boldsymbol \alpha})=\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha_j X_j\bigg)_\sharp \mathbb{P}$.
	A function which is 
	jointly convex with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ is also called
	\textbf{totally convex}.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:generalized-geo}
	    Let us now 
	consider $\mathscr{X}=\mathscr{P}_2(H)$, $H$ a Hilbert space.
	For a given reference measure
	$\bar \mu\in \mathscr{X}$ we consider the sets 
	$${\ensuremath{\mathcal O}}_{\bar\mu,J}:=
	\Big\{(\bar X,X_1,X_2,\cdots,X_J)\in (L^2(\Omega,\mathbb{P},H))^{J+1}\normalcolor:
	\bar X_\sharp \mathbb{P}=\bar \mu,\ 
	(\bar X,X_j)_\sharp\mathbb{P}\text{ optimal in }\mathscr{X}\Big\}.$$
	For every ${\boldsymbol X}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal O}}_{\bar\mu,J}$ 
	we set 
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol X};{\boldsymbol \alpha}):=\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha_j X_j\bigg)_\sharp \mathbb{P}$.
	The collection ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar\mu}$
	(depending on the reference measure $\bar\mu$) of these maps
	provides a natural extension
	to the notion of generalized geodesics.
	Notice that 
	$\mu\mapsto \frac 12 \mathscr W_2^2(\mu,\bar\mu)$ is
	$1$-convex with respect to 
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar\mu}$
	and 
	the examples considered in 
	\cite[Sec. 9.2]{AGS08}
	are also barycentrically convexlike 
	with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar\mu}$ 
	for every choice of $\bar\mu$. Indeed, the barycentric map $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol X};{\boldsymbol \alpha})$ is the push-forward of the convex combination $\sum_{j}\alpha_j X_j$ of the optimal maps $X_j$, which range in a convex subset of $L^2(\Omega,\mathbb{P},H)$. Since these energies lift to functionals of the map, their convexity along two-point interpolations---the case established in \cite[Sec.~9.2]{AGS08}---is convexity in the usual sense, and therefore extends to the barycenter $\sum_{j}\alpha_j X_j$ of arbitrarily many maps.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:NNCC}
        According to 
        \cite{Leger-Todeschi-Vialard25}
        a metric space $({{\mathrm X}},{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}})$ 
        endowed with the cost function 
        ${\mathsf c}(x,y):={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)$
        has nonnegative cross curvature (NNCC)
        if 
        for every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm X}}$
        the collection of functions
        \begin{displaymath}
            x\mapsto {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,\bar x)-
            {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y),\quad y\in {{\mathrm X}},
        \end{displaymath}
        are jointly convexlike
        (with respect to a common system $\mathcal{G}_{\bar x,2}$
        of $2$-barycentric maps called \emph{variational $c$-segments}, which may depend on $\bar x$, and function as generalized geodesics).
        It is worth noticing that 
        in NNCC spaces 
        the collection
        $x\mapsto \frac 12{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,\bar x)$
        are jointly $1$-convex
        with respect to 
        ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_{\bar x,2}$.  The space of probability measures endowed with the spherical Hellinger metric is an example of an NNCC space; see Example~\ref{ex:convexity-spherical-Hellinger}.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
Consider the product space ${{\mathrm X}}=\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d) \times 2.30^d$. Such a space was used for the system describing the dynamics of strategic agents interacting with algorithms, studied in \cite{conger_strategic_2023}. We can define a different interpolation for the component of $\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)$ than that in $2.30^d$, resulting many different interpolation options. We can select the barycentric maps defined in 6. for $\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)$ above with reference measure $\rho\in\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)$  and the barycentric maps defined in 1. for $2.30^d$,
    \begin{align*}
        \boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}) :=\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^J {\boldsymbol \alpha}_j \boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j} ^{(1)}\bigg)_\sharp \mathbb{P} \times  \sum_{j=1}^J {\boldsymbol \alpha}_j \boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j} ^{(2)}\,,  \qquad (\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j} , \rho)_\sharp \mathbb{P} \text{ optimal in }\mathscr W_2\,.
    \end{align*}
    Then $x \mapsto \frac{1}{2}\mathscr W_2^2(x^{(1)},\rho)+\frac 12\norm{x^{(2)}}^2$ is 1-convex with respect to
    ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ parameterized by $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}$ above.
    Alternatively, we could select 4. for $\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)$ and 3. for $2.30^d$,
    \begin{align*}
        \boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}) :=\sum_{j=1}^J {\boldsymbol \alpha}_j \boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j} ^{(1)}\times  \mathop{\rm argmin}\limits_{x^{(2)}\in2.30^d}\sum_{j=1}^J {\boldsymbol \alpha}_j \norm{\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{j} ^{(2)}-x^{(2)}}^2_V\,,
    \end{align*}
     where $\norm{\cdot}_V$ is any Euclidean norm. However, while this interpolant results in 1-convexity for the family $x^{(2)} \mapsto \frac12 \norm{x^{(2)}-\bar x^{(2)}}^2$ for any $\bar x^{(2)}\in2.30^d$, the family $x^{(1)} \mapsto \mathscr W_2^2(x^{(1)},\rho)$ for any $\rho\in\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)$ is not 1-convex, which precludes the conditions required for taking $\tau\to 0$ in the movement scheme.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
Consider the setting ${{\mathrm X}}=\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)$ endowed with $\mathscr W_2$ and energies $E_1(\rho),E_2(\rho):\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^d)\to 2.30\cup \{+\infty\}$ defined by 
    \begin{align*}
        E_1(\rho)=\int V(z){\mathrm d}\rho(z)\,, \quad E_2(\rho)=\begin{cases}
            \int \rho(z)\log \rho({\mathrm d} z) & \text{if } \rho\in L^1(2.30^d)\,, \\
            +\infty & \text{otherwise}
        \end{cases}\,,
    \end{align*}
     with $V\in C^2(2.30^d,2.30)$ satisfying $\nabla^2 V \succeq \kappa \text{Id}$. We set $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}$ according to Wasserstein-2 geodesics ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$, and $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}$ according to linear interpolation.
     Checking the convexity conditions with respect to each of these barysystems,
     \begin{align*}
         E_1(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x} (\alpha)) &\le \alpha_1 E_1(x_1) + \alpha_2 E_1(x_2) -\frac{\kappa}{2} \alpha_1 \alpha_2 \mathscr W_2^2(x_1,x_2) \\
         E_1(\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}(\alpha)) &= \alpha_1 E_1(y_1) + \alpha_2 E_1(y_2) \\
          E_2(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x} (\alpha)) &\le \alpha_1 E_2(x_1) + \alpha_2 E_2(x_2)  \\
           E_2(\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}(\alpha)) &\le \alpha_1 E_2(y_1) + \alpha_2 E_2(y_2) \,.
     \end{align*}
     If $\kappa>0$, then for $E_1$ $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}$ has a "better" (more positive) barycentric convexity parameter; if $\kappa<0$, then since $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}$ results in 0-convexity, it is a better choice. $E_1$ is barycentrically quasi-convexlike with respect to both $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}$. For $E_2$, geodesics and linear interpolations both result in 0-barycentric convexity.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:hemicontinuity}
	Let ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}'$ be a collection of barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$
	(e.g.~a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$ of $J$-barycentric maps or a system
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ of barycentric maps, as in
	Definition~\ref{def:barycentric maps}).
	We say that $\varphi:{{\mathrm D}}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is upper
	hemicontinuous with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}'$ if for every
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}'$ the composition
	$\varphi\circ\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}:
	{\boldsymbol \alpha}\mapsto \varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}))$
	is upper semicontinuous in its simplex of definition.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
We say that a function $\varphi:{{\mathrm D}}\to
    (-\infty,+\infty]$ 
    has 	
	complete sublevels if
	for every $c\in 2.30$ the corresponding sublevel set 
	$\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:\varphi(x)\le c\}$ 
	is complete (possibly empty). 
	In particular $\varphi$ is lower  semicontinuous.
	
	$\psi:{{\mathrm D}} \to [-\infty,+\infty)$ has complete superlevels 
	if
	for every $c\in 2.30$ the corresponding superlevel set 
	$\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:\psi(x)\ge c\}$ 	is complete. 
	In particular $\psi$ is upper semicontinuous.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:trivial}
	If ${{\mathrm X}}$ is complete
    and 
     ${{\mathrm D}}$ is closed, 
     then $\varphi$ has complete sublevels 
	(resp.~superlevels) iff $\varphi$ 
	is lower (resp.~upper) semicontinuous. 

     
    If ${{\mathrm X}}$ is complete but 
    ${{\mathrm D}}$ is not closed, 
    these conditions are in general stronger than
    lower (resp.~upper) semicontinuity: in fact, 
    they are 
    respectively equivalent to the following property
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:complet-sub}
        \begin{aligned}
            x_n\in {{\mathrm D}},\ x\in {{\mathrm X}},\ x_n\to x
        \text{ as }n\to\infty,\ 
        \ \varphi(x_n)\le c<\infty 
        \quad
        &\Rightarrow
        \quad
        x\in {{\mathrm D}},\ \varphi(x)\le c,\\
        x_n\in {{\mathrm D}},\ x\in {{\mathrm X}},\ x_n\to x
        \text{ as }n\to\infty,\ 
        \ \varphi(x_n)\ge c>-\infty
        \quad
        &\Rightarrow
        \quad
        x\in {{\mathrm D}},\ \varphi(x)\ge c.
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{le:obvious}
	If $\varphi_\alpha:{{\mathrm X}}\to (-\infty,+\infty]$, $\alpha\in {\mathrm A}$, is a collection of 
	functions with complete sublevels, also
	$\varphi:=\sup_{\alpha\in {\mathrm A}}\varphi_\alpha$ has complete sublevels.
	Similarly, if
	$\psi_\alpha:{{\mathrm X}}\to [-\infty,+\infty)$, $\alpha\in {\mathrm A}$, is a collection of 
	functions with complete superlevels, then
	$\psi:=\inf_{\alpha\in {\mathrm A}}\psi_\alpha$ has complete superlevels.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For every $c\in 2.30$ we have
	\begin{displaymath}
		\{x\in {{\mathrm X}}:\varphi(x)\le c\}=
		\bigcap_{\alpha\in {\mathrm A}}\{x\in {{\mathrm X}}:\varphi_\alpha(x)\le c\},
	\end{displaymath}
	so that all the sublevels are intersection of complete subsets of ${{\mathrm X}}$ 
	and are therefore complete as well. The same follows for $\psi$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:minima}
	Let
	$\varphi: {{\mathrm D}}  \to (-\infty,+\infty] $ be a proper function
	with complete sublevels.
	If $\varphi$ is $\kappa$-convexlike
	for some $\kappa>0$ 
	with respect to some system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of 
	$2$-barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$, 
	then 
	\begin{enumerate}
	\item there exists a unique minimizing point 
	$\bar x\in{{\mathrm D}} $ such that $\varphi(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in {{\mathrm D}} }\varphi(x)$;
	\item 
	every infimizing sequence
	$(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in ${{\mathrm D}} $ converges to $\bar x$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\textbf{1.} follows by \cite[Lemma 2.4.8]{AGS08}.
	To show \textbf{2.},
	let $\bar \varphi:=\inf_{x\in {{\mathrm D}} }\varphi(x)\in 2.30.$ Fix any $1>0$.
	We argue as in the proof of Lemma 2.4.8 \cite{AGS08}
	using the estimate
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:inf-estimate}
		\varphi(x_0)\le \bar\varphi+1,\quad
		\varphi(x_1)\le \bar\varphi+1\quad\Rightarrow\quad
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x_1)\le \frac {81}\kappa\,, \quad \text{for all } x_0,x_1 \in {{\mathrm D}}\,,
	\end{equation}
    which holds due to the convexity inequality, for any $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x} \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ such that $x_0 =\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\mathsf e}_2^1)$ and $x_1 = \boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\mathsf e}_2^2)$,
\begin{align*}
    \bar \varphi \le \varphi(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}(1/2,1/2)) \le \frac{1}{2}\varphi(x_0) + \frac{1}{2}\varphi(x_1) - \frac{\kappa}{8}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x_1) \quad 
    \Rightarrow  \quad \frac{\kappa}{8}
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x_1)  \le \varepsilon \,.
\end{align*}
	\eqref{eq:inf-estimate} immediately shows that 
	an infimizing sequence
	satisfies the Cauchy condition and therefore converges to 
	a point $\bar x\in{{\mathrm D}}$ 
    (since the sequence belongs to a sublevel of $\varphi$, which is complete) and $\bar x$ is a minimizing point for $\varphi$ 
	thanks to its lower semicontinuity. 
    \eqref{eq:inf-estimate}
	also shows that minimizing points are unique.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let ${\mathsf u}:(a,b)\to {{\mathrm X}}$ be a curve. The upper/lower right/left metric derivatives and the metric derivative
of ${\mathsf u}$ (if they exist) are defined by
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:urmder}
	\begin{alignedat}{2}
		|\dot{{\mathsf u}}^+|(t):=
		{}&\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf u}(t+h),{\mathsf u}(t))}h,&\quad
		|\dot{{\mathsf u}}_+|(t):=
		{}&\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf u}(t+h),{\mathsf u}(t))}h,\\
				|\dot{{\mathsf u}}^-|(t):=
		{}&\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf u}(t),{\mathsf u}(t-h))}h,&\quad
		|\dot{{\mathsf u}}_-|(t):=
		{}&\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf u}(t),{\mathsf u}(t-h))}h,\\
			 |\dot{{\mathsf u}}|(t):={}&\lim_{h\to0}\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf u}(t+h),{\mathsf u}(t))}{|h|}.
	\end{alignedat}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
For a real function $\zeta:(a,b)\to 2.30$ and $t\in (a,b)$ 
we consider the upper and lower right/left Dini derivatives
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:Dini}
	\begin{aligned}
{\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t}\!\!}^+\zeta(t):={}&\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\zeta(t+h)-\zeta(t)}h,&
	{\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\!}_+ \zeta(t):={}&\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\zeta(t+h)-\zeta(t)}h\\
	{\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t}\!\!}^-\zeta(t):={}&\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\zeta(t)-\zeta(t-h)}h,&
	{\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\!}_- \zeta(t):={}&\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\zeta(t)-\zeta(t-h)}h
	\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{le:ulDini}
	
    Let $\zeta:(a,b)\to [0,\infty)$ be continuous
	and let $\upsilon:(a,b)\to 2.30$ be 
    a function satisfying
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\upsilon(t)=0$
        in $Z:=\{t\in (a,b): \zeta(t)=0\}$,
        \item 
        $\upsilon$ is upper semicontinuous
        in $(a,b)\setminus Z$,
        \item $\upsilon$ is locally bounded from above in $(a,b).$
    \end{enumerate}
    If 
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:lower-Dini}
        {\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\!}_- \zeta(t)\le \upsilon(t)
        \quad \text{for every }t\in (a,b)\setminus Z,
    \end{equation}
	then $\upsilon$ is locally integrable in $(a,b)$
    and for every 
    $a_0\in (a,b)$ 
    the function
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:auxiliary}
		\tilde\zeta(t):=\zeta(t)-\int_{a_0}^t \upsilon(s)\,{\mathrm d} s
		\quad\text{is nonincreasing and continuous.}
	\end{equation}
    In particular 
    \eqref{eq:lower-Dini} 
    is equivalent to the 
    inequality with the upper left Dini derivative
     \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:upper-Dini}
        {\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t}\!\!}^- \zeta(t)\le \upsilon(t)
        \quad \text{for every }t\in (a,b),
    \end{equation}
    and to the distributional inequality
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:ddistributional}
		\frac{\mathrm d}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\zeta\le \upsilon \quad\text{in }\mathscr D'(a,b),
	\end{equation}
    where $\mathscr D'(a,b)$ is the space of distributions dual to $C_c^\infty((a,b),2.30)$.
    
	Finally, if $\zeta$ is locally absolutely continuous 
	(in particular if $\zeta$ is locally Lipschitz) 
	then the above conditions are equivalent to
	\begin{equation}
		\frac{\mathrm d}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\zeta(t)\le \upsilon(t)\quad \text{for a.e. }t\in (a,b)
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The proof 
	can be obtained as an adaptation of 
    \cite[Lemma A.1]{Muratori-SavareI}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:equilibrium-1}
	We say that $x^*\in{{\mathrm D}}$
	is a solution of the Primal Equilibrium Problem if 
	\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:equilibrium}
	\tag{EP}
		\mathsf b(y,x^*)\ge 0
		\quad \text{for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$.}
\end{equation}
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:primal_soln}
    Let us suppose $\mathsf b:{{\mathrm D}} \times {{\mathrm D}} \to 2.30$ satisfies \eqref{eq:diagonal} and that 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item
		the functions $y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
		are jointly barycentrically quasi-convexlike with respect to
		a system of
		barycentric maps ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ in ${{\mathrm D}};$
		\item
		for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the function $x\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$ is
		upper hemicontinuous with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$
		(Definition~\ref{def:hemicontinuity});
		\item
		the superlevels $\sigma^+(y):=\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:
		\mathsf b(y,x)\ge 0\}$ are
		closed in ${{\mathrm D}}$ and at least one of them is compact.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then Problem \ref{prob:equilibrium-1}
	has a solution.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{le:KKM}
    Let $\bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$ be the $J-1$-dimensional simplex with $J$ vertices and let $C_1,\dots,C_J \subset \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$ be a closed 
    KKM covering of $\bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$, i.e.~satisfying 
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:KKM}
        \operatorname{co}({\mathsf e}_J^{k}:k\in B)\subset 
        \bigcup_{k\in B} C_{k}\quad\text{for every subset } 
        B\subset \{1,\dots,J\}.
    \end{equation}
    Then $\cap_{j=1}^J C_j \neq \emptyset$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
It is sufficient to check that the collection
	of 
	sets $\sigma^+(y)$, $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	have the finite intersection property.
	Let $y_1,\cdots,y_J\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y} \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$
	such that $y_k=\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\mathsf e}_J^k)$,
	and consider the 
	sets 
	$${\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)\subset \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J},\quad 
	{\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k):=
	\Big\{{\boldsymbol \beta}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}:
	\mathsf b( y_k,\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \beta}) )\ge0\Big\}.$$
	Thanks to Condition 2, the compositions
	${\boldsymbol \beta}\mapsto \mathsf b(y_k,\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \beta}))$ are upper semicontinuous, so
	that every ${\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)$ is closed. \normalcolor
	Let us check that $\{{\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)\}_{k=1}^J$ satisfies the assumption of the 
	KKM lemma (see Lemma \ref{le:KKM} above):
	if  $B$
    is a subset of 
	 $\{1,\cdots, J\}$
	we need to prove that 
	$\operatorname{co}({\mathsf e}_J^{k}:k\in B
    )\subset 
	\cup_{k\in B} {\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)$.
	By contradiction, if 
	$\bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}\ni {\boldsymbol \alpha} =
	\sum_{k=1}^{ J} \alpha_k {\mathsf e}_J^{k}
	\not\in \cup_{k\in B} {\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)$, 
	for some 
	coefficients 
	$\alpha_k$ with $\alpha_k=0$ if $k\not\in B$, 
	then 
	$\mathsf b ( y_{k},\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \alpha}) )<0$
	for every $k\in B$
	and therefore, since
	$y\mapsto \mathsf b( y,\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \alpha}) )$ is
	quasi-convexlike 
    with respect to
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$, 
	$\mathsf b(\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \alpha}),\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \alpha}))
	\le \max_{k\in B}
	\mathsf b (y_{k},\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}({\boldsymbol \alpha}))<0$,
	a contradiction with \eqref{eq:diagonal}. Hence, $\{{\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)\}_{k=1}^J$ is a KKM covering and there exists $\beta^*\in \cap_{k=1}^J {\ensuremath{\mathcal S}}(k)$. Let $x^*=
    \boldsymbol{\mathsf y}(\beta^*) $. 
    Then $
    \mathsf b ({y_k}, {x^*})  \ge 0$ for all $k\in [1,\dots,J]$,
    i.e.~$x^*\in \cap_{k=1}^J \sigma^+(y_k).$
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:coercive-primal}
    If ${\mathsf a}$ is $\xi$ radially convex according to Definition~\ref{def:radial-convexity} and ${\mathsf a}(x^*,x^*)=0$, then
	the primal inequality \eqref{eq:equilibrium} improves to a coercive
	one: any solution $x^*$ of Problem~\ref{prob:equilibrium-1} satisfies
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:coercive-primal-remark}
		\mathsf b(y,x^*)\ge \frac\xi2\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x^*)
		\qquad\text{for every }y\in{{\mathrm D}}.
	\end{equation}
	Indeed, taking \eqref{eq:radial-convex} with $x=x^*$, using
	$\mathsf b(x^*,x^*)=0$ and $\mathsf b(z_t,x^*)\ge0$ (since $z_t\in{{\mathrm D}}$ and $x^*$
	solves \eqref{eq:equilibrium}), we get
	$0\le t\,\mathsf b(y,x^*)-\frac\xi2\,t(1-t)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x^*)$ for $t\in(0,1]$;
	dividing by $t$ and letting $t\downarrow0$ gives
	\eqref{eq:coercive-primal-remark}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
\label{prob:equilibrium-2}
	We say that $y_*\in {{\mathrm D}}$
	is a solution of the Dual Equilibrium Problem if 
	\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:equilibrium'}
	\tag{EP'}
		\mathsf b(y_*,x)\le 0
		\quad \text{for every $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:saddle}
	$x_*=x^*$ is a joint solution
	of the two Equilibrium Problems
	\ref{prob:equilibrium-1} and
	\ref{prob:equilibrium-2} 
    if and only if
	$x_*$ is a diagonal saddle point of $\mathsf b$, i.e.
	\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:saddle}
	\tag{Saddle}
		\mathsf b(y,x_*)\ge 0=\mathsf b(x_*,x_*)\ge \mathsf b(x_*,x)
		\quad \text{for every $x,y\in {{\mathrm D}}$.}
\end{equation}
Let us observe that we are looking for saddle points of $\mathsf b$ 
on the diagonal of ${{\mathrm D}}\times {{\mathrm D}}$.
Therefore, if we introduce the marginal functions
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:marginals}
	f(x):=\inf_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x),\quad
	g(y):=\sup_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x)
\end{equation}
which satisfy
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:minmax1}
	\max_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}f(x)=\max_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}
	\inf_{y\in{{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x),\quad
	\min_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}}g(y)=\min_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}}
	\sup_{x\in{{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x),
\end{equation}
it is immediate to observe that 
\eqref{eq:diagonal} yields
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:lu-bounds}
	g(y)\ge 0\ge f(x)\quad\text{for every }x,y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
\end{equation}
\eqref{eq:saddle} is thus equivalent to
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:saddle2}
	g(x_*)=f(x_*).
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:int-dissipative}
Given $\eta\in2.30$, we say that $\mathsf b$
is \emph{$\eta$-interaction dissipative} if
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:bif-monotone}
	\mathsf b(x,y)+\mathsf b(y,x)\le \eta {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x)\quad\text{for every }
	x,y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{le:metric-Minty}
	Let
    $y_*$ be a solution
    of the dual equilibrium problem 
    \eqref{eq:equilibrium'}
    and let us suppose that 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item [(1)] 
		the functions $y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, 
		are jointly convexlike with respect to
		a 
        system of 
		$2$-barycentric maps ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ in ${{\mathrm D}}.$
		\item [(2)] for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the function $x\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$ is
        upper hemicontinuous with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then $y_*$ is 
	also a solution of 
	Problem \ref{prob:equilibrium-1}.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $y_*$ be a solution to 
	Problem \ref{prob:equilibrium-2}, let $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$
	and let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$
	satisfying 
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{1}=y_*$, $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}_{2}=y$.
	We set $x_t:=\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((1-t),t)$.
	Since $y_*$ is a solution to Problem \ref{prob:equilibrium-2}
	we have
	\begin{displaymath}
		\mathsf b(y_*,x_t)\le 0.
	\end{displaymath}
	On the other hand \eqref{eq:diagonal}
	yields 
	\begin{displaymath}
		\mathsf b(x_t,x_t)\ge 0.
	\end{displaymath}
	Since the functions $y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$ are jointly convexlike,
	applying \eqref{eq:B2-convex} to $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}$ with ${\boldsymbol \alpha}=(1-t,t)$
	gives
	\begin{displaymath}
		\mathsf b(x_t,x_t)\le (1-t)\,\mathsf b(y_*,x_t)+t\,\mathsf b(y,x_t).
	\end{displaymath}
	Since $\mathsf b(x_t,x_t)\ge0$, $\mathsf b(y_*,x_t)\le0$ and $1-t>0$, we obtain
	$0\le t\,\mathsf b(y,x_t)$, hence $\mathsf b(y,x_t)\ge0$.
	Passing to the limit as $t\downarrow0$ and 
	using the upper-semicontinuity of 
	$t\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x_t)$ at $t=0$ we 
	obtain $\mathsf b(y,y_*)\ge0$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:primal-implies-dual}
	Suppose $\mathsf b$ satisfies the $\eta$-interaction dissipativity
	\eqref{eq:bif-monotone}, and let $x^*\in{{\mathrm D}}$ be a solution of the
	primal problem \eqref{eq:equilibrium}.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)] If $\eta\le0$, then $x^*$ is also a solution of the
		dual problem \eqref{eq:equilibrium'}.
		\item[(ii)] If $\eta>0$ and, in addition, $\mathsf b$ satisfies the
		radial convexity \eqref{eq:radial-convex} with $\xi\ge 2\eta$,
        then $x^*$
		is also a solution of the dual
		problem \eqref{eq:equilibrium'}.
	\end{enumerate}
	In either case $x^*$ is a diagonal saddle point \eqref{eq:saddle}.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For every $x\in{{\mathrm D}}$, \eqref{eq:bif-monotone} for the pair $(x^*,x)$ gives
	\begin{displaymath}
		\mathsf b(x^*,x)\le \eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x^*,x)-\mathsf b(x,x^*).
	\end{displaymath}
	If $\eta\le0$, then $\mathsf b(x,x^*)\ge0$ because $x^*$ solves
	\eqref{eq:equilibrium}, hence $\mathsf b(x^*,x)\le\eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x^*,x)\le0$.
	If $\eta>0$, recall that interaction dissipativity (no matter the sign of $\eta$) together with the standing assumption \eqref{eq:diagonal} yield ${\mathsf a}(x,x)=0$ for all $x\in{{\mathrm D}}$; then \eqref{eq:coercive-primal-remark} of
	Remark~\ref{rem:coercive-primal} with $y=x$ gives
	$\mathsf b(x,x^*)\ge\frac\xi2\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,x^*)$, so
	\begin{displaymath}
		\mathsf b(x^*,x)\le\Big(\eta-\frac\xi2\Big){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x^*,x)\le0,
	\end{displaymath}
	because $\xi\ge2\eta$. In both cases $x^*$ solves
	\eqref{eq:equilibrium'}, and being a solution of both problems it is a
	diagonal saddle point by Remark~\ref{rem:saddle}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:equilibrium2}
	Let $\xi> 2\eta_+$ 
    and  
	let $\mathsf b:{{\mathrm D}}\times {{\mathrm D}}\to 2.30$ 
	be
	a function
	satisfying 
	the following properties:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)] $\mathsf b$ is $\eta$-interaction dissipative
		according to \eqref{eq:bif-monotone};
		\item[(ii)] The maps
		$y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, 
		have complete sublevels $\sigma_-(x)$ and are jointly
		barycentrically {$\xi$}-convexlike with respect to a system of 
		 barycentric maps ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$. 
	\end{enumerate}
	 Then Problem \ref{prob:equilibrium-2} has a unique solution $y_*$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
It is not restrictive to assume $\eta\ge0$: the $\eta$-interaction dissipativity \eqref{eq:bif-monotone} implies the $\eta_+$-interaction dissipativity, and the assumption $\xi>2\eta_+$ only involves $\eta_+$.
Notice that applying 
\cite[Lemma 2.4.8]{AGS08} we 
deduce that 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:lower-bound}
    \text{for every }x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}
		 \text{ we have $\inf_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x_0)>-\infty.$}
\end{equation}
   


\textbf{Step 1.} \emph{The sets $\sigma_-(x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	have the finite intersection property.}
	
	Let $x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_J\in {{\mathrm D}}$
    and let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{J}$ such that $x_k=\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\mathsf e}_J^k)$, $k=1,\cdots,J$. 
	We consider 
    the function $S({\boldsymbol \alpha}):= 
    \sum_{j,k}\alpha_j\alpha_k {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_j,x_k)$.
    For $k=1,\cdots,J$ we define the sets
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:sets}
        C(k):=\Big\{{\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}:
        \sum_j\alpha_j\mathsf b(x_j,x_k) \le \tfrac \xi 4\, S({\boldsymbol \alpha})\Big\}.
    \end{equation}
    and we want to prove that the collection $(C_k)_k$ is a closed KKM covering according to the definition in \eqref{eq:KKM}. 
    
    Clearly, each $C_k$ is closed.
    Whenever ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \mathrm{co}({\mathsf e}_J^k:k\in B)$ for some subset $B\subset \{1,\cdots,J\}$ (so that $\alpha_k=0$ if $k\not\in B$) we get 
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{k\in B} \alpha_k\Big[\sum_j \alpha_j\mathsf b(x_j,x_k) \Big]
        &= \sum_{j,k} \alpha_j\alpha_k \mathsf b(x_j,x_k)
        =
        \frac 12 \sum_{j,k} \alpha_j\alpha_k 
        \Big[\mathsf b(x_j,x_k)+\mathsf b(x_k,x_j)\Big]\\
        &\le  \frac{\eta}{2}  \sum_{j,k} \alpha_j\alpha_k 
        {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_j,x_k) = \frac \eta 2 S({\boldsymbol \alpha})\,\le \frac \xi 4 S({\boldsymbol \alpha})\,.
    \end{align*} 
    It follows that there exists $k\in B$ such that
    \begin{displaymath}
        \sum_j \alpha_j\mathsf b(x_j,x_k) \le \frac \xi 4 S({\boldsymbol \alpha}),
    \end{displaymath}
    i.e.~${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in C(k)$, so that $\mathrm{co}({\mathsf e}_J^k:k\in B)\subset \cup_{k\in B} C(k)$ and the KKM property is satisfied. By Lemma \ref{le:KKM} we deduce that there exists ${\boldsymbol \alpha}^*\in \cap_{k=1}^J C(k)$, so that 
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:sets2}
        \sum_j \alpha_j^*\mathsf b(x_j,x_k) \le \tfrac \xi 4 S({\boldsymbol \alpha}^*)\quad\text{for every }k=1,\cdots,J.
    \end{equation}  
    Setting $x_*:=\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}({\boldsymbol \alpha}^*)$, since $y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x_k)$ are jointly $\xi$ barycentrically convexlike we have 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathsf b(x_*,x_k) \le \sum_j \alpha_j^*\mathsf b(x_j,x_k) - \tfrac \xi 4 S({\boldsymbol \alpha}^*)
        \le 0\quad\text{for every }k=1,\cdots,J\,,
    \end{align*}
   and therefore $x_*\in \bigcap_{k=1}^J \sigma_-(x_k)$.
	
	
	\smallskip\noindent
	\textbf{Step 2.} \emph{$\bigcap_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}\sigma_-(x)$ is nonempty and contains a unique element}.

    Fix $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}$.
    For every $\Omega\subset {{\mathrm D}}$ with $\Omega\ni x_0$, where $\inf_{y} \mathsf b( y,{x_0})>-\infty$ from
    \eqref{eq:lower-bound}, 
	 we
	set 
	\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:marginal}
	\mathsf b_\Omega(y):=\sup_{x\in \Omega}\mathsf b(y,x),\quad
	\sigma_-(\Omega):=
	\Big\{y\in {{\mathrm D}}:\mathsf b_\Omega(y)\le 0\Big\}\,.
	\end{equation}
	The function $\mathsf b_\Omega$ is $\xi$-convexlike and uniformly bounded from below since
	$\mathsf b_\Omega\ge \mathsf b(\cdot,x_0)\ge \inf_y {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x_0)}>-\infty$, and together with \eqref{eq:bif-monotone}, we conclude that $\mathsf b_\Omega(\cdot)$ is proper.
	Using the assumption that $\mathsf b(\cdot,x)$ has complete sublevel sets, $\mathsf b_\Omega$  has a unique minimizer $y_\Omega$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:minima}.
	In the particular case when $\Omega={{\mathrm D}}$ 
	we recover the marginal 
	function $g$ of \eqref{eq:marginal} with $g(y)=\mathsf b_{{\mathrm D}}(y)=
	\sup_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x)
	\ge \mathsf b(x,x)\ge0$. 
	Therefore $\sigma_-({{\mathrm D}})$ 
	is nonempty if $\min \mathsf b_{{\mathrm D}}=0$.
	
		Let $\Lambda=\{\Omega\subset {{\mathrm D}}\, : \, x_0\in \Omega\}$, restricted such that $\Omega_1,\Omega_2\in \Lambda$ implies $\Omega_1 \subseteq \Omega_2$ or $\Omega_2 \subseteq \Omega_1$, be  the collection of 
	 subsets with a finite number of elements in ${{\mathrm D}}$, containing $x_0$, and ordered by inclusion.
	$\Lambda$ is a directed set. 
	Every set $\sigma_-(\Omega)$, $\Omega\in \Lambda$,
	 is nonempty by Step 1 because each $\Omega\in\Lambda$ is finite and it is 
	 included in $\sigma_-(x_0)$, which is a complete set.
	We have $m_\Omega:=\mathsf b_\Omega(y_\Omega)\le 0$ since $\sigma_-(\Omega)$ is nonempty by Step 1;
	in particular $y_\Omega\in \sigma_-(\Omega)$
	for every $\Omega\in \Lambda$.
	
	
	The claim of Step 2 then follows if we show that $\Omega\mapsto y_\Omega$ is a Cauchy net.
	We know that $\Omega\mapsto m_\Omega$ is bounded from above and increasing: if $\Omega_1 \subseteq \Omega_2$, then
    \begin{align*}
        m_{\Omega_1} =\min_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}} \mathsf b_{\Omega_{1}}(y) \le \min_{y \in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b_{\Omega_2}(y) = m_{\Omega_{2}}\,.
    \end{align*}
    From this, $\lim_{\Omega\in \Lambda}m_\Omega=\sup_{\Omega\in \Lambda}m_\Omega=:m\le 0$, where the limit is taken in the sense of nets. 
	Given $1>0$ we can find $\Omega^1\in \Lambda$ such that 
	$m_{\Omega^1}\ge m-1$
	and therefore
	for every $\Omega_1,\Omega_2$ containing $\Omega^1$ 
	with $y_k:=y_{\Omega_k}$ we have
	$$ m_{\Omega^1}\le \mathsf b_{\Omega^1}(y_k)\le
	\mathsf b_{\Omega_k}(y_k)=m_{\Omega_k}\le m
	\le m_{\Omega^1}+1\,.
	$$
    We now use that $y \mapsto \mathsf b( y,x)$  is $\xi$-barycentrically convexlike, selecting $J=2$ and test points $y_1,y_2$:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathsf b ({\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}(0.5,0.5)}, x) \le \frac12 \mathsf b( { {y_1}}, x) + \frac12 \mathsf b({ {y_2}}, x) - \frac{\xi\normalcolor}{8} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y_1,y_2)\,.
    \end{align*}
    Using that for all $x\in \Omega^1$, $\mathsf b ({y_1},x) \le m_{\Omega^1} + 1$ and $\mathsf b({y_2},x) \le m_{\Omega^1} + 1$, along with $\mathsf b ( {\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}(0.5,0.5)} ,x) \ge \mathsf b_{\Omega^1}(y_{\Omega^1})$, we have  
    \begin{align*}
        {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y_1,y_2) \le \frac{81}\xi\,.
    \end{align*}
    The above estimate in combination with $y_\Omega\in\sigma_-(x_0)$, a complete set, allows us to conclude that $\Omega\mapsto y_\Omega$ is a Cauchy net converging to a limit $\bar y \in \sigma_-(x_0)$. Since $\Omega \cup \{x\} \mapsto y_{\Omega \cup \{x\}}$ is a subnet of $\Omega\mapsto y_\Omega$ for any $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, if $\Omega \mapsto y_\Omega$ converges to $\bar y$, then $\Omega \cup \{x\} \mapsto y_{\Omega\cup \{x\}}$ also converges to $\bar y$. Lower semicontinuity of $\mathsf b( \cdot, x)$ follows from the assumption that $\sigma_-(x)$ are complete. Therefore,
	for every $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, 
	$\mathsf b(\bar y,x)\le \liminf_{\Omega\in \Lambda}\mathsf b(y_\Omega,x)
	\le \liminf_{\Omega\in \Lambda}
	\mathsf b_\Omega(y_\Omega)=m\le 0$
	so that $\bar y\in \bigcap_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}\sigma_-(x)$. Hence, $\bar y$ solves the Dual Equilibrium Problem \ref{prob:equilibrium-2}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
\emph{The sets $\sigma_-(x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	have the finite intersection property.}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
\emph{$\bigcap_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}\sigma_-(x)$ is nonempty and contains a unique element}.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:primal-consequences}
	Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2}, let $y_*$ be
	the unique solution of the dual problem \eqref{eq:equilibrium'}.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)] The primal problem \eqref{eq:equilibrium} has at most
		one solution, which must coincide with $y_*$.
		\item[(ii)] If in addition the upper-hemicontinuity
		condition~(2) of Lemma~\ref{le:metric-Minty} holds, then $y_*$
		solves \eqref{eq:equilibrium} as well; it is then the unique
		solution of both problems and the unique diagonal saddle point
		\eqref{eq:saddle} of $\mathsf b$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The barycentric $\xi$-convexity assumed in
	Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2} implies the radial convexity
	\eqref{eq:radial-convex} (Remark~\ref{rem:coercive-primal}), with
	$\xi>2\eta_+$.

	\emph{(i)} If $x^*$ solves \eqref{eq:equilibrium}, then
	Proposition~\ref{prop:primal-implies-dual} shows that $x^*$ solves
	\eqref{eq:equilibrium'} (the case $\eta\le0$ needs no convexity, the
	case $\eta>0$ uses $\xi>2\eta$); by uniqueness of the dual solution
	$x^*=y_*$.

	\emph{(ii)} The convexity condition~(1) of
	Lemma~\ref{le:metric-Minty} follows from the $\xi$-convexity, so if
	condition~(2) holds as well, Lemma~\ref{le:metric-Minty} shows that
	$y_*$ solves \eqref{eq:equilibrium}. Together with \emph{(i)} and
	Remark~\ref{rem:saddle}, $y_*$ is the unique solution of both
	problems and the unique diagonal saddle point.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:antisymmetric}
	Let $\mathsf b:{{\mathrm D}}\times {{\mathrm D}}\to 2.30$ 
	be 
	a function
	satisfying 
	the antisymmetric identity
	\eqref{eq:antisymmetry}.
	If 
	\begin{quote}
		the maps
		$y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, 
		have complete sublevels 
		and are jointly 
        $\xi$-convexlike 
         with respect to some family 
        of 
        $2$-barycentric maps ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2$
        for some $\xi>0.$
        \end{quote}
	then Problems
	\ref{prob:equilibrium-1} and 
	\ref{prob:equilibrium-2} have a unique saddle solution $x^*=y_*$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We adapt the argument of \cite[Chapter 1, Theorem 1.1]{Brezis73}
	and \cite[Chap. 6, Theorem 2.1]{Ekeland-Temam74} due to Shiffman.
    
    Let us first observe that 
    for $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}$ 
		 we have $
		 -I:=\inf_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x_0)>-\infty$
         thanks to Proposition \ref{prop:minima}. 

	Let us define $
	g(y)=\sup_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}}\mathsf b(y,x)$
	as in \eqref{eq:marginals}.
	Notice that \eqref{eq:antisymmetry}
	yields $f(x)=-g(x)$.
	We observe that the function
	$y\mapsto g(y)$ is $\xi$-convexlike,
	it has complete sublevels, and it is 
	bounded from below since
	$g(y)\ge \mathsf b(y,y)=0$.
	Moreover
	\begin{displaymath}
		\mathsf b(x_0,x)=
		-\mathsf b(x,x_0)\le I\quad\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}},
	\end{displaymath}
	so that 
	$g(x_0)\le I<+\infty$ and therefore
	$g$ is not identically $+\infty$
	it attains its minimum at some point $\bar y\in {{\mathrm D}}.$ We want to show that 
	$g(\bar y)=0$.
	Let us fix  
	$y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and 
	let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ 
	satisfy $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}_1=\bar y$,
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}_2=y$;
	for every $\vartheta \in (0,1)$ 
	we set $y_\vartheta =\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}((1-\vartheta),\vartheta)$.
	Since $g(y_\vartheta)=
	\sup_x \mathsf b(y_\vartheta,x)$,
	and $x\mapsto -\mathsf b(y,x)=\mathsf b(x,y)$ 
	is $\xi$-convexlike with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$, 
	there exists a unique point $x_\vartheta$
	such that 
	$g(y_\vartheta)=\mathsf b(y_\vartheta,x_\vartheta)$.
	We have
	\begin{align*}
		g(\bar y)&\le g(y_\vartheta)=
		\mathsf b(y_\vartheta,x_\vartheta)
		\stackrel{(1)}\le 
		(1-\vartheta)
				\mathsf b(\bar y,x_\vartheta)
				+\vartheta \mathsf b(y,x_\vartheta)
				\stackrel{(2)}\le 
				(1-\vartheta)
			g(\bar y)
				+\vartheta \mathsf b(y,x_\vartheta)
	\end{align*}
	where we used the convexity inequality 
	in (1)
	and the minimality property of $g$ in (2) ($g(\bar y)\ge 
	{{{\mathsf b}}(\bar y,x)}$ for every $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$).
	We deduce that 
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:1bis}
		g(\bar y)\le \mathsf b(y,x_\vartheta)
		\quad\text{for every }\vartheta\in (0,1).
	\end{equation}
	\sloppy As $\vartheta\downarrow0$ 
	$y_\vartheta$ is a minimizing 
	sequence for $g$ since
	$g(y_\vartheta)\le 
	(1-\vartheta)g(\bar y)+\vartheta g(y)$ 
	so that 
	$\liminf_{\vartheta\downarrow0}g(y_\vartheta)=g(\bar y)$.
	We deduce that $y_\vartheta\to \bar y$ as $\vartheta\downarrow0$.
	
	We claim that $x_\vartheta$ 
	converges to 
	the unique maximizer $\bar x$ 
	of $x\mapsto \mathsf b(\bar y,x)$
	as $\vartheta\downarrow0$. In fact
	\begin{align*}
			(1-\vartheta)\mathsf b (\bar y,x_\vartheta)+
		\vartheta g(y)&\ge 
		(1-\vartheta)\mathsf b(\bar y,x_\vartheta)+
		\vartheta \mathsf b(y,x_\vartheta)
		\ge \mathsf b (y_\vartheta,x_\vartheta)
		=g(y_\vartheta)
		\\&\ge \mathsf b(y_\vartheta,x)\quad\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}},
	\end{align*}
	so that 
	\begin{displaymath}
		\limsup_{\vartheta\downarrow0}
		\mathsf b(\bar y,x_\vartheta)\ge 
\limsup_{\vartheta\downarrow0}
\mathsf b(y_\vartheta,x)\ge \mathsf b(\bar y,x)
		\quad\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}},
	\end{displaymath}
	and therefore
	\begin{displaymath}
		\limsup_{\vartheta\downarrow0}
		\mathsf b(\bar y,x_\vartheta)\ge 
		\sup_{x\in {{\mathrm D}}} \mathsf b(\bar y,x)=g(\bar y)
	\end{displaymath}
	showing that $x_\vartheta$ is a maximizing sequence
	for 
	the $\xi$-concavelike function 
	$x\mapsto \mathsf b(\bar y,x)$. Proposition \ref{prop:minima}
	then shows that $x_\vartheta\to \bar x$.
	We can eventually pass to the limit in \eqref{eq:1bis}
	as $\vartheta\downarrow0$ using the lower semicontinuity of $\mathsf b$ w.r.t.~$x$
	obtaining
	\begin{displaymath}
			g(\bar y)=\mathsf b(\bar y,\bar x)\le 
	\mathsf b (\bar x,y)
		\quad \text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}},
	\end{displaymath}
	so that $g(\bar y)\le f(\bar x)\le 0$.
	
	To show uniqueness, if $(y',y')$ 
	is another saddle point for $\mathsf b$,
	then 
    \begin{equation*}
	g(y')=\mathsf b(y',y') =0 
    \end{equation*}
    yields
	$g(y')=g(\bar y)=0$ 
	showing that $\bar y=y'$ thanks to the 
	$\xi$-convexity of $g$.

    The fact that $\bar y$ is also
    a solution of the primal problem follows
    by Lemma 
    \ref{le:metric-Minty},
    since the map 
    $x\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)=
    -\mathsf b(x,y)$ is upper semicontinuous.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{le:B-structure}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-regular}, let $\tau>0$, $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	and let ${\mathsf B}$ be defined by \eqref{eq:generating}.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(1)] For every $x,y\in {{\mathrm D}}$
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:B-symmetrized}
			{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;x,x)=0,\qquad
			{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)+{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;x,y)={{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}.
		\end{equation}
		In particular, for every $\eta\in2.30$,
		${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$ satisfies the $\eta$-interaction
		dissipativity \eqref{eq:bif-monotone} if and only if ${\mathsf b}$ does,
		and ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$ is antisymmetric
		\eqref{eq:antisymmetry} if and only if ${\mathsf b}$ is.
		\item[\rm(2)] If the sublevels of ${\mathsf b}(\cdot,x)$ are complete, i.e.
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:b-sublevels}
			\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}}\quad
			\text{the map }y\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}\ \text{has complete sublevels,}
		\end{equation}
		then for every $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the map
		$y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$ has complete sublevels as well.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Claim (1) follows by a direct computation, since the terms
	$\frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,\cdot)$ cancel in the symmetrized sum.

	(2) The map $y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$ is the sum of the lower
	semicontinuous map $y\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$, of the continuous map
	$y\mapsto \frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,y)$, and of a constant, so that
	its sublevels are closed in ${{\mathrm D}}$. Since ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,\cdot)\ge 0$,
	for every $c'\in2.30$
	\begin{displaymath}
		\Big\{y\in {{\mathrm D}}:{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)\le c'\Big\}\subset
		\Big\{y\in {{\mathrm D}}:{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}\le c'+\tfrac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x)\Big\};
	\end{displaymath}
	the latter set is complete by \eqref{eq:b-sublevels} and a closed
	subset of a complete set is complete.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:B-convexity}
	Let $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, $\kappa\in2.30$, $\tau>0$, let ${\mathsf B}$ be defined by
	\eqref{eq:generating}, and let $\xi:=\dfrac 1\tau+\kappa$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(1)] If the two-point conditions \eqref{eq:gg-dist-2}
		and \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2} hold, then the maps
		$y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, are jointly
		$\xi$-convexlike with respect to the same system
		${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x,2}$:
        for every $x_0,x_1\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the family
		$(z_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ of \eqref{eq:gg-dist-2}, \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2}
		satisfies, for every $t\in[0,1]$,
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:B-two-convex}
			\tag{$\mathrm{C}^{{\mathsf B}}_{\xi,2}$}
			\begin{aligned}
				{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;z_t,x)\le{}&
				(1-t)\,{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;x_0,x)+t\,{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;x_1,x)
				\\&-\frac\xi2\,t(1-t)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x_1)
				\qquad\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}}.
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		In particular ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$ satisfies the
		radial convexity \eqref{eq:radial-convex} with the same $\xi$.
		\item[\rm(2)] If a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ of barycentric
		maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:gg-dist} and
		\eqref{eq:gg-bif}, then the maps
		$y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, are jointly
		barycentrically $\xi$-convexlike with respect to
		${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$: for every
		$\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ and ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:B-bary-convex}
			\tag{$\mathrm{C}^{{\mathsf B}}_{\xi}$}
			{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}({\boldsymbol \alpha}),x)\le
			\sum_{j=1}^J \alpha_j\,{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}_{j},x)
			-\frac{\xi}{4}\sum_{j,k=1}^J
			\alpha_j\alpha_k\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}_{j},\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}_{k})
			\quad\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}}.
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(1) Given $x_0,x_1\in {{\mathrm D}}$, let $(z_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ be a family
	satisfying \eqref{eq:gg-dist-2} and \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2}. Multiplying
	\eqref{eq:gg-dist-2} by $\frac 1{2\tau}$, adding \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2},
	and subtracting the constant $\frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x)$ from
	both sides, we obtain \eqref{eq:B-two-convex}. The choice $x_0:=x$,
	$x_1:=y$, together with ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;x,x)=0$, yields the radial
	convexity \eqref{eq:radial-convex} of
	Remark~\ref{rem:coercive-primal}.

	(2) Let us fix $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, $J\in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}$,
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$, and ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$.
	Multiplying \eqref{eq:generalized_metric_convexity}, written for
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}$, by $\frac 1{2\tau}$, adding the inequality
	\eqref{eq:convex} for the maps $y\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$, and subtracting
	the constant $\frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x)$ from both sides, we
	obtain \eqref{eq:B-bary-convex}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rm:metric_space_curvature}
	Condition \eqref{eq:gg-dist} constrains the geometry of
	$({{\mathrm X}},{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}})$ rather than the driving bifunction, and it captures the
	part of the convexity of ${\mathsf B}$ which is uniform with respect to the
	time step. Indeed, suppose that for a base point $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, a
	system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ independent of $\tau$, and a vanishing sequence
	$\tau_n\downarrow 0$, the maps $y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau_n,\bar x;y,x)$,
	$x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, are jointly barycentrically
	$(\tau_n^{-1}+\kappa)$-convexlike with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$.
	Writing \eqref{eq:convex} for these maps along a fixed
	$\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}\in {\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ and ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$, multiplying
	by $2\tau_n$, and letting $n\to\infty$, the contribution of the
	real-valued ${\mathsf b}$ vanishes in the limit and we recover exactly
	\eqref{eq:generalized_metric_convexity}.
	For $J=2$ and geodesic interpolants,
	\eqref{eq:generalized_metric_convexity} is the NPC comparison
	inequality \eqref{eq:cn} of Example~\ref{ex:NPC}: it holds with
	equality along linear interpolants in Hilbert (and all flat) spaces,
	and it fails in positively curved spaces. This is the reason for
	allowing the system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ to depend on the base point
	and to collect non-geodesic interpolants: in the Wasserstein space
	$(\mathscr{P}_2(H),\mathscr W_2)$, which is positively curved, the generalized
	geodesics based at $\bar x$ of Example~\ref{ex:generalized-geo}
	satisfy \eqref{eq:gg-dist}, whereas geodesics do not; NNCC spaces
	(Example~\ref{ex:NNCC}) exhibit the same mechanism.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:VMS-compact}
	Let $\tau>0$ and $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, and assume that
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(i)] the maps $y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$,
		$x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, are jointly barycentrically quasi-convexlike with
		respect to a {\em continuous} system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ 
        of barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$;
		\item[\rm(ii)] for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the map $x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ is
		upper semicontinuous; 
		\item[\rm(iii)] there exists $y_0\in {{\mathrm D}}$ such that the
		superlevel set
		$\sigma^+(y_0)=\big\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y_0,x)\ge 0\big\}$
		is compact.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then the primal problem \eqref{eq:B-primal} has at least one solution.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln} to
	${\mathsf a}:={\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$, which vanishes on the diagonal
	by Lemma~\ref{le:B-structure}(1). Note that the first assumption of Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln} is precisely (i) in the statement above.
	For every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the map $x\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$ is the
	sum of the upper semicontinuous map $x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ by assumption (ii) above, of the
	continuous map $x\mapsto -\frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x)$, and of a
	constant, hence it is upper semicontinuous; since the system
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ is continuous, the second assumption of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln} follows, and every superlevel
	$\sigma^+(y)$ is closed in ${{\mathrm D}}$. By (iii) one of them is compact,
	so Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln} provides a solution of
	\eqref{eq:B-primal}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:compact}
Assume
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:b-growth}
        \text{for some $y_0\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and $\tau_o>0$,
	the superlevel of $x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y_0,x)}-\tfrac1{2\tau_o}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y_0,x)$
	is compact.}
    \end{equation}
 Then Condition (iii) in Theorem~\ref{thm:VMS-compact} holds for every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and every
	$\tau\in(0,\tau_o)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:generating}, $\sigma^+(y_0)$ is a
	superlevel set of $x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y_0,x)}-\tfrac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x)$. From Young's inequality for $p,q\in2.30$ and $\theta>0$,
    \begin{align*}
        (p+q)^2 \le (1+\theta) p^2 + (1+\theta^{-1})q^2\,,
    \end{align*}
	applied with $q={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(y_0,\bar x)$, $p={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\bar x,x)$, and $\theta=\frac {\tau_o}\tau-1$ and dividing by $1/2\tau_o$, we have
 \begin{align*}
        \frac1{2\tau_o}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y_0,x)\le \tfrac{1}{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x)+C\,, \quad C=C(y_0,\bar x, \tau_o, \tau):=\frac{1+\theta^{-1}}{2\tau_o}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y_0,\bar x)\,.
    \end{align*}
    Hence, 
	\begin{displaymath}
		\sigma^+(y_0)\subset
		\Big\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:{{{\mathsf b}}(y_0,x)}-\tfrac1{2\tau_o}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y_0,x)
		\ge c\Big\}
	\end{displaymath}
    for any small enough constant $c\in2.30$. Then, using  \eqref{eq:b-growth}, it follows that Condition (iii) holds for every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and every
	$\tau\in(0,\tau_o)$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:discrete-SEVI}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-sublevels} and the $\eta$-interaction
	dissipativity
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:b-dissipative}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}\le \eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)
		\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in {{\mathrm D}},
	\end{equation}
	let $\tau>0$, $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, $\xi>2\eta_+$, and assume that
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(i)] the convexity condition \eqref{eq:B-bary-convex}
		holds for a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ of barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$,
		possibly depending on $\tau$ and $\bar x$;
		\item[\rm(ii)] for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the map
		$x\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$ is upper hemicontinuous with
		respect to the system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of $2$-barycentric maps of
		${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ (Definition~\ref{def:hemicontinuity}).
	\end{enumerate}
	Then the primal problem \eqref{eq:B-primal} and the dual problem
	\eqref{eq:B-dual} have a unique common solution $x_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}$, and
	$(x_\tau,x_\tau)$ is the unique diagonal saddle point
	\eqref{eq:saddle} of ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We set ${\mathsf a}:={\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$ and check the assumptions
	of Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2}: ${\mathsf a}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:diagonal}
	and the $\eta$-interaction dissipativity \eqref{eq:bif-monotone} by
	Lemma~\ref{le:B-structure}(1) and \eqref{eq:b-dissipative}; the maps
	$y\mapsto {\mathsf a}(y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, have complete sublevels by
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels} and Lemma~\ref{le:B-structure}(2), and are
	jointly barycentrically $\xi$-convexlike with $\xi>2\eta_+$ by (i).
	Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2} thus yields a unique solution $x_\tau$
	of the dual problem \eqref{eq:B-dual}. By (ii), ${\mathsf a}$ satisfies the
	upper hemicontinuity condition (2) of Lemma~\ref{le:metric-Minty} with
	respect to the system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of condition (1) of that Lemma
	(guaranteed by (i)); Corollary~\ref{cor:primal-consequences}(ii) then
	shows that $x_\tau$ is also the unique solution of the primal problem
	\eqref{eq:B-primal} and the unique diagonal saddle point of
	${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:B-hemicontinuity}
	When the maps of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ are continuous, condition
	{\rm(ii)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} is equivalent to the
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$-upper hemicontinuity of the maps
	$x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$, $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$, since the squared-distance terms in
	\eqref{eq:generating} are then continuous along each map.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:VMS-antisym}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-sublevels} and the antisymmetry
	condition \eqref{eq:antisymmetry}, let $\tau>0$, $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
	$\xi>0$, and assume that the convexity condition
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds for a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of
	$2$-barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$, possibly depending on $\tau$ and
	$\bar x$. Then the problems \eqref{eq:B-primal} and \eqref{eq:B-dual}
	have a unique common solution $x_\tau$, and $(x_\tau,x_\tau)$ is the
	unique diagonal saddle point \eqref{eq:saddle} of
	${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{le:B-structure}, ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$ is
	antisymmetric and the maps $y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$ have
	complete sublevels; by \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} they are jointly
	$\xi$-convexlike with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:antisymmetric}
	then applies.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:discrete-EVI}
	Let $\tau>0$, $\kappa\in2.30$, $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, set
	$\xi:=\dfrac 1\tau+\kappa>0$, and suppose that the convexity condition
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds. Then every solution $x_\tau$ of the
	primal problem \eqref{eq:B-primal} satisfies
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:resolvent-evi}
		\frac1{2\tau}
		\Big({\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_\tau,y)
		-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,y)+
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x_\tau)\Big)
		\le {{{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,x_\tau)}
		\qquad\text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}, condition
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} implies the radial convexity
	\eqref{eq:radial-convex} of ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$ with the
	same $\xi$; Remark~\ref{rem:coercive-primal} then improves the primal
	inequality \eqref{eq:B-primal} to the coercive form
	\eqref{eq:coercive-primal-remark}
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x_\tau)\ge
		\frac{\xi}2\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x_\tau)
		\qquad\text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}},
	\end{displaymath}
	which coincides with \eqref{eq:resolvent-evi} thanks to
	\eqref{eq:generating} and \eqref{eq:s-variant1}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:radial-enough}
	The proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-EVI} only uses the radial
	convexity \eqref{eq:radial-convex} of ${\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;\cdot,\cdot)$
	with $\xi=\frac 1\tau+\kappa$, which is weaker than \eqref{eq:B-two-convex}
	and implied by it (Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}); we have stated
	the assumption as \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} only because radial convexity
	is less transparent. Relaxing to radial convexity is useful, for example, when ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ are variational $c$-segments in a nonnegative cross curvature metric setting (see Example~\ref{ex:NNCC}) where \eqref{eq:gg-dist-2} does not hold in general; it holds only for maps in ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ with starting or ending point $\bar x$. 
    In turn, \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} follows from the
	two-point conditions \eqref{eq:gg-dist-2} and \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2}
	thanks to Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}(1). Inequality
	\eqref{eq:resolvent-evi} is precisely a single step of the discrete
	Evolution Variational Inequality \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:explain}
	In the typical situation where \eqref{eq:gg-dist} and
	\eqref{eq:gg-bif} hold for every base point $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ with
	$\xi=\tfrac1\tau+\kappa$, Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity} provides
	both the barycentric convexity \eqref{eq:B-bary-convex} required by
	Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} and the two-point condition
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} of Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-EVI}. When
	${\mathsf b}$ is $\eta$-interaction dissipative, the requirement
	$\xi>2\eta_+$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} then reduces to a
	constraint on the step size only: $\tau<\tau_o$, where
	$\tau_o^{-1}:=2\eta_+-\kappa$ if $\kappa<2\eta_+$ and $\tau_o:=+\infty$
	otherwise.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:VMS}
	Let $\tau>0$ be a given step size and let $X^0_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}$.
	A sequence $(X^n_\tau)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in ${{\mathrm D}}$ is a solution
	of the recursive Variational Movement Scheme (VMS) if for every $n>0$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:explicit-VMS-primal}
		{\mathsf B}(\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau; y,X^{n}_\tau)\ge 0
		\quad\text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:discrete-bEVI}
	Let $\tau>0$ and $\kappa\in2.30$. A sequence $(X^n_\tau)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in
	${{\mathrm D}}$ is a solution of the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-Evolution Variational
	Inequality if for every $n>0$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:D-SEVI2}
		\frac1{2\tau}\Big({\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_\tau,y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^{n-1}_\tau,y)\Big)
		+
		\frac1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)
		\le
		{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,X^n_\tau)}
		\qquad\text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:saddle-sEVI}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-regular}, let $\tau>0$, and suppose
	that for every base point $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the assumptions of one of
	Theorems~\ref{thm:VMS-compact}, \ref{thm:discrete-SEVI},
	or~\ref{thm:VMS-antisym} hold. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[\rm(i)] 
    For every initial datum
	$X^0_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the VMS scheme \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-primal}
	admits a solution $(X^n_\tau)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. 
    \item[\rm(ii)] If the assumptions of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} or of Theorem~\ref{thm:VMS-antisym}
	hold at every step, the solution is unique and each iterate
	$X^n_\tau$ also solves the dual problem
    \begin{equation}
		\label{eq:explicit-VMS-dual}
		{\mathsf B}(\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau; X^{n}_\tau,x)\le 0
		\quad\text{for every }x\in {{\mathrm D}}.
	\end{equation}
     \item[\rm(iii)] 
	If
    for some $\kappa\in2.30$ and every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, the
	convexity condition \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds with
	$\xi=\tfrac1\tau+\kappa>0$ (see also 
	Remark~\ref{rem:radial-enough}), then $(X^n_\tau)$ defined via the VMS scheme \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-primal} also
	solves the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
At each step $n>0$ we apply one of Theorems~\ref{thm:VMS-compact},
	\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI}, or~\ref{thm:VMS-antisym} to the bifunction
	${\mathsf B}(\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau;\cdot,\cdot)$, obtaining $X^n_\tau$ solving the
	primal problem \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-primal}.
    
    In the cases of
	Theorems~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} and~\ref{thm:VMS-antisym} the
	solution is unique and also solves \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-dual}. 
    
    Under the
	additional convexity assumption, Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-EVI}
	applied with
	$\bar x:=X^{n-1}_\tau$ turns \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-primal} into a
	single step of \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rmk:choice-scheme}
Recall the choice of bifunction for multispecies coupled gradient flows \eqref{intro:bifunction_multispecies}:
\begin{align*}
    {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)} = \sum_{i=1}^N 
    F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},
    x^{(-i)} )-F^{(i)}(x^{(i)}, x^{(-i)} )\,, \quad \text{for all }x,y\in{{\mathrm D}}\,.
\end{align*}
 From a discrete-time gradient flow perspective, consider the following two natural options for how each species $(i)$ can update to move in the direction of steepest descent of $F^{(i)}$. One option is minimizing $F^{(i)}(\cdot,(X_\tau^{(-i),n-1}))$ with a distance penalty,
\begin{align*}
         X_\tau^{(i),n}= \mathop{\rm argmin}\limits_{x^{(i)}\in{{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}}\Big\{  F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},X_\tau^{(-i),n-1} ) + \frac{1}{2\tau} {\mathsf d}_{{{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}}^2(x^{(i)},X_\tau^{(i),n-1})\Big\} \,, \quad \text{for every }i\in[1,\dots,N]\,.
\end{align*}
This update is implicit in $x^{(i)}$ but explicit in $x^{(-i)}$ because of the dependence on $X_\tau^{(-i),n-1}$. The second option is to solve
\begin{align*}
        X_\tau^{n} \quad \text{is a Nash equilibrium of} \quad \Big\{x \mapsto F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) + \frac{1}{2\tau} {\mathsf d}_{{{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}}^2(x^{(i)},X_\tau^{(i),n-1}) \Big\}_i\,, 
\end{align*}
which is a fully implicit update. Proving the existence of minimizers for the partially-explicit update is easier than proving existence of a Nash equilibrium for a set of energies. On the other hand, we expect better stability properties from the fully implicit method. In \cite{di_francesco_measure_2013}, the implicit-explicit update scheme was used along with Lipschitz bounds on the energy functionals to prove existence of solutions for a two-species PDE system with nonlocal interaction potentials and linear coupling potentials. 
To illustrate the lack of stability of the first method, consider the min-max game where ${{\mathrm X}}^{(1)}={{\mathrm X}}^{(2)}=2.30$, and $F^{(1)}(x^{(1)},x^{(2)})=-F^{(2)}(x^{(2)},x^{(1)}) = \frac{b}{2} (x^{(1)})^2+ax^{(1)}x^{(2)}-\frac{b}{2}(x^{(2)})^2$ with $b>0$ and $a\in2.30$. The corresponding continuous-time gradient flow solution converges exponentially to the Nash equilibrium $x=0$ with rate $b$.
The schemes via the implicit-explicit and the Nash updates are
\begin{align*}
   &\text{(implicit-explicit) }&\ X^{n+1}_\tau &= (1+\tau b)^{-1} \begin{bmatrix}
         1 & -\tau a \\ \tau a & 1 
    \end{bmatrix} X_\tau^n\,,\\
    &\text{(fully implicit) }&\ X^{n+1}_\tau &= ((1+\tau b)^2 + \tau^2 a^2) ^{-1} \begin{bmatrix}
         1+\tau b & -\tau a \\ \tau a & 1+\tau b
    \end{bmatrix} X^{n}_\tau\,. 
\end{align*}
The maximum eigenvalue magnitudes  for each system are $\sqrt{a^2 \tau^2 + 1}(b \tau + 1)^{-1}$ and $[\tau^2 (a^2 + b^2) + 2 b \tau + 1]^{-1/2}$, with exponential stability if the magnitudes are less than one. If the coupling term $a$ is larger than the convexity parameter $b$, the first system is exponentially stable only for a small enough $\tau$, dependent on $a$ and $b$, whereas the  second system is exponentially stable for all $\tau > 0$, $a \in 2.30$, and $b>0$.
This mirrors the need for an upper-Lipschitz bound on the gradient of the energy for explicit Euler for the stability of gradient descent, along with a small enough time step relative to the Lipschitz constant. This observation motivates our choice of saddle point scheme (VMS) for general bifunctions ${\mathsf b}$, which is precisely the fully implicit Nash equilibrium scheme above in the case of multispecies coupled gradient flows.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{le:simple-but-tricky}
	If a sequence $(X^n_\tau)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a solution
	of \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} then it also solves
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:D-SEVI1}
		\frac1{\tau}\Big({\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,Y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^{n-1}_\tau,Y)\Big)
	\le
		{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(Y,X^n_\tau)}
		\qquad\text{for every }Y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let us first suppose $Y\neq X^n_\tau.$
	Setting $a:={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,Y)$,
	$b:={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^{n-1}_\tau,Y)$,
	$c={{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(Y,X^n_\tau)}$,
	since $|a-b|\le {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)$,
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} implies
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac 1{2\tau} (a^2-b^2+(a-b)^2)\le c a,
	\end{displaymath}
	which, after developing the squares, yields
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac 1{\tau} (a^2-ab)\le c a;
	\end{displaymath}
	dividing by $a>0$ we get \eqref{eq:D-SEVI1}.
	The case $Y=X^n_\tau$ is trivial, since the left-hand side of
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI1} is nonpositive and
	${{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X^n_\tau,X^n_\tau)}=0$ by \eqref{eq:link}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:bounded_Delta}
    For every $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and $\kappa\in2.30$ we set
   \begin{gather}
	\label{eq:local-slope}
	\Delta(x):=\limsup_{y\to x}
	\frac{\big({{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}\big)_-}{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)},\qquad 
	\Delta^{\kappa}(x):=
    \sup_{y\in {{\mathrm D}}}\frac{{\big({{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,x)}\big)}_-}{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)},
\end{gather}
with values in $[0,+\infty]$.
 We set ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa}):=\Big\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:
\Delta^{\kappa}(x)<\infty\Big\}$ and ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{}):=\Big\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:
\Delta(x)<\infty\Big\}$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
In order to better understand
    the role of $\Delta(x)$
    it could be useful to observe that
    in the simple case
    ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}=\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)$,
    $\Delta(x)$ coincides with
    the metric slope of $\varphi$
    \cite{AGS08}
    \begin{displaymath}
        \Delta(x)=
        |\partial\varphi|(x)=
        \limsup_{y\to x}
        \frac{(\varphi(y)-\varphi(x))_-}{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(y,x)}
    \end{displaymath}
    and $\Delta^{\kappa}(x)=|\partial\varphi|(x)$  
    whenever $\varphi$ is $\kappa$-convex (this follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:local-global-slope} below). 
    In the operator-Hilbertian case
    ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}=\langle A(x),y-x\rangle$
    where $A$ is globally defined,
    $\Delta^{\kappa}(x)=\Delta(x)=\|A(x)\|$
    for every $\kappa\le 0$.
    In both cases ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{})$
    is dense in ${{\mathrm D}}$; see also Corollary~\ref{cor:slope-density} for a more general statement.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:local-global-slope}
	Let $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, $\kappa\in2.30$, $\tau_o>0$, and suppose that there
	exists a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of $2$-barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$,
