	independent of $\tau$, such that the convexity condition
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds at the base point $\bar x:=x$ with
	$\xi:=\frac1\tau+\kappa$ for every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o)$. Then
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:local-global-slope}
		\Delta^{\kappa}(x)=\Delta(x).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:loc-le-glob} it is sufficient to prove that
	$\Delta^{\kappa}(x)\le \Delta(x)$, and we may assume that
	$S:=\Delta(x)$ is finite.
	Let us fix $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$, $y\neq x$, and a $2$-barycentric map of
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ connecting $x_0:=x$ to $x_1:=y$; we set
	$z_t:=\boldsymbol{\mathsf z}((1-t),t)$, $t\in [0,1]$.
	Evaluating \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} at the point $x$, since
	${\mathsf B}(\tau,x;x,x)=0$ and
	${\mathsf B}(\tau,x;z,x)={{{\mathsf b}}(z,x)}+\frac1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,z)$
	by \eqref{eq:generating}, we obtain, for every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o)$
	and $t\in[0,1]$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:radial-B-at-x}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(z_t,x)}+\frac1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,z_t)\le
		t\,{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+\frac{t^2}{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)
		-\frac\kappa2\,t(1-t)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y).
	\end{equation}
    Multiplying \eqref{eq:radial-B-at-x} by $2\tau$ and letting
	$\tau\downarrow0$, the contribution of the real-valued ${\mathsf b}$ vanishes
	and, as in Remark~\ref{rm:metric_space_curvature}, we recover the
	metric control
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,z_t)\le t\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y);
	\end{displaymath}
	in particular $z_t\to x$ as $t\downarrow0$. On the other hand, keeping
	$\tau$ fixed in \eqref{eq:radial-B-at-x}, neglecting the nonnegative
	term $\frac1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,z_t)$, and recalling
	\eqref{eq:s-variant1}, we get
	\begin{displaymath}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(z_t,x)}\le
		t\,{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,x)}
		+\Big(\frac\kappa2+\frac1{2\tau}\Big)\,t^2\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y). 
	\end{displaymath}
	For every $1>0$ there exists $r>0$ such that
	$\big({{{\mathsf b}}(z,x)}\big)_-\le (S+1)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,z)$ whenever
	$z\in {{\mathrm D}}$, ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,z)\le r$; hence, for $t$ small enough,
	\begin{displaymath}
		-t\,{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,x)}
		-\Big(\frac\kappa2+\frac1{2\tau}\Big)\,t^2\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)\le
		-{{{\mathsf b}}(z_t,x)}\le
		\big({{{\mathsf b}}(z_t,x)}\big)_-\le
		(S+1)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,z_t)\le
		(S+1)\,t\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y).
	\end{displaymath}
	Dividing by $t>0$ and passing to the limit as $t\downarrow0$ we obtain
	$\big({{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,x)}\big)_-\le (S+1)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)$. Dividing by ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)$ and taking the supremum
	with respect to $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and letting $1\downarrow0$ we conclude.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:local-global-weaker}
	By Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}(1), the assumption of
	Proposition~\ref{prop:local-global-slope} is satisfied when the
	two-point conditions \eqref{eq:gg-dist-2} and \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2}
	hold at the base point $\bar x:=x$, since they provide
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} for every $\tau>0$ along the same system.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:iterates-slope}
	Let $\kappa\in2.30$, $\tau>0$, and let $(X^n_\tau)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a
	solution of the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}. Then
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:iterates-slope}
		\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X^n_\tau)\le {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)
		\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1.
	\end{equation}
	In particular $X^n_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ for every $n\ge 1$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:D-SEVI1} and the triangle inequality, for every
	$Y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ we have
	\begin{displaymath}
		-{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(Y,X^n_\tau)}\le
		\frac1{\tau}\Big({\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^{n-1}_\tau,Y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^{n}_\tau,Y)\Big)
		\le \frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)}\tau;
	\end{displaymath}
	taking the supremum with respect to
	$Y\in {{\mathrm D}}\setminus\{X^n_\tau\}$ and recalling
	\eqref{eq:local-slope} we obtain \eqref{eq:iterates-slope}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{le:MY-convex}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-regular} and \eqref{eq:b-sublevels},
	let $\bar\tau>0$, $\kappa\in2.30$, $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ with
	$\xi=\frac 1{\bar \tau}+\kappa>0$,
    and assume that the convexity condition
	\eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds for a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of
	$2$-barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$.
    Then the map
	$y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\bar \tau,\bar x;y,\bar x)$ attains its minimum on
	${{\mathrm D}}$; in particular \eqref{eq:MY} holds at $\bar x$ with step
	size $\bar \tau$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} with $x:=\bar x$, the map
	$\psi(y):={\mathsf B}(\bar \tau,\bar x;y,\bar x)$ is $\xi$-convexlike with
	$\xi=\bar \tau^{-1}+\kappa>0$ with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$; it is
	proper, since $\psi(\bar x)=0$ by \eqref{eq:b-regular}, and it has
	complete sublevels by \eqref{eq:b-sublevels} and
	Lemma~\ref{le:B-structure}(2). Proposition~\ref{prop:minima} then
	shows that $\psi$ attains its minimum on ${{\mathrm D}}$, so that
	$\mathsf b_{\bar \tau}(\bar x)>-\infty$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{le:one-step}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-regular} and the $\eta$-interaction
	dissipativity \eqref{eq:b-dissipative}, let $\bar\tau>0,\,\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ satisfy
	\eqref{eq:MY} and 
    $\bar \tau(2\eta-\kappa)_+ \le 1$.  
    If
	$\tau\in(0,\bar\tau/2)$ and $x_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}$ solves a single step of the
	discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI \eqref{eq:resolvent-evi},
    then
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:one-step-rate}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x_\tau)\le
		2\,\big({-}\mathsf b_{\bar \tau}(\bar x)\big)\,\tau.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Choosing $y:=\bar x$ in \eqref{eq:resolvent-evi} and recalling
	\eqref{eq:s-variant1} and \eqref{eq:b-regular} we obtain
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac1{\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_\tau,\bar x)\le
		{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(\bar x,x_\tau)}=
		{{{\mathsf b}}(\bar x,x_\tau)}-\frac\kappa2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_\tau,\bar x).
	\end{displaymath}
	The dissipativity \eqref{eq:b-dissipative} gives
	${{{\mathsf b}}(\bar x,x_\tau)}\le
	\eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x_\tau)-{{{\mathsf b}}(x_\tau,\bar x)}$, while \eqref{eq:MY}
	yields
	$-{{{\mathsf b}}(x_\tau,\bar x)}\le
	\frac1{2\bar \tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\bar x,x_\tau)-\mathsf b_{\bar \tau}(\bar x)$; hence
	\begin{displaymath}
		\Big(\frac1\tau+\frac\kappa2-\eta-\frac1{2\bar \tau}\Big)
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_\tau,\bar x)\le -\mathsf b_{\bar \tau}(\bar x).
	\end{displaymath}
	Since $\tau<\bar\tau/2$ we have
	$\frac1\tau+\frac\kappa2-\eta-\frac1{2\bar \tau}\ge \frac 1{2\tau}+
    \frac1{2\bar \tau}
    +\frac\kappa2-\eta\ge \frac 1{2\tau}$ and we
	obtain \eqref{eq:one-step-rate}; notice that
	$\mathsf b_{\bar \tau}(\bar x)\le {\mathsf B}(\bar \tau,\bar x;\bar x,\bar x)=0$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:slope-density}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-regular}, \eqref{eq:b-sublevels}, and \eqref{eq:b-dissipative},
    and assume that for every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ there exist
	$\bar\tau>0$ with $\xi=\frac 1{\bar \tau}+\kappa>0$ and a system
	${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2}$ of $2$-barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$ for which the
	convexity condition \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds.
	If for every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ there exists a sequence
	$\tau_\ell\downarrow0$ such that the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} admits a one-step solution with initial datum
	$\bar x$ and step size $\tau_\ell$, then ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ is dense in
	${{\mathrm D}}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$. Lemma~\ref{le:MY-convex} provides
	\eqref{eq:MY} at $\bar x$ and, since \eqref{eq:MY} is stable under
	reducing the step size, we can also assume
	$\bar\tau(2\eta-\kappa)_+\le1$. Since the first step of
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} coincides with \eqref{eq:resolvent-evi}, the
	solutions $X^1_{\tau_\ell}$ belong to ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ by
    Proposition~\ref{prop:iterates-slope}
    and converge to $\bar x$ by
	Lemma~\ref{le:one-step}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
\label{ex:convexity-spherical-Hellinger}
    Consider a system of coupled gradient flows with respect to the spherical Hellinger metric $\mathscr{H}$, which gives rise to a space with nonnegative cross curvature (see Example~\ref{ex:NNCC} in Section~\ref{sec:convexity-ex}): for all $i\in [1,\dots,N]$,
    \begin{align*}
        \partial_t \rho^{(i)}(x) = -\nabla_{\mathscr{H},\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}[\rho^{(1)},\dots, \rho^{(N)} ] = -\Big(\delta_{\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}[\rho](x) -\int \delta_{\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}[\rho]\, {\mathrm d}\rho^{(i)}\Big) \rho^{(i)}(x)\,.
    \end{align*}
    We would like to prove well-posedness of the solutions to the above system of evolutions. While results in \cite{carrillo_fisher-rao_2024} show that a class of $f$-divergences are geodesically convex in the Hellinger metric, existence of solutions was left as an open problem because ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\cdot,\rho)$ is not 1-convex along geodesics in the spherical Hellinger metric. In \cite{lascu_fisher-rao_2024}, the authors propose a min-max flow system for use in machine learning applications, studying its long time behavior.
    In recent work, \cite{Leger-Todeschi-Vialard25} showed the existence of (non-unique) curves along which the squared spherical Hellinger distance is 1-convex. These curves could serve as condidates for a suitable choice of barycentric system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$. However, it is not known which nontrivial energy functionals are convex with respect to these curves. 
    This illustrates how the choice of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ can be challenging for spaces that lack non-positive curvature.
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
For $\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)}\in\mathscr{P}_2(2.30)$, $a_1,a_2\in2.30$, and $\kappa>0$, consider the energy functionals
    \begin{align*}
        F^{(1)}(\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)}) &= \frac{\kappa}{2}\int z_1^2{\mathrm d} \rho^{(1)}(z_1)+ 2a_1\iint z_1 z_2 {\mathrm d} \rho^{(1)}(z_1) {\mathrm d} \rho^{(2)}(z_2)\,, \\
        F^{(2)}(\rho^{(2)},\rho^{(1)}) &=\frac{\kappa}{2}\int z_2^2 {\mathrm d} \rho^{(2)}(z_2)+ 2a_2\iint z_1  z_2 {\mathrm d} \rho^{(1)}(z_1) {\mathrm d} \rho^{(2)}(z_2) \,.
    \end{align*}
    It was shown in \cite[Example 4.5]{conger_monotone_2025} that this system is not necessarily monotone, even though $F^{(1)}$ and $F^{(2)}$ are strongly $\kappa$-displacement convex in $\rho^{(1)}$ and $\rho^{(2)}$ respectively.  In fact, for the choice of $a_1=a_2$, the corresponding coupled Wasserstein-2 gradient flow can be written as a joint gradient flow of an energy functional that has no minimizer.  In other words, the static game has no solution (no Nash equilibrium). However, the existence theorems in Section~\ref{sec:resolvent}
     can still be applied to provide existence of solutions to the dynamic game (see Section~\ref{sec:metric_dissipative_evolutions}). Here, let us discuss existence of solutions to the VMS scheme \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-primal} and the discrete EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} approximating the solutions to the dynamic game.
     Let ${{{\mathsf b}}(\mu,\rho)} =\sum_{i=1}^2 F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)})-F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)})$. Computing the interaction dissipativity according to Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order}, we have, with $\gamma^{(1)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(1)},\mu^{(1)})$ and $\gamma^{(2)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(2)},\mu^{(2)})$ optimal transport plans,
     \begin{align*}
         {{{\mathsf b}}(\rho,\mu)} + {{{\mathsf b}}(\mu,\rho)} &=  2(a_1+a_2)\iiiint \left( z_1 z_2'+ z_1'z_2-z_1z_2- z_1'z_2' \right){\mathrm d} \gamma^{(1)}(z_1,z_1') {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(2)} (z_2,z_2') \\
         &= 2(a_1+a_2) \iiiint (z_1-z_1')(z_2'-z_2){\mathrm d} \gamma^{(1)}(z_1,z_1') {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(2)} (z_2,z_2')  \le |a_1+a_2| {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\rho,\mu)\,,
     \end{align*}
     where the inequality follows from Young's inequality. Therefore, ${\mathsf b}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:b-dissipative} with $\eta=|a_1+a_2|$. In particular, ${\mathsf b}$ is not antisymmetric, unless $a_1+a_2=0$ or one of the pairs $(\rho^{(i)}, \mu^{(i)})$ has the same means. Thus, we consider the existence of discrete iterates using Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI} via the dissipativity conditions in Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI}. For this example, we select ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ as generalized geodesics (Example~\ref{ex:generalized-geo}), then $y \mapsto {\mathsf b}(y,x)$ is $\kappa$-barycentrically convexlike with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ and \eqref{eq:B-bary-convex} holds. Therefore, $\lambda=|a_1+a_2|-\kappa$. Depending on the choice of $a_1$, $a_2$, and $\kappa$, it is possible that $\lambda>0$. 
     Selecting $\tau_o:=(2\eta_+)^{-1}$ results in $\xi=\tau^{-1}+\kappa > 2\eta_+$ for every $\tau<\tau_o$. For any $\rho_n \to \rho$ we have ${\mathsf b}(\rho_n,\mu) \to {\mathsf b}(\rho,\mu)$ because $\mathscr W_2$ convergence implies convergence of second moment terms  
     and the linear terms have Lipschitz integrands. Thus, the map $y \mapsto {\mathsf b}(y,x)$ is $\mathscr W_2$-continuous, and 
    it has complete sublevels due to the coercive quadratic terms and continuity of $y \mapsto {\mathsf b}(y,x)$. The map $x\mapsto {\mathsf b}(y,x)$ is continuous along all curves in ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$.
      The requirements for Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} are thus satisfied and we can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI}.
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
The main difference in applying Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2} to ${\mathsf a}={\mathsf B}$ rather than ${\mathsf a}={\mathsf b}$ to achieve the result in Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} is the presence of $\frac{1}{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\cdot,\bar x)$ in the bifunction. In order for ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)} = \<{\mathsf A}(x),y-x>$ to satisfy the criteria for Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI}, we can simply apply the same requirements as discussed in Section~\ref{sec:ex-existence}, because norms on Hilbert spaces satisfy the desired 1-convexity property and continuity properties.
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
In the single species gradient flow setting, ${{\mathrm X}}={{\mathrm X}}^{(1)}$ and energy $\varphi:{{\mathrm X}} \to 2.30$. Solving the primal equilibrium problem \eqref{eq:B-primal} for ${\mathsf B}(\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau;y,x)$ reduces to solving
\begin{align*}
     &\frac{1}{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^{n-1}_\tau,y) - \frac{1}{2\tau} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^{n-1}_\tau,X^n_\tau)+\varphi(y) - \varphi(X^n_\tau) \ge 0\,, \quad \forall\, y\in {{\mathrm X}}\,,  \\
     &\quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^{n-1}_\tau,y)+\varphi(y) \ge \frac{1}{2\tau} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^{n-1}_\tau,X^n_\tau) + \varphi(X^n_\tau) \,, \quad \forall\, y\in {{\mathrm X}}\,,
\end{align*}
which is the same minimizing movement scheme \eqref{eq:JKO} in \cite{AGS08}, known as the JKO scheme in Wasserstein-2 spaces \cite{JordanKinderlehrerOtto98}.
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
The bifunction is given by ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)} = F(y^{(1)},x^{(2)})-F(x^{(1)},y^{(2)})$, and the generating bifunction is
\begin{align*}
    \begin{split}
        {\mathsf B}(\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau;y,x):=
	\frac 1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,X_\tau^{n-1})-
    \frac1{2\tau}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,X_\tau^{n-1}) + F(y^{(1)}, x^{(2)})-F(x^{(1)},y^{(2)})\,.
    \end{split}
\end{align*}
Let us assume sufficient regularity of $F$ so that ${\mathsf b}(\cdot,x)$ has complete sublevels, and $F$ is convex-concave such that the convexity condition \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} holds for some ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x,2}$. 
Since ${\mathsf b}$ is antisymmetric, we can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:VMS-antisym} to obtain existence of $(X_\tau^n)$ solving \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-primal} with 2-point barycentric convexity instead of the stronger barycentric convexity required for Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI}. By Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI}, $(X_\tau^n)$ also solves the discrete EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}.
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
We will check the convexity along generalized geodesics in the multispecies coupled gradient flow setting. 
    Let $(F^{(i)})$ be a coupled gradient flow with each species evolving in the Wasserstein-2 metric space. To show existence of a global Nash equilibrium, we can 
    check conditions on $(F^{(i)})$ so that the maps $y \mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ are $\kappa$-barycentrically convexlike with respect to $\mathscr W_2$  generalized geodesics (Example~\ref{ex:generalized-geo}). 
    This choice of curves applies to Examples (II)-(III) as well in the Wasserstein-2 metric setting. Dissipativity \eqref{eq:b-dissipative} in combination with upper-semicontinuity of each $F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},\cdot)-F^{(i)}(\cdot,\cdot)$ is sufficient to satisfy the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI}. Then by Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI}, the VMS scheme admits a solution $(X_\tau^n)$, each iterate $X_\tau^n$ solves the dual equilibrium problem \eqref{eq:explicit-VMS-dual}, and since $\frac12 \mathscr W_2^2(\cdot,x)$ is $1$-convex with respect to generalized geodesics, $(X_\tau^n)$ solves the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI1}.
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:solutions}
	A \emph{strong solution} to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} is a locally absolutely
	continuous curve ${\mathsf x}:[0,+\infty)\to {{\mathrm D}}$ satisfying
	\eqref{eq:SEVI2} pointwise a.e.~in $(0,+\infty)$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{le:V-estimates}
	Let $\kappa\in2.30$, let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:lyapunov},
    and let
	$\tau_o>0$ satisfy $\tau_o\,(C_2-\kappa/2)_+\le 1/4$. Every solution
	$(X^n_\tau)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} with $\tau\in(0,\tau_o]$ satisfies
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:V-energy}
		V(X^n_\tau)+\frac1{2\tau}\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)\le
		V(X^{n-1}_\tau)+\tau C_1^2
		\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, setting for a given time horizon $T>0$
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:V-constants}
		N_\tau:=\lceil T/\tau\rceil,\quad
		V_T:=V(X^0_\tau)+(T+\tau_o)C_1^2,\quad
		E_T:=2\Big(V(X^0_\tau)-\inf_{{\mathrm D}} V+(T+2\tau_o)C_1^2\Big),
	\end{equation}
	we have
	\begin{gather}
		\label{eq:V-bound}
		V(X^n_\tau)\le V_T,\qquad
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)\le \tau\,E_T
		\qquad\text{for every }1\le n\le N_\tau,
		\\
		\label{eq:V-energy-sum}
		\sum_{n=1}^{N_\tau}
		\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)}{\tau}\le E_T,
		\\
		\label{eq:V-hoelder}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_\tau(t),\overline{X}_\tau(s)\big)\le
		\sqrt{(t-s+\tau)\,E_T}
		\qquad\text{for every }0\le s\le t\le T.
	\end{gather}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Choosing $Y:=X^{n-1}_\tau$ in \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} and recalling
	\eqref{eq:s-variant1} we obtain, with
	$d_n:={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)$,
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac1\tau\,d_n^2\le
		{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(X^{n-1}_\tau,X^n_\tau)}
		={{{\mathsf b}}(X^{n-1}_\tau,X^n_\tau)}-\frac\kappa2\,d_n^2.
	\end{displaymath}
	By \eqref{eq:lyapunov} and Young's inequality
	$C_1\,d_n\le \frac1{4\tau}d_n^2+\tau C_1^2$,
	\begin{displaymath}
		\Big(\frac3{4\tau}-C_2+\frac\kappa2\Big)d_n^2\le
		V(X^{n-1}_\tau)-V(X^n_\tau)+\tau C_1^2,
	\end{displaymath}
	and since $\tau\,(C_2-\kappa/2)_+\le 1/4$ we have
	$\frac3{4\tau}-C_2+\frac\kappa2\ge \frac1{2\tau}$, which yields
	\eqref{eq:V-energy}.
	Summing \eqref{eq:V-energy} over $l$ for $1\le l\le n\le N_\tau$ and using
	$n\tau\le T+\tau_o$ we get
	\begin{displaymath}
		V(X^n_\tau)+\frac12\sum_{l=1}^n \frac{d_l^2}\tau\le
		V(X^0_\tau)+n\tau C_1^2\le V_T,
	\end{displaymath}
	which gives the first bound in \eqref{eq:V-bound} and, since
	$V(X^n_\tau)\ge \inf_{{\mathrm D}} V$, also \eqref{eq:V-energy-sum}. The
	second bound in \eqref{eq:V-bound} follows from
	\eqref{eq:V-energy}, \eqref{eq:V-bound}, and
	$V(X^n_\tau)\ge\inf_{{\mathrm D}} V$.
	Finally, if $0\le s\le t\le T$ with $s\in ((m-1)\tau,m\tau]$ and
	$t\in ((n-1)\tau,n\tau]$, then $(n-m)\tau\le t-s+\tau$ and the
	Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2\big(\overline{X}_\tau(t),\overline{X}_\tau(s)\big)\le
		\Big(\sum_{l=m+1}^n d_l\Big)^2\le
		(n-m)\sum_{l=m+1}^n d_l^2\le
		\frac{t-s+\tau}\tau\,\tau\,E_T=(t-s+\tau)\,E_T.
		\qedhere
	\end{displaymath}
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{le:discrete-to-continuous}
	Let $\kappa\in2.30$, let $\tau_j\downarrow0$, and for every $j\in\mathbb{N}$ let
	$(X^n_{\tau_j})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a solution of the discrete
	${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} with step size $\tau_j$.
	Suppose that there exists a curve ${\mathsf x}:[0,+\infty)\to {{\mathrm D}}$ such
	that for every $T>0$:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(i)] $\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t)\to {\mathsf x}(t)$ as $j\to\infty$,
		for every $t\in [0,T]$;
		\item[\rm(ii)] There exists $\tilde E_T<\infty$ such that $\displaystyle
		\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\
		\sum_{n=1}^{\lceil T/\tau_j\rceil}
		\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_{\tau_j},X^{n-1}_{\tau_j})}{\tau_j}
		\le \tilde E_T$;
		\item[\rm(iii)] for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$,
		$\displaystyle\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(y,\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t))}<+\infty$;
		\item[\rm(iv)] for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and a.e.~$t\in (0,T)$,
		$\displaystyle\limsup_{j\to\infty}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(y,\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t))}\le {{{\mathsf b}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then ${\mathsf x}$ is a strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2}; moreover its
	metric derivative satisfies
	$\int_0^T|\dot{\mathsf x}|^2(t)\,{\mathrm d} t\le \tilde E_T$ for every $T>0$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Throughout the proof we fix $T>0$ and set
	$d_n^j:={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_{\tau_j},X^{n-1}_{\tau_j})$.

	\emph{Step 1: Regularity of ${\mathsf x}$.}
	From (ii), arguing as in the proof of \eqref{eq:V-hoelder}, we have for large enough $j\in\mathbb{N}$ that 
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:hoelder-j}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(s)\big)\le
		\sqrt{(t-s+\tau_j)\tilde E_T}\qquad\text{for }0\le s\le t\le T,
	\end{equation}
	so that, by (i), ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(s))\le \sqrt{(t-s)\tilde E_T}$: ${\mathsf x}$
	is continuous. Let
	$m_j:(0,T)\to[0,+\infty)$ be the piecewise constant function equal
	to $d^j_n/\tau_j$ on $((n-1)\tau_j,n\tau_j)$; by (ii)
	$\|m_j\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \tilde E_T$, so a subsequence (not relabelled)
	converges weakly in $L^2(0,T)$ to some $m$ with
	$\|m\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \liminf_j \|m_j\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \tilde E_T$. 
	For $0\le s\le t\le T$, the triangle inequality gives
	${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(s))\le
	\int_{s'}^{t'} m_j(r)\,{\mathrm d} r$ for some $s',t'$ with $|s'-s|,|t'-t|\le \tau_j$, and
	passing to the limit
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(s))\le \int_s^t m(r)\,{\mathrm d} r,
	\end{displaymath}
    so that ${\mathsf x}$ is absolutely continuous in $[0,T]$ with metric
	derivative $|\dot{\mathsf x}|\le m$ a.e.

	\emph{Step 2: Integral form of the discrete EVI.}
	Fix $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and let $\zeta_j(\cdot,y):[0,T]\to2.30$ be the
	piecewise affine interpolant of the values
	$\big({\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_{\tau_j},y)\big)_n$ at the nodes $(n\tau_j)_n$.
	For $t\in ((n-1)\tau_j,n\tau_j)$, the inequality
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} gives
	\begin{displaymath}
		\partial_t \zeta_j(t,y)=
		\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_{\tau_j},y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^{n-1}_{\tau_j},y)}{\tau_j}
		\le 2\,{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,X^n_{\tau_j})}-\frac{(d^j_n)^2}{\tau_j}
		\le 2\,{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t))},
	\end{displaymath}
	so that, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:integrated-discrete}
		\zeta_j(t,y)-\zeta_j(s,y)\le
		2\int_s^t {{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(r))}\,{\mathrm d} r.
	\end{equation}

	\emph{Step 3: Passage to the limit.}
    By the triangle inequality and \eqref{eq:hoelder-j} applied with $s=0$, we have
    	\begin{equation*}
        {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),y\big)
        \le 
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(0)\big)
        +  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(0),y\big)
        \le
		\sqrt{(T+\tau_j)\tilde E_T} +  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(0),y\big)\,,
	\end{equation*}
    which is bounded above uniformly in $t\in[0,T]$ and $j\in\mathbb{N}$.
	Since $\max_n d^j_n\le \sqrt{\tau_j \tilde E_T}\to0$ by (ii) and
	$\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}} \sup_{[0,T]}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(\cdot),y)$ is bounded, we have
	$\sup_{[0,T]}\big|\zeta_j(\cdot,y)-
	{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(\cdot),y)\big|\to 0$, so that by (i) the
	left-hand side of \eqref{eq:integrated-discrete} converges to
	${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(s),y)$.
	The integrands in the right-hand side are measurable (being
	piecewise constant) and uniformly bounded above by (iii) and the
	boundedness of ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(\cdot),y)$; Fatou's Lemma
	(in limsup form) then yields
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(s),y)\le
		2\int_s^t g_y(r)\,{\mathrm d} r,\qquad
		g_y(r):=\limsup_{j\to\infty}{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(r))},
	\end{displaymath}
	where $g_y$ is measurable, locally bounded above, and satisfies
	$g_y(r)\le {{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(r))}$ for a.e.~$r\in (0,T)$ by (iv) and (i).
	Since $t\mapsto {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)$ is absolutely continuous,
	differentiating at every $t$ which is both a differentiability
	point and a Lebesgue point of $g_y$ we obtain
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac12\frac{\mathrm d}{{\mathrm d} t} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)\le g_y(t)\le
		{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}
		\qquad\text{for a.e.~}t\in (0,T).
	\end{displaymath}
	As $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and $T>0$ are arbitrary, ${\mathsf x}$ is a strong solution
	to \eqref{eq:SEVI2}.
    Finally, since $|\dot{\mathsf x}|(t)\le m(t)$ for a.e. $t\in[0,T]$ by Step 1, and $\|m\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \tilde E_T$, we conclude $\int_0^T|\dot{\mathsf x}|^2(t)\,{\mathrm d} t\le \int_0^T|m(t)|^2\,{\mathrm d} t\le\tilde E_T$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->
From (ii), arguing as in the proof of \eqref{eq:V-hoelder}, we have for large enough $j\in\mathbb{N}$ that 
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:hoelder-j}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(s)\big)\le
		\sqrt{(t-s+\tau_j)\tilde E_T}\qquad\text{for }0\le s\le t\le T,
	\end{equation}
	so that, by (i), ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(s))\le \sqrt{(t-s)\tilde E_T}$: ${\mathsf x}$
	is continuous. Let
	$m_j:(0,T)\to[0,+\infty)$ be the piecewise constant function equal
	to $d^j_n/\tau_j$ on $((n-1)\tau_j,n\tau_j)$; by (ii)
	$\|m_j\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \tilde E_T$, so a subsequence (not relabelled)
	converges weakly in $L^2(0,T)$ to some $m$ with
	$\|m\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \liminf_j \|m_j\|^2_{L^2(0,T)}\le \tilde E_T$. 
	For $0\le s\le t\le T$, the triangle inequality gives
	${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(s))\le
	\int_{s'}^{t'} m_j(r)\,{\mathrm d} r$ for some $s',t'$ with $|s'-s|,|t'-t|\le \tau_j$, and
	passing to the limit
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(s))\le \int_s^t m(r)\,{\mathrm d} r,
	\end{displaymath}
    so that ${\mathsf x}$ is absolutely continuous in $[0,T]$ with metric
	derivative $|\dot{\mathsf x}|\le m$ a.e.
<!-- end head-7 -->

<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:existence-compact}
	Let $\kappa\in2.30$ and let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:b-regular} and the
	Lyapunov decomposition \eqref{eq:lyapunov} with compact sublevels
	$\big\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}: V(x)\le c\big\}$, $c\in2.30$.
	Let $\tau_o>0$ satisfy $\tau_o\,(C_2-\kappa/2)_+\le 1/4$,
	$2\tau_o C_2<1$, and
	$\tau_o^{-1}+\kappa>0$, and suppose that for every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o]$
	and every base point $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(1)] 
        the maps $y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$,
		$x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, are jointly barycentrically quasi-convexlike with
		respect to a {\em continuous} system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{}$ of barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$;
		\item[\rm(2)] the convexity condition \eqref{eq:B-two-convex}
		holds with $\xi:=\dfrac1\tau+\kappa$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then for every $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}$ there exist a vanishing sequence
	$\tau_j\downarrow0$ and a strong solution ${\mathsf x}$ to \eqref{eq:SEVI2}
	such that ${\mathsf x}(0)=x_0$, $|\dot{\mathsf x}|\in L^2_{\rm loc}([0,+\infty))$,
	and
	$\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t)\to{\mathsf x}(t)$ locally uniformly in $[0,+\infty)$,
	where $(X^n_{\tau_j})$ solve \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} with
	$X^0_{\tau_j}=x_0$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Since $2\tau_oC_2<1$, we can choose $\tau_o'>\tau_o$ with
	$2\tau_o'C_2<1$; as explained in the paragraph after \eqref{eq:V-lsc-map}, the Lyapunov decomposition \eqref{eq:lyapunov} with
	compact sublevels implies \eqref{eq:b-growth} 
    with the threshold
	$\tau_o'$, so that, by Lemma~\ref{lem:compact}, condition (iii) of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:VMS-compact} holds for every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o]$
	and every base point $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$. Moreover, under
	\eqref{eq:lyapunov} the map $x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}=V(y)-V(x)+\mathsf b'(y,x)$
	is upper semicontinuous for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$, since $V$ is lower
	semicontinuous and $\mathsf b'(y,\cdot)$ is upper semicontinuous; hence
	condition (ii) of Theorem~\ref{thm:VMS-compact} holds as well.
	Together with (1), all the assumptions of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:VMS-compact} are thus satisfied at every base point;
	by (2) and Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI}, for every
	$\tau\in(0,\tau_o]$ there exists a solution $(X^n_\tau)$ of the VMS
	with $X^0_\tau=x_0$, which solves the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI
	\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}.
    
    Let $V_T,E_T$ be
	defined as in \eqref{eq:V-constants} (they do not depend on $\tau$).
	By Lemma~\ref{le:V-estimates}, for every $T>0$ the iterates
	$X^n_\tau$, $0\le n\le N_\tau$, belong to the compact sublevel
	$K_T:=\{V\le V_T\}$, and the interpolants satisfy the H\"older
	bound \eqref{eq:V-hoelder}.

    By a refined version of Ascoli-Arzel\`a Theorem (see, e.g., \cite[Thm.~3.3.1]{AGS08}),
    we can find a sequence $\tau_j\downarrow0$ and a continuous curve ${\mathsf x}:[0,+\infty)\to {{\mathrm D}}$ such that
    (i) of Lemma~\ref{le:discrete-to-continuous} holds, and the convergence is locally uniform in $[0,+\infty)$.

	It remains to check conditions (ii)--(iv) of
	Lemma~\ref{le:discrete-to-continuous}: (ii) follows from \eqref{eq:V-energy-sum} with $\tilde E_T=E_T$. For (iii), the
	Lyapunov decomposition \eqref{eq:lyapunov} gives, for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$
	and $t\in [0,T]$,
	\begin{displaymath}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(y,\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t))}\le
		V(y)-\inf_{{\mathrm D}} V+C_1\,R_T+C_2 \,R_T^2,\qquad
		R_T:=\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),y\big)<+\infty.
	\end{displaymath}
    Here, the finiteness of $R_T$ follows since $       {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),y\big)
        \le 
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t),x_0\big)
        +  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(x_0,y\big)
        \le
		\sqrt{(T+\tau_o)\tilde E_T} +  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}\big(x_0,y\big)$ by \eqref{eq:hoelder-j}.
	Finally, (iv) follows from \eqref{eq:V-usc}, since
	$\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t)\to{\mathsf x}(t)$ for every $t$.
	Lemma~\ref{le:discrete-to-continuous} then shows that ${\mathsf x}$ is a
	strong solution.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:skew-symmetric}
The simplest situation is when $\mathsf b$ is \emph{skew-symmetric}, i.e.
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:skew-symmetric}
	{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}=0,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad
	{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}=-{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)},\quad\text{for every }
	x,y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
\end{equation}
In this case $\eta=0$ and ${\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}}(y,x)=-{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}={{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$, so
that $\mathsf b$ is \emph{self-conjugate}; moreover $x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ is upper semicontinuous
and therefore the conditional upper semicontinuity
\eqref{eq:conditional-usc}
is a consequence of \eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:slope-lsc}
It is worth noticing that \eqref{eq:conditional-usc}
implies that
$\Delta^{\kappa}(\cdot)$ is lower semicontinuous.
In fact, if $(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence in ${{\mathrm D}}$ converging to $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$
such that
$\Delta^{\kappa}(x_n)\le L$, then
we have
\begin{displaymath}
    \frac{\kappa}2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x_n)\le
    L{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(y,x_n)+{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x_n)}
\end{displaymath}
and we can pass to the limit in the inequality
as $n\to\infty$ thanks to \eqref{eq:conditional-usc},
obtaining $\Delta^{\kappa}(x)\le L$ as well.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:weak-solutions}
    Let us assume that $\mathsf b$ satisfies 
    {\em (\ref{subeq:structure-dissipativity}a-d)}.
    A \emph{weak dual} solution is a continuous curve
	${\mathsf x}:[0,+\infty)\to \overline{{\mathrm D}}$ that satisfies
	\eqref{eq:cSEVI2} in the distributional sense.


	A ${\mathsf s}$-$\mathrm{EVI}$\ flow in ${{\mathrm D}}\subset {{\mathrm X}}$ is a family of continuous maps
	${\mathsf S}_t:
    \overline{{{\mathrm D}}}\to \overline{{{\mathrm D}}}$ such that for every $x_0\in \overline{{{\mathrm D}}}$ 
	\begin{equation}
		{\mathsf S}_{t+h}(x_0)={\mathsf S}_h({\mathsf S}_t(x_0)),\quad 
		\lim_{h\downarrow0}{\mathsf S}_h(x_0)=x_0,\quad
		t\mapsto {\mathsf S}_t(x_0)\text{ is a weak solution to\ } \eqref{eq:cSEVI2}
	\end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:strong-solution}
       t\mapsto  {\mathsf S}_t(x_0)\text{ is a strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} whenever $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$.}
    \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:Lip-slope}
    If ${\mathsf x}$ is a strong solution
    which is locally Lipschitz continuous
     in $(0,+\infty)$ 
    and $L_{a,b}$ is its Lipschitz constant
    in $[a,b]\subset (0,+\infty)$
    we easily deduce
    \begin{displaymath}
        -{{{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}\le L_{a,b}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))
        \quad\text{for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}},\ t\in [a,b],
    \end{displaymath}
    so that 
    $\sup_{t\in [a,b]}\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))\le L_{a,b}$.
    It follows that the map 
    $t\mapsto {{{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}$
    is upper semicontinuous in $(0,+\infty)$ and in particular
    locally bounded from above for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}.$ Thus, it satisfies the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{le:ulDini}.

    If ${\mathsf x}$ is a weak solution,
    the map $t\mapsto {{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}$ is upper semicontinuous,
    so that Lemma~\ref{le:ulDini}
    can be applied as well.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:weak-in-D}
    If ${\mathsf x}$ is a weak solution, then ${\mathsf x}(t)\in {{\mathrm D}}$ for
    a.e.~$t>0$. Indeed, the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:integral} is
    finite and, by \eqref{eq:above}, the integrand is locally bounded
    from above, so that $t\mapsto {{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}$ is locally
    integrable in $(0,+\infty)$; in particular, 
     it is finite for a.e.~$t>0$, i.e.\ ${\mathsf x}(t)\in{{\mathrm D}}$ for a.e.~$t>0$.
     Moreover, ${\mathsf x}(\bar t)\notin{{\mathrm D}}$, i.e.\ ${{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(\bar t))}=-\infty$, may only occur at times $\bar t$ where the upper
    left Dini derivative of $t\mapsto \frac12{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,{\mathsf x}(t))$ is
    $-\infty$  (by the upper semicontinuity of $t\mapsto{{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}$ and Lemma~\ref{le:ulDini}), i.e.~where ${\mathsf x}$ has infinite left metric speed; it is
    thus excluded for locally Lipschitz weak solutions.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:exponential-trick}
    Notice that we can obtain a more symmetric
    formulations of \eqref{eq:SEVI2}
    and \eqref{eq:cSEVI2}
    by multiplying both inequalities by
    ${\mathrm e}^{-\lambda t}$ obtaining
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:more-symm}
        \begin{aligned}
            \frac 12\frac {\mathrm d}{{\mathrm d} t}
            \Big({\mathrm e}^{-\lambda t}
            {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)\Big)
            &\le 
            {\mathrm e}^{-\lambda t}
            \mathsf b^{\eta}(y,{\mathsf x}(t)),
            \\
            \frac 12\frac{\mathrm d}{{\mathrm d} t}
            \Big({\mathrm e}^{-\lambda t}
            {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)\Big)
            &\le 
            {\mathrm e}^{-\lambda t}
            \skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}^{\eta}(y,{\mathsf x}(t)),
        \end{aligned}
        \qquad
        \mathsf b^{\eta}(y,x)+\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}^{\eta}(x,y)= 0.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{le:equivalence12}
	A locally absolutely continuous
    curve ${\mathsf x}:[0,+\infty)\to
    {{\mathrm D}}$ is a strong solution to
	\eqref{eq:SEVI2}
	if and only if it is a solution to
	\begin{equation}
\label{eq:SEVI1}
	\frac{\mathrm d} {{\mathrm d} t} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}\quad\text{ a.e.~in $(0,\infty)$, 
    for every }y\in {{\mathrm D}}.
	\tag{EVI$_{1,\kappa}$}
\end{equation}
(or, equivalently, according to one of the forms of Lemma \ref{le:ulDini}).

A continuous curve ${\mathsf x}:[0,+\infty)\to \overline{{\mathrm D}}$ 
is a weak solution to 
	\eqref{eq:cSEVI2}  
	if and only if it is a solution to 
	\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cSEVI1}
	\frac{\mathrm d} {{\mathrm d} t} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)\le {{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}_1^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}
    \quad\text{for every }y\in
     {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa}).
	\tag{d-EVI$_{1,\kappa}$}
\end{equation}
according to one of the equivalent forms of Lemma \ref{le:ulDini}.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
For strong solutions, the equivalence
is easy since
the local absolute continuity implies
\begin{displaymath}
    \frac 12\frac{\mathrm d}{{\mathrm d} t}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),y)
    =
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)
    \cdot
    \frac{\mathrm d}{{\mathrm d} t}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y),\quad
    \frac{\mathrm d}{{\mathrm d} t}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)=0
    \text{ a.e.\ where ${\mathsf x}(t)=y$}.
\end{displaymath}
In the case of weak solutions, 	we apply 
	Lemma \ref{le:ulDini} and we prove the equivalence 
	of \eqref{eq:cSEVI1} and \eqref{eq:cSEVI2}
	using the lower left Dini derivative.

	The implication \eqref{eq:cSEVI1}$\Rightarrow$\eqref{eq:cSEVI2}
	is an immediate consequence of the formula
	\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:liminf}
		\frac 12 {\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\!}_-\zeta^2(t)=
		\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\zeta^2(t)-\zeta^2(t-h)}{2h}=
		\zeta(t)		\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\zeta(t)-\zeta(t-h)}{h}=
		\zeta(t)\,{\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\!}_-\zeta(t)
	\end{equation}
	which holds for every nonnegative continuous function $\zeta$.
	
	Let us now prove the converse implication:
	we suppose that 
     \eqref{eq:cSEVI2} holds, 
    we fix $y\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, and we want to prove that
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:toprove}
		{\frac{ {\mathrm d}}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\!}_- {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)\le
        {{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}_1^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}  \quad\text{for every }t\in (0,\infty)\text{ such that }{\mathsf x}(t)\neq y,
	\end{equation} 
    and that 
    the right-hand side of 
    \eqref{eq:cSEVI1} is locally bounded from above.
	\eqref{eq:toprove} can be obtained by applying
	\eqref{eq:liminf}.
    We also have
    \begin{align*}
        {{\skew{-6}{\hat}{{\mathsf b}}_1^{\kappa}}(y,{\mathsf x}(t))}
        =
        -{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)}
        +\lambda {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y)
        \le \Delta^{\kappa}(y)
        +\lambda {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),y),
    \end{align*}
    which clearly shows the 
    required local boundedness.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:strong-solutions}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy the dissipativity \eqref{eq:S-lambda}  
    and let 
	$\lambda=\eta-\kappa$. The following properties hold.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item\label{item:strong-contraction}
		If ${\mathsf x},{\mathsf y}$ are strong solutions to \eqref{eq:SEVI2}, then
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:estimate-strong}
			{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(t))\le
			{\mathrm e}^{\lambda(t-s)}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(s),{\mathsf x}(s))
			\quad\text{whenever}\quad 0\le s\le t;
		\end{equation}
		in particular, for every initial datum there is at most one
		strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2}.
		\item\label{item:mder-decay}
		Every strong solution ${\mathsf x}$ to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} satisfies
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:mder-decay}
			|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)\le {\mathrm e}^{\lambda(t-s)}
			|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(s)
			\quad \text{whenever}\quad
			0\le s\le t;
		\end{equation}
        in particular ${\mathsf x}$ is locally Lipschitz in $(0,+\infty)$.
        \item\label{item:Lip-at-zero}
		If ${\mathsf x}(0)\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, then any strong solution ${\mathsf x}$ is
		locally Lipschitz in $[0,+\infty)$ and
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:Lip-at-zero}
			|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)\le {\mathrm e}^{\lambda t}\,\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(0))
			\quad\text{for every }t\ge0.
		\end{equation}
		\item 
        \label{item:slope} Finally, if in addition the conditional upper semicontinuity \eqref{eq:conditional-usc} holds, then
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:slope-mder}
			\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))= |\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)
			\quad\text{for every }t\ge0,
		\end{equation}
		so that ${\mathsf x}$ takes values in ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ for $t>0$ whenever ${\mathsf x}(0)\in{{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
{\em Claim \ref{item:strong-contraction}.}
	Since ${\mathsf x}$ and ${\mathsf y}$ are locally absolutely continuous,
	using \cite[Lemma 4.3.4]{AGS08}, setting $g(t,s)={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y} (t), {\mathsf x}(s))$ and using the equivalence of right- and left-hand derivatives,
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} g(t,t) &\le \limsup_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf y}(t))-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t-h),{\mathsf y}(t))}{h} + \limsup_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf y}(t+h))-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf y}(t))}{h} \\
        & = {\frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} s}} \big[{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(s),{\mathsf y}(t)) \big]\big|_{s=t} + {\frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} s}} \big[{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf y}(s)) \big]\big|_{s=t}\,,
    \end{align*}
    we get by Lemma \ref{le:equivalence12} and \eqref{eq:S-lambda1}
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:d-inequality}
		\frac{\mathrm d}{{{\mathrm d} t}}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(t))\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(t))}+
		{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf y}(t))}
		\le \lambda {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(t))
		\quad\text{a.e.~in }(0,+\infty),
	\end{equation}
	which immediately yields \eqref{eq:estimate-strong}.

	{\em Claim \ref{item:mder-decay}.}
	Applying \eqref{eq:estimate-strong} to the strong solutions ${\mathsf x}(t)$ and ${\mathsf x}_h(t):={\mathsf x}(t+h)$
	we get
	\begin{equation*}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t+h),{\mathsf x}(t))\le {\mathrm e}^{\lambda(t-s)}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(s+h),{\mathsf x}(s))
		\quad\text{if }0\le s\le t;
	\end{equation*}
	dividing by $h$ and passing to the limit as $h\downarrow0$ we get
	\eqref{eq:mder-decay}.
    The fact that ${\mathsf x}$ is locally
	Lipschitz in $(0,+\infty)$ follows: 
    \eqref{eq:mder-decay} shows that
	$|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)
    <\infty$ for every $t>0$ and that the restriction of
	${\mathsf x}$ to every interval $[t,T]$, $0<t\le T$, is Lipschitz with
	constant
	$L_{t,T}\le 
    \inf_{0<s\le t}{\mathrm e}^{\lambda_+(T-s)}\,|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(s)$.
	
	{\em Claim \ref{item:Lip-at-zero}.}
	Let us set $S:=\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(0))$ and
	$\delta(t):={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(0))$.
	Choosing $y:={\mathsf x}(0)$ in \eqref{eq:SEVI1} and using
	\eqref{eq:S-lambda1} and the definition \eqref{eq:local-slope} of
	the global slope, we get
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac{\mathrm d}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\delta(t)\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf x}(0),{\mathsf x}(t))}\le
		\lambda\,\delta(t)+S
		\quad\text{a.e.~in }(0,+\infty).
	\end{displaymath}
	since $\delta(0)=0$, a
	standard comparison argument yields
	$\delta(h)\le S\int_0^h{\mathrm e}^{\lambda (h-r)}\,{\mathrm d} r$.
    Dividing by $h>0$ and taking the superior limit as $h\downarrow0$ we obtain
    \begin{displaymath}
        |\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(0)=\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\delta(h)}{h}\le S.
    \end{displaymath}
	Applying \eqref{eq:mder-decay}  
    we obtain \eqref{eq:Lip-at-zero} 
    and the fact that ${\mathsf x}$ is Lipschitz in every
	bounded interval $[0,T]$.

    {\em Claim \ref{item:slope}.}   
     Assuming $|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)<\infty$, we can apply Remark~\ref{rem:Lip-slope} together with Remark~\ref{rem:slope-lsc}
     (which needs \eqref{eq:conditional-usc})
     we obtain $\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))\le 
     {\mathrm e}^{\lambda_+(T-t)}|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)$,
	and 
    $\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))\le 
    |\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)$ follows 
    letting $T\downarrow t$. 
    \eqref{eq:slope-mder} then follows from \eqref{eq:mder-decay} and \eqref{eq:Lip-at-zero} 
    (for the curve $s\mapsto {\mathsf x}(t+s)$).
    \normalcolor
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- head-10: body_md -->
Applying \eqref{eq:estimate-strong} to the strong solutions ${\mathsf x}(t)$ and ${\mathsf x}_h(t):={\mathsf x}(t+h)$
	we get
	\begin{equation*}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t+h),{\mathsf x}(t))\le {\mathrm e}^{\lambda(t-s)}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(s+h),{\mathsf x}(s))
		\quad\text{if }0\le s\le t;
	\end{equation*}
	dividing by $h$ and passing to the limit as $h\downarrow0$ we get
	\eqref{eq:mder-decay}.
    The fact that ${\mathsf x}$ is locally
	Lipschitz in $(0,+\infty)$ follows: 
    \eqref{eq:mder-decay} shows that
	$|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)
    <\infty$ for every $t>0$ and that the restriction of
	${\mathsf x}$ to every interval $[t,T]$, $0<t\le T$, is Lipschitz with
	constant
	$L_{t,T}\le 
    \inf_{0<s\le t}{\mathrm e}^{\lambda_+(T-s)}\,|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(s)$.
<!-- end head-10 -->
<!-- head-11: body_md -->

	$\delta(t):={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(0))$.
	Choosing $y:={\mathsf x}(0)$ in \eqref{eq:SEVI1} and using
	\eqref{eq:S-lambda1} and the definition \eqref{eq:local-slope} of
	the global slope, we get
	\begin{displaymath}
		\frac{\mathrm d}{{{\mathrm d} t}}\delta(t)\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf x}(0),{\mathsf x}(t))}\le
		\lambda\,\delta(t)+S
		\quad\text{a.e.~in }(0,+\infty).
	\end{displaymath}
	since $\delta(0)=0$, a
	standard comparison argument yields
	$\delta(h)\le S\int_0^h{\mathrm e}^{\lambda (h-r)}\,{\mathrm d} r$.
    Dividing by $h>0$ and taking the superior limit as $h\downarrow0$ we obtain
    \begin{displaymath}
        |\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(0)=\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\delta(h)}{h}\le S.
    \end{displaymath}
	Applying \eqref{eq:mder-decay}  
    we obtain \eqref{eq:Lip-at-zero} 
    and the fact that ${\mathsf x}$ is Lipschitz in every
	bounded interval $[0,T]$.
<!-- end head-11 -->
<!-- head-12: body_md -->
Assuming $|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)<\infty$, we can apply Remark~\ref{rem:Lip-slope} together with Remark~\ref{rem:slope-lsc}
     (which needs \eqref{eq:conditional-usc})
     we obtain $\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))\le 
     {\mathrm e}^{\lambda_+(T-t)}|\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)$,
	and 
    $\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))\le 
    |\dot{{\mathsf x}}^+|(t)$ follows 
    letting $T\downarrow t$. 
    \eqref{eq:slope-mder} then follows from \eqref{eq:mder-decay} and \eqref{eq:Lip-at-zero}

<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:cEVI_solutions}
    Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:S-lambda},
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis} and \eqref{eq:conditional-usc} with
	$\lambda:=\eta-\kappa$.
	Let ${\mathsf x}$ be a strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} and let ${\mathsf y}$
	be a weak solution to \eqref{eq:cSEVI2}. Then
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:estimate}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(t))\le {\mathrm e}^{\lambda(t-s)}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(s),{\mathsf x}(s))\quad\text{whenever}\quad
		0\le s\le t.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, a strong and a weak solution starting from the same
	initial datum coincide.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions}, ${\mathsf x}$ is locally Lipschitz
	in $(0,+\infty)$ and ${\mathsf x}(t)\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ for every $t>0$.
	Since ${\mathsf x}$ and ${\mathsf y}$ are continuous, it is sufficient to prove
	\eqref{eq:estimate} when $0<s\le t$; up to replacing the two
	solutions with ${\mathsf x}(s+\cdot)$ and ${\mathsf y}(s+\cdot)$, we can assume
	that $s=0$, that ${\mathsf x}(0)\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, and that ${\mathsf x}$
	is Lipschitz in $[0,T]$ for every $T>0$.
	We argue by a standard doubling variables
	technique\normalcolor\ (see e.g.~\cite{Nochetto-Savare06}
    and Appendix~\ref{app:cauchy_estimate_proof}).
    We extend ${\mathsf x}$ in the interval $(-\infty,0)$
    by setting ${\mathsf x}(t):={\mathsf x}(0)$ for $t<0.$
    Let us set
    $\zeta(s,t):=
    {\mathrm e}^{-\frac 12\lambda(s+t)}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(s),
    {\mathsf y}(t))$;  we easily see from \eqref{eq:SEVI1}, \eqref{eq:cSEVI1} and \eqref{eq:above} that
    \begin{displaymath}
        \frac{\partial}{\partial s}
        \zeta(s,t)+
        \frac{\partial}{\partial t}
        \zeta(s,t)\le f(s,t)
        \quad\text{in }\mathscr D'(2.30\times (0,+\infty))
    \end{displaymath}
    where
    \begin{displaymath}
        f(s,t):=
        \begin{cases}
            0&\text{if }s>0,\\
            -
            {\mathrm e}^{-\frac\lambda 2(s+t)}
            {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(0))}
            &\text{if }s\le 0.
        \end{cases}
    \end{displaymath}
    Indeed, since ${\mathsf x}$ is Lipschitz, for a.e.~$t$ (where
    ${\mathsf y}(t)\in{{\mathrm D}}$, Remark~\ref{rem:weak-in-D}) the map
    $s\mapsto\zeta(s,t)$ satisfies the corresponding a.e.~inequality by
    \eqref{eq:SEVI1}, while for every $s$ the map $t\mapsto\zeta(s,t)$
    satisfies the distributional inequality given by \eqref{eq:cSEVI1}
    and Lemma~\ref{le:ulDini}, whose right-hand side is locally
    integrable in $t$ and, by \eqref{eq:above} and
    \eqref{eq:Lip-at-zero}, locally uniformly bounded from above;
    testing with a nonnegative $\phi\in C^\infty_{\mathrm c}(2.30\times(0,+\infty))$
    and combining the two inequalities via Fubini's theorem, the
    first-order form of the identity \eqref{eq:general-skew-symmetry}
    yields $f$ as above. Notice that for a.e.~$t>0$ we have
    $-{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf x}(0))}\le \Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(0))$ by
    Definition~\ref{def:bounded_Delta}.
    For $0<\sigma<T$ we integrate the inequality over the strip
    $\{(s,t):\sigma<t<T,\ t-1<s<t\}$; the flux of the field
    $(\zeta,\zeta)$ through the two oblique edges vanishes, and, letting
    $\sigma\downarrow0$, by the continuity of $\zeta$ up to $t=0$ we obtain,
    for every $0<1\le T$,
    \begin{displaymath}
        \int_{T-1}^{T}\zeta(s,T)\,{\mathrm d} s\le
        \int_{-1}^{0}\zeta(s,0)\,{\mathrm d} s
        +\iint_{Q(1)}f(s,t)\,{\mathrm d} s\,{\mathrm d} t,
    \end{displaymath}
    where $Q(1):=\{(s,t):-1<s<0,\ 0<t<s+1\}$ is the portion of
    the strip where $s\le 0$. Using \eqref{eq:above} and ${\mathsf x}(0)\in{{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, $f$ is bounded from above by $e^{\lambda 1/2}\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(0))$ on
    $Q(1)$. Since ${\mathsf x}(0)\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, and
    $|Q(1)|=1^2/2$, dividing by $1>0$ and passing to the limit
    as $1\downarrow0$ we obtain
    ${\mathrm e}^{-\lambda T}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(T),{\mathsf x}(T))\le {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(0),{\mathsf x}(0))$,
    i.e.~\eqref{eq:estimate}.\normalcolor
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:EVI-flow}
    Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:S-lambda},
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis} and \eqref{eq:conditional-usc} with
	$\lambda:=\eta-\kappa$.
	Let us suppose that the domain of the global slope is dense
	in ${{\mathrm D}}$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:domain-slope}
		\text{the set }{{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})\text{ (Definition~\ref{def:bounded_Delta}) is dense in }{{\mathrm D}},
	\end{equation}
	and that\normalcolor\ for every $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ there
	exists a strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} starting from $x_0$.
	Then there exists a unique ${\mathsf s}$-$\mathrm{EVI}$\ flow
	${\mathsf S}_t:\overline{{\mathrm D}}\to\overline{{\mathrm D}}$ according to
	Definition~\ref{def:weak-solutions}; it satisfies the contraction
	property
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:flow-contraction}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf S}_tx_0,{\mathsf S}_ty_0)\le {\mathrm e}^{\lambda t}\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x_0,y_0)
		\quad\text{for every }x_0,y_0\in \overline{{\mathrm D}},\ t\ge0,
	\end{equation}
	and for every $x_0\in \overline{{\mathrm D}}$ the curve
	$t\mapsto {\mathsf S}_tx_0$ is the unique weak solution to
	\eqref{eq:cSEVI2} starting from $x_0$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
If $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, the strong solution starting from
	$x_0$ is unique by
	Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions}(\ref{item:strong-contraction})
	and we denote it by $t\mapsto {\mathsf S}_tx_0$;
	\eqref{eq:estimate-strong} yields \eqref{eq:flow-contraction} for
	initial data in ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$. Since
	${\mathsf S}_hx_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ for every $h>0$ by
	Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions}(\ref{item:slope}) and
	$t\mapsto {\mathsf S}_{t+h}x_0$ is a strong solution starting from
	${\mathsf S}_hx_0$, uniqueness yields the semigroup property
	${\mathsf S}_{t+h}x_0={\mathsf S}_t({\mathsf S}_hx_0)$.

	If $x_0\in \overline{{\mathrm D}}$, the density \eqref{eq:domain-slope} of
	${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ in ${{\mathrm D}}$ (and thus in $\overline{{\mathrm D}}$) provides
	a sequence $x_{0,n}\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ converging to $x_0$; by
	\eqref{eq:flow-contraction} the curves $t\mapsto {\mathsf S}_tx_{0,n}$
	converge locally uniformly to a continuous curve
	$t\mapsto {\mathsf S}_tx_0$ starting from $x_0$, which does not depend on
	the approximating sequence and still satisfies
	\eqref{eq:flow-contraction} and the semigroup property. Being a
	locally uniform limit of strong solutions, it is a weak solution
	to \eqref{eq:cSEVI2} by the stability observed after
	\eqref{eq:integral}.

	Finally, if ${\mathsf y}$ is a weak solution starting from
	$x_0\in \overline{{\mathrm D}}$, then Theorem~\ref{thm:cEVI_solutions}
	yields 
	\begin{displaymath}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf S}_tx_0)=
		\lim_{n\to\infty}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf y}(t),{\mathsf S}_tx_{0,n})\le
		\limsup_{n\to\infty}{\mathrm e}^{\lambda t}\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x_0,x_{0,n})=0,
	\end{displaymath}
	so that ${\mathsf y}(t)$ coincides with ${\mathsf S}_t x_0$ for all $t\ge 0$: for every initial
	datum in $\overline{{\mathrm D}}$ there is exactly one weak solution. The
	uniqueness of the ${\mathsf s}$-$\mathrm{EVI}$\ flow follows as well: any two ${\mathsf s}$-$\mathrm{EVI}$\
	flows consist of weak solutions, so that they coincide on ${{\mathrm D}}$,
	and thus on $\overline{{\mathrm D}}$ by the continuity of the maps
	${\mathsf S}_t$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:which-assumptions}
	Claims (\ref{item:strong-contraction})--(\ref{item:Lip-at-zero})
	of Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions} 
    rely on the dissipativity
	\eqref{eq:S-lambda} only; the conditional upper semicontinuity
	\eqref{eq:conditional-usc} enters just in the proof of
	\eqref{eq:slope-mder}, through Remark~\ref{rem:Lip-slope}. The
	density condition \eqref{eq:domain-slope} is only needed to
	generate the flow on the whole of $\overline{{\mathrm D}}$ in
	Theorem~\ref{thm:EVI-flow}. Let us
	recall that, by Corollary~\ref{cor:slope-density}, it is
	automatically satisfied whenever every ${\mathsf b}(\cdot,\bar x)$,
	$\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, is quadratically bounded from below \eqref{eq:MY}
	and the scheme admits one-step solutions from $\bar x$ for
	arbitrarily small step sizes.\normalcolor
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{le:apriori}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy the dissipativity condition \eqref{eq:S-lambda},
	let $\lambda:=\eta-\kappa$, and let $\tau>0$ with $\lambda\tau<1$,
	$\tilde\tau:=\big(\frac1\tau-\lambda\big)^{-1}$. Every solution
	$(X^n_\tau)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} with
	$X^0_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$ takes values in ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$
	and satisfies, for every $n\ge1$,
	\begin{gather}
		\label{eq:discrete-Lipschitz}
		\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X_\tau^n)\le
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_\tau^n,X_\tau^{n-1})\le
		\tilde\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X_\tau^{n-1}),
		\\
		\label{eq:slope-stability}
		\Delta^{\kappa}(X^n_\tau)\le
		(1-\lambda\tau)^{-n}\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X^0_\tau).
	\end{gather}
	In particular, for every $T>0$ and $\tau_o>0$ with
	$\lambda\tau_o<1$ we have
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:monotonicity}
		\Delta^{\kappa}(X^n_\tau)\le c_0\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X^0_\tau)
		\qquad\text{for every }\tau\in(0,\tau_o],\
		0\le n\le\Big\lceil\frac T\tau\Big\rceil,
	\end{equation}
	where
	\begin{equation*}
		c_0=c_0(\tau_o,T,\lambda):=
		\begin{cases}
			1&\text{ if }\lambda\le0,\\
			(1-\lambda\tau_o)^{-(T/\tau_o+1)}&\text{ if }\lambda>0.
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Choosing $Y:=X^{n-1}_\tau$ in \eqref{eq:D-SEVI1} and using
	\eqref{eq:S-lambda1} we get
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:discrete-derivative}
		\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)}\tau
		\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X^{n-1}_\tau,X^n_\tau)}
		\le -{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X^{n}_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)}
		+\lambda\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_\tau^n,X_\tau^{n-1})
		\le \Delta^{\kappa}(X^{n-1}_\tau)
		+\lambda\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_\tau^n,X_\tau^{n-1}),
	\end{equation}
	where the last inequality follows from the definition
	\eqref{eq:local-slope} of the global slope. Since $\lambda\tau<1$,
	\eqref{eq:discrete-derivative} yields the second inequality of
	\eqref{eq:discrete-Lipschitz}; the first one is
	\eqref{eq:iterates-slope}. Combining the two inequalities we obtain
	\begin{equation*}
		\Delta^{\kappa}(X^n_\tau)\le
		\frac{\tilde\tau}\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X^{n-1}_\tau)
		=(1-\lambda\tau)^{-1}\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X^{n-1}_\tau),
	\end{equation*}
	and an induction gives \eqref{eq:slope-stability}. If $\lambda\le0$
	then $(1-\lambda\tau)^{-n}\le1$; if $\lambda>0$, for every
	$n\le\lceil T/\tau\rceil$ an elementary computation shows that
	$(1-\lambda\tau)^{-n}\le(1-\lambda\tau)^{-(T/\tau+1)}\le
	(1-\lambda\tau_o)^{-(T/\tau_o+1)}$, whence \eqref{eq:monotonicity}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:cauchy_condition}
Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy the dissipativity condition
\eqref{eq:S-lambda} and let $\lambda:=\eta-\kappa$.\ Fix $T>0$ and $\tau_o$ small enough such that $\lambda<1/\tau_o$. For any $\tau_1, \tau_2\in (0,\tau_o]$,
	if $X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2}$ belong to ${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, then the curves
	$\overline X_{\tau_1}(t), \overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)$  constructed from  the discrete solution to \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}
	satisfy the Cauchy condition
    \begin{align*}
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))
    \le  e^{\lambda T}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2}) + C_\tau(T)\,.
\end{align*}
where for $\tilde\tau:=\max\{\tilde\tau_1, \tilde\tau_2\}$ and $\tilde\tau_i := \left(\frac{1}{\tau_i}- \lambda \right)^{-1}$ we define
\begin{gather*}
    C_\tau(T)= a_\tau(T) +\lambda \int_0^T a_\tau(t) e^{\lambda(T-t)}{\mathrm d} t\\
    a_\tau(T)= 2c_T \sqrt{\tilde\tau} \left[\sqrt{\tilde\tau} +
  \sqrt{\left(1+\frac{\tilde \tau}{\tau_1 }\right)(h_{\tau_1}(T)+h_{\tau_2}(T))}
  \right]
\left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right)\,.
\end{gather*}
with $h_\tau(T)=\frac{T}{2}+\frac \tau2\ell_\tau(T)(1-\ell_\tau(T))$ for $\ell_\tau(T):=T/\tau-n$ if $n\tau< T\le (n+1)\tau$, and $c_T>0$ a constant that only depends on $\tau_o, T, \lambda$ and increases in $T$. In particular, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Cauchy-est}
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))-e^{\lambda T}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})=\mathcal{O}\left(\max\{\tau_1,\tau_2\}/\sqrt{\tau_1}\right)\to 0
\end{equation}
for any $\tau_1,\tau_2 \to 0$ satisfying  $\tau_2^2/\tau_1\to 0$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:tau_to_zero}
	Let ${\mathsf b}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:S-lambda},
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis} and \eqref{eq:conditional-usc}, and
	assume that ${\mathsf b}(\cdot,\bar x)$ is quadratically bounded from below
	\eqref{eq:MY} for every $\bar x\in{{\mathrm D}}$. Let
	$\lambda:=\eta-\kappa$, $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, and let $\tau_o>0$
	with $\lambda\tau_o<1$. If for every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o]$ there
	exists a solution $(X^n_\tau)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2} with
	$X^0_\tau=x_0$, then \eqref{eq:SEVI2} admits a unique strong
	solution ${\mathsf x}$ with ${\mathsf x}(0)=x_0$ and for every $T>0$ we have
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:tau-rate}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_\tau(t),{\mathsf x}(t))\le C\sqrt\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(x_0)
		\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],\ \tau\in(0,\tau_o],
	\end{equation}
	with a constant $C=C(\tau_o,T,\lambda)$; in particular
	$\overline{X}_\tau,\underline{X}_\tau\to{\mathsf x}$ uniformly in $[0,T]$ as
	$\tau\downarrow0$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Throughout the proof we fix $T>0$, we set
	$\Delta_0:=\Delta^{\kappa}(x_0)$, and we denote by $C$ a generic
	positive constant depending only on $\tau_o,T,\lambda$.

	{\em Step 1: Convergence of the interpolants.}
	Let $0<\tau_2\le\tau_1\le\tau_o$. The two discrete solutions with time steps $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ share
	the initial datum $x_0$; applying
	Proposition~\ref{prop:cauchy_condition} in the interval $[0,t]$,
	$t\le T$, and using the monotonicity of the constants with respect
	to the time horizon, the explicit form of the error term
	$C_\tau(t)$ (where now $\tilde\tau=\tilde\tau_1\le
	C\tau_1$ and $h_{\tau_i}(t)\le C$) yields
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:Cauchy-rate}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{X}_{\tau_2}(t))\le
		C\sqrt{\tau_1}\,\Delta_0
		\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],
	\end{equation}
	so that $(\overline{X}_\tau(t))_{\tau\in(0,\tau_o]}$ satisfies the Cauchy
	condition as $\tau\downarrow0$, uniformly with respect to $t\in[0,T]$.
	Moreover, \eqref{eq:discrete-Lipschitz} and \eqref{eq:monotonicity}
	give, for $t\in((n-1)\tau,n\tau]\cap[0,T]$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:interp-bounds}
		\Delta^{\kappa}(\overline{X}_\tau(t))\le L:=c_0\Delta_0,\qquad
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_\tau(t),x_0)\le
		\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^i_\tau,X^{i-1}_\tau)\le
		\frac{L\,(t+\tau)}{1-\lambda\tau}\le R,
	\end{equation}
	with $R:=\max\{1,(1-\lambda\tau_o)^{-1}\}\,L\,(T+\tau_o)$. We claim
	that the values of all the interpolants lie in a complete sublevel
	of ${\mathsf b}(\cdot,x_0)$: indeed, by \eqref{eq:S-lambda} and the
	definition \eqref{eq:local-slope} of the global slope, every
	$x\in{{\mathrm D}}$ with $\Delta^{\kappa}(x)\le L$ and ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,x_0)\le R$
	satisfies
	\begin{equation*}
		{\mathsf b}(x,x_0)\le \eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,x_0)-{\mathsf b}(x_0,x)
		\le |\eta|\,R^2+LR+\frac{|\kappa|}2R^2=:b^*,
	\end{equation*}
	since $-{\mathsf b}(x_0,x)\le \big({{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(x_0,x)}\big)_-
	+\frac{|\kappa|}2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x)\le
	\Delta^{\kappa}(x)\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x_0,x)+\frac{|\kappa|}2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_0,x)$. The
	sublevel $\{y\in{{\mathrm D}}:{\mathsf b}(y,x_0)\le b^*\}$ is complete by
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}; therefore for every $t\in[0,T]$ the
	limit ${\mathsf x}(t):=\lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\overline{X}_\tau(t)$ exists in ${{\mathrm D}}$,
	the convergence is uniform in $[0,T]$, and \eqref{eq:tau-rate}
	follows from \eqref{eq:Cauchy-rate} letting $\tau_2\downarrow0$ with
	$\tau_1=\tau$. Since
	${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_\tau(t),\underline{X}_\tau(t))\le\tilde\tau L\to0$ by
	\eqref{eq:discrete-Lipschitz}, the interpolants $\underline{X}_\tau$
	converge to the same limit; clearly ${\mathsf x}(0)=x_0$.

	{\em Step 2: Regularity of the limit.} If $0\le s<t\le T$ with
	$s\in((m-1)\tau,m\tau]$ and $t\in((n-1)\tau,n\tau]$, then
	$(n-m)\tau < t-s+\tau$ and \eqref{eq:discrete-Lipschitz},
	\eqref{eq:monotonicity} give
	\begin{equation*}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_\tau(t),\overline{X}_\tau(s))\le
		\sum_{i=m+1}^n{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^i_\tau,X^{i-1}_\tau)\le
		(n-m)\,\tilde\tau\,L<\frac{L\,(t-s+\tau)}{1-\lambda\tau};
	\end{equation*}
	passing to the limit as $\tau\downarrow0$ we obtain
	${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}({\mathsf x}(t),{\mathsf x}(s))\le L\,(t-s)$, so that ${\mathsf x}$ is Lipschitz in
	$[0,T]$. Since $\Delta^{\kappa}(\cdot)$ is lower semicontinuous
	(Remark~\ref{rem:slope-lsc}), \eqref{eq:interp-bounds} also yields
	$\Delta^{\kappa}({\mathsf x}(t))\le L$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

	{\em Step 3: The limit is a strong solution.} 
    We apply
	Lemma~\ref{le:discrete-to-continuous} along any sequence
	$\tau_j\downarrow0$. Condition~(i) is the uniform convergence of Step~1.
	For~(ii), by \eqref{eq:discrete-Lipschitz} and
	\eqref{eq:monotonicity} we have
	${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)\le\tilde\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(X^{n-1}_\tau)
	\le\tilde\tau L$, whence
	\begin{equation*}
		\sum_{n=1}^{\lceil T/\tau\rceil}
		\frac{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(X^n_\tau,X^{n-1}_\tau)}{\tau}
		\le \Big\lceil\tfrac T\tau\Big\rceil\,\frac{\tilde\tau^2}{\tau}\,L^2
		\le \frac{(T+\tau_o)\,L^2}{(1-\lambda_+\tau_o)^2}=:E_T'.
	\end{equation*}
	 For~(iii), writing $R_Y:=R+{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x_0,Y)$ and choosing
	$\bar\tau=\bar\tau(Y)$ as in \eqref{eq:MY}, the dissipativity
	\eqref{eq:S-lambda}, the lower bound \eqref{eq:MY} at $\bar x:=Y$,
	and the uniform bounds \eqref{eq:interp-bounds} give,
	for every $Y\in{{\mathrm D}}$ and $t\in[0,T]$,
	\begin{equation*}
		{{{\mathsf b}}(Y,\overline{X}_\tau(t))}\le
		\eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(\overline{X}_\tau(t),Y)-{{{\mathsf b}}(\overline{X}_\tau(t),Y)}
		\le \Big(|\eta|+\tfrac1{2\bar\tau}\Big)R_Y^2-\mathsf b_{\bar\tau}(Y),
	\end{equation*}
	which is finite and independent of $\tau,t$. Finally, condition~(iv)
	is precisely the conditional upper semicontinuity
	\eqref{eq:conditional-usc}, valid at every $t$ because
	$\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t)\to{\mathsf x}(t)$ and
	$\sup_j\Delta^{\kappa}(\overline{X}_{\tau_j}(t))\le L<\infty$ by
	\eqref{eq:interp-bounds}. Lemma~\ref{le:discrete-to-continuous} then
	shows that ${\mathsf x}$ is a strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} (with
	$|\dot{\mathsf x}|\in L^2(0,T)$); uniqueness follows from
	Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions}(\ref{item:strong-contraction}).
<!-- end proof-32 -->
