\label{thm:main_existence}
	Let ${\mathsf b}:{{\mathrm D}}\times {{\mathrm D}}\to2.30$ satisfy \eqref{eq:S-lambda},
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}, and \eqref{eq:conditional-usc}, let
	$\lambda:=\eta-\kappa$, and let 
    $\tau_o^{-1}:=2\eta_+-\kappa$ if
	$\kappa<2\eta_+$ and $\tau_o:=+\infty$ otherwise. Suppose that for
	every $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ there exists a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$
	of \emph{continuous} barycentric maps in ${{\mathrm D}}$ such that
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(1)] the convexity conditions \eqref{eq:gg-dist} and
		\eqref{eq:gg-bif} hold for ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$;
		\item[(2)] for every $y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the map
		$x\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ is upper hemicontinuous with
		respect to the system of $2$-barycentric maps of
		${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ (Definition~\ref{def:hemicontinuity}). 
	\end{enumerate}
	Then the following hold.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(i)] For every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o)$ and every
		$X^0_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}$ 
        the scheme (VMS) admits a unique solution
		$(X^n_\tau)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, which solves the discrete EVI
		\eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}.
		\item[\rm(ii)] For every $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{})$ there
		exists a unique strong solution ${\mathsf x}$ to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} with
		${\mathsf x}(0)=x_0$; the interpolants $\overline{X}_\tau$ of the discrete
		solutions starting from $x_0$ converge to ${\mathsf x}$ uniformly on
		compact intervals as $\tau\downarrow0$, with the rate 
        	\begin{equation*}
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_\tau(t),{\mathsf x}(t))\le C\sqrt\tau\,\Delta^{\kappa}(x_0)
		\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],\ \tau\in(0,\tau_o],
	\end{equation*} 
        and the contraction estimate \eqref{eq:estimate-strong} holds
		between any two strong solutions.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}, Condition (1) implies that for
	every $\tau>0$ and $\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ the maps
	$y\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$, $x\in {{\mathrm D}}$, satisfy the
	barycentric convexity \eqref{eq:B-bary-convex} and the two-point
	condition \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} with $\xi=\frac1\tau+\kappa$; if
	$\tau<\tau_o$ then $\xi>2\eta_+$ by Remark~\ref{rem:explain}.
	Since the maps of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$ are continuous, Condition (2)
	and Remark~\ref{rem:B-hemicontinuity} yield the upper
	hemicontinuity of $x\mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar x;y,x)$ with respect to
	the $2$-barycentric maps of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar x}$. Together with
	\eqref{eq:S-lambda} and \eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}, the assumptions
	of Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete-SEVI} thus hold for every base point,
	so that Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI} provides a unique solution of
	(VMS), which solves \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}: this proves {\rm(i)}.

	Since $\tau_o^{-1}\ge 2\eta_+-\kappa\ge \eta-\kappa=\lambda$, every
	$\tau<\tau_o$ satisfies $\lambda\tau<1$: the existence and
	convergence in claim {\rm(ii)} then follow from
	Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_to_zero},  whose lower bound \eqref{eq:MY}
	at every $\bar x\in{{\mathrm D}}$ is provided by Lemma~\ref{le:MY-convex}
	thanks to Condition (1) and \eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}, while its uniqueness and the
	contraction estimate follow from
	Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions}(\ref{item:strong-contraction}).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:antisym_existence}
	Let ${\mathsf b}:{{\mathrm D}}\times {{\mathrm D}}\to2.30$ be antisymmetric
	\eqref{eq:antisymmetry} and satisfy \eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}, let
	$\kappa\in2.30$, $\lambda:=-\kappa$, and suppose that for every
	$\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and every $x_0,x_1\in {{\mathrm D}}$ there exists a family
	$(z_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ satisfying the two-point convexity conditions
	\eqref{eq:gg-dist-2} and \eqref{eq:gg-bif-2}. Then the conclusions
	{\rm(i)--(ii)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:main_existence} hold with
	$\eta=0$ and $\tau_o$ characterized by
	$\tau_o^{-1}=(-\kappa)_+=\lambda_+$ if $\kappa<0$, and $\tau_o=+\infty$ otherwise.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The antisymmetry implies the $0$-interaction dissipativity and the
	diagonal condition, i.e.~\eqref{eq:S-lambda} with $\eta=0$;
	moreover, by Remark~\ref{rem:skew-symmetric}, the conditional upper
	semicontinuity \eqref{eq:conditional-usc} is a consequence of
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}. By
	Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}(1), the two-point conditions
	imply \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} with $\xi=\frac1\tau+\kappa$, which is
	positive if and only if $\lambda\tau<1$, i.e.~$\tau<\tau_o$.
	Theorems~\ref{thm:VMS-antisym} and~\ref{thm:saddle-sEVI} then
	provide, for every $X^0_\tau\in {{\mathrm D}}$, a unique solution of (VMS)
	solving \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}, and we conclude as in the proof of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:main_existence} by applying
	Theorems~\ref{thm:tau_to_zero}
	and~\ref{thm:strong-solutions}(\ref{item:strong-contraction}).
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:compact-dissipative}
	Theorem~\ref{thm:existence-compact} provides strong solutions to
	\eqref{eq:SEVI2} starting from \emph{every} $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}$ under
	compactness and convexity assumptions, with no dissipativity of
	${\mathsf b}$, but without uniqueness. If ${\mathsf b}$ is in addition
	$\eta$-interaction dissipative, i.e.~\eqref{eq:S-lambda} holds,
	then Theorem~\ref{thm:strong-solutions} immediately upgrades that
	existence result: strong solutions are unique, satisfy the
	contraction estimate \eqref{eq:estimate-strong}, and enjoy the
	regularizing estimates \eqref{eq:mder-decay} and
	\eqref{eq:Lip-at-zero} (recall
	Remark~\ref{rem:which-assumptions}). If moreover
	\eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis} and \eqref{eq:conditional-usc} hold,
	then for every $x_0\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{})$ the \emph{whole} family of
	interpolants $\overline{X}_\tau$ converges to the solution with the rate
	\eqref{eq:tau-rate}, by Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_to_zero}: notice that
	the possible non-uniqueness of the discrete iterates plays no role
	there.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:well-posed-flow}
	Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main_existence} or of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:antisym_existence}, there exists a unique
	${\mathsf s}$-$\mathrm{EVI}$\ flow ${\mathsf S}_t:\overline{{\mathrm D}}\to\overline{{\mathrm D}}$ in the sense of
	Definition~\ref{def:weak-solutions}, satisfying the contraction
	property \eqref{eq:flow-contraction}. In particular, for every
	$x_0\in \overline{{\mathrm D}}$ there exists a unique weak solution to
	\eqref{eq:cSEVI2} starting from $x_0$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The convexity and completeness assumptions of  Theorems~\ref{thm:main_existence} and \ref{thm:antisym_existence}
	guarantee, via Proposition~\ref{prop:B-convexity}(1), the two-point
	convexity \eqref{eq:B-two-convex} at every base point
	$\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$; since both theorems also provide, for every
	$\bar x\in {{\mathrm D}}$ and every $\tau\in(0,\tau_o)$, a one-step solution
	of the discrete ${\mathsf b}^\kappa$-EVI \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}, the density
	condition \eqref{eq:domain-slope} follows from
	Corollary~\ref{cor:slope-density}.
	Theorems~\ref{thm:main_existence} and~\ref{thm:antisym_existence}
	provide a strong solution starting from every initial datum in
	${{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, so that all the assumptions of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:EVI-flow} are satisfied.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
A set of energy functionals $(F^{(i)})$ are $(\eta,\kappa)$-monotone, with rate $\lambda = \eta-\kappa$,  if
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\kappa$ convexity: $y\mapsto \mathsf b(y,x)$ is barycentrically $\kappa$-convexlike with respect to a system ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$.
        \item $\eta$ dissipativity: ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)} + {{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)} \le \eta {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)$.
    \end{itemize}
    Equivalently, each 
    $F^{(i)}(\cdot,x^{(-i)})$
    is barycentrically $\kappa$-convexlike and for every $x,y \in {{\mathrm D}}$,
        \begin{align*}
    \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})+
   F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},y^{(-i)})-  F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) \le \eta {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)\,.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:eta_ge0}
    Let ${\mathsf b}$ take the coupled gradient flow form \eqref{eq:sk_coupled_gradient_flow}. Then $\eta\ge 0$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Suppose ${\mathsf b}$ is $\eta$-interaction dissipative according to \eqref{eq:bif-monotone},
    \begin{align*}
        {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)} + {{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)} \le \eta {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)\,, \qquad \forall\, x,y\in {{\mathrm D}} \,,
    \end{align*}
    and fix $x,y\in {{\mathrm D}}$ with ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)>0$. Let the swap operator $S^{(i)}:{{\mathrm D}} \times {{\mathrm D}} \to {{\mathrm D}} \times {{\mathrm D}}$, which switches the $i$-th entry in the two input elements, be defined as
    \begin{align*}
        S^{(i)}(x,y) = (\tilde x, \tilde y) \,, \qquad \tilde x^{(j)}= x^{(j)}, \ \tilde y^{(j)}=y^{(j)} \quad \forall j\ne i\,, \quad \text{and }\tilde x^{(i)}=y^{(i)}, \ \tilde y^{(i)} = x^{(i)}\,.
    \end{align*}
    Since ${{\mathrm D}}=\prod_i{{\mathrm D}}^{(i)}$ is a product, $S^{(i)}(x,y)\in{{\mathrm D}}\times{{\mathrm D}}$, and swapping coordinates leaves ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)$ unchanged. We rewrite
    \begin{align*}
       {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}&= \sum_{i=1}^N G_i(x,y)\,,\\
       G_i(x,y)&:=   F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},y^{(-i)})-F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) +F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)})- F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)})\,,
    \end{align*}
    and note that each $G_i$ changes sign when its own coordinate is swapped: $G_i(S^{(i)}(x,y))=-G_i(x,y)$.

    We consider the case $N=2$ for simplicity. Then the single swap $S^{(1)}$ flips \emph{both} terms: $G_1$ by the identity above, and $G_2$ because species $1$ is the opponent of species $2$, so $S^{(1)}$ swaps precisely the two values $x^{(1)},y^{(1)}$ appearing in $G_2$. Hence ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}$ is antisymmetric under $S^{(1)}$,
    \begin{align*}
        \big({{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(x,y)}\big)+\big({{{\mathsf b}}(\tilde y,\tilde x)}+{{{\mathsf b}}(\tilde x,\tilde y)}\big)=0\,,\qquad (\tilde x,\tilde y):=S^{(1)}(x,y)\,.
    \end{align*}
    Applying \eqref{eq:bif-monotone} to the pairs $(x,y)$ and $(\tilde x,\tilde y)$ and adding, the left-hand side vanishes while, since ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\tilde x,\tilde y)={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)$, the right-hand side equals $2\eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)$; therefore $0\le 2\eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)$ and $\eta\ge 0$.

     For general $N$ one sums \eqref{eq:bif-monotone} over the $2^N$ pairs $S^A(x,y)$, $A\subset\{1,\dots,N\}$, where $S^A$ composes the swaps $S^{(i)}$, $i\in A$ (all pairs lie in ${{\mathrm D}}\times{{\mathrm D}}$ at the same distance ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y)$, since ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2=\sum_i{\mathsf d}^2_{{{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}}$): as $G_i\circ S^{A\triangle\{i\}}=-G_i\circ S^A$, pairing $A$ with $A\triangle\{i\}$ cancels the contributions of $G_i$ for every $i$, and $0\le 2^N\eta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x,y)$ follows.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
\label{rem:steady-nash}
	Let $x_*\in{{\mathrm D}}$ be a Nash equilibrium of $(F^{(i)})$, i.e.\
	${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x_*)}\ge0$ for every $y\in{{\mathrm D}}$. Then the constant curve
	${\mathsf x}\equiv x_*$ is a steady state of \eqref{eq:SEVI2} in either of
	the following situations.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(i)] If $y\mapsto{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x_*)}$ is $\kappa$-barycentrically
		convexlike, then applying the two-point convexity inequality to
		the interpolation between $x_*$ and $y$, using ${{{\mathsf b}}(x_*,x_*)}=0$
		and ${{{\mathsf b}}(\cdot,x_*)}\ge0$, and letting the interpolation parameter
		tend to $0$, gives ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x_*)}\ge\frac\kappa2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x_*)$ for
		every $y$, which is the steady-state form of \eqref{eq:SEVI2}.
		\item[\rm(ii)] If ${\mathsf b}$ is $\eta$-interaction dissipative and the
		flow of \eqref{eq:SEVI2} is well posed,  and $x_*\in{{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$
		(automatic if $\kappa\le0$, or under the convexity of (i)),
		so that the strong solution issued from $x_*$ exists, then the solution ${\mathsf x}$
		issued from $x_*$ is stationary: testing \eqref{eq:SEVI2} at
		$y=x_*$ and using ${{{\mathsf b}}({\mathsf x}(t),x_*)}\ge0$ and the dissipativity,
		\begin{displaymath}
			\tfrac12\frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),x_*)\le
			{{{\mathsf b}}(x_*,{\mathsf x}(t))}-\tfrac\kappa2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),x_*)
			\le\Big(\eta-\tfrac\kappa2\Big){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),x_*),
		\end{displaymath}
		so that ${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2({\mathsf x}(t),x_*)\le{\mathrm e}^{(2\eta-\kappa)t}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(x_*,x_*)=0$.
		More generally, this holds whenever
		${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x_*)}+\beta\,{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,x_*)\ge0$ for every $y$ and some $\beta\in2.30$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Conversely, if $\kappa\ge0$, every steady state $\bar x$ satisfies
	${{{\mathsf b}}(y,\bar x)}\ge\frac\kappa2{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}^2(y,\bar x)\ge0$ and is therefore a
	Nash equilibrium; steady states and Nash equilibria then coincide.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:ss_is_Nash}
  Let $(F^{(i)})$ be $(\eta,\kappa)$-monotone according to Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order} with respect to some ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$, with rate $\lambda=\eta-\kappa$ and $\kappa>2\eta_+$. Assume that the maps $y\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$, $x\in{{\mathrm D}}$, have complete sublevels and that, for every $y\in{{\mathrm D}}$, the map $x\mapsto{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ is upper hemicontinuous with respect to the $2$-barycentric maps ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2$ of ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$.\normalcolor 
   Then there exists a unique steady state $x_\infty\in {{\mathrm D}}$, which is also the unique Nash equilibrium of $(F^{(i)})$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
From Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2}, there exists a unique $y_*\in{{\mathrm D}}$ such that 
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)}_*,x^{(-i)})- F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})\le 0 \quad \text{for all }x\in{{\mathrm D}}\,.
    \end{align*}
    In order for $y_*$ to be a solution to the primal problem, we need that for $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}(t)\in{\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2$ such that $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((1,0)) =y_*$ and $\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((0,1))=y$, we have $t \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((1-t,t))^{(-i)})- F^{(i)}(\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((1-t,t))^{(i)},\boldsymbol{\mathsf x}((1-t,t))^{(-i)})$ is upper-hemicontinuous at $t=0$ for all $y\in{{\mathrm D}}$, which we obtain from the upper-hemicontinuity assumption.  By Lemma~\ref{le:metric-Minty}, $y_*$ solves the primal problem. Conversely, every solution $x^*$ of the primal problem is a solution of the dual problem by Proposition~\ref{prop:primal-implies-dual}, since the $\kappa$-barycentric convexity of $y\mapsto{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ yields the radial convexity \eqref{eq:radial-convex} with $\xi=\kappa\ge 2\eta_+$; the uniqueness part of Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2} then gives $x^*=y_*$. Thus $x^*:=y_*$ is the unique solution of the primal problem and satisfies
    \begin{align*}
    \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{*(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{*(i)},x^{*(-i)})\ge 0 \quad \text{for all } y\in {{\mathrm D}}\,,
    \end{align*}
    showing that $x^*\in{{\mathrm D}}$ is the unique Nash equilibrium for $(F^{(i)})$. 

    Finally, since $y\mapsto{{{\mathsf b}}(y,x^*)}$ is $\kappa$-barycentrically convexlike, Remark~\ref{rem:steady-nash}{\rm(i)} shows that $x^*$ is a steady state; and, since $\kappa>2\eta_+\ge0$, the converse in Remark~\ref{rem:steady-nash} shows that every steady state is a Nash equilibrium, hence coincides with $x^*$. Therefore $x^*$ is the unique steady state.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:ss_is_Nash-2}
   Assume $(F^{(i)})$ satisfies for every $J\ge 2$, $x\in{{\mathrm D}}$, $\boldsymbol{\mathsf y}\in{\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_J$ and ${\boldsymbol \alpha}\in \bm{\bigtriangleup}_{J}$,
     \begin{align*} 
        \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\boldsymbol{\mathsf y^{(i)}}({\boldsymbol \alpha}),x^{(-i)})\le
        \max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\boldsymbol{\mathsf y^{(i)}}_j ,x^{(-i)}):
	j\in \{1,\cdots,J\},
	\alpha_j>0\right\}
    \end{align*}
    Further, assume that the superlevel sets
    \begin{align*}
        \sigma^+(y):=\left\{x\in {{\mathrm D}}:
		 \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)})\ge \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})\right\}
    \end{align*} are
		closed in ${{\mathrm D}}$ and at least one of them is compact. 
        Assume moreover that, for every $y\in{{\mathrm D}}$, the map $x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})$ is upper hemicontinuous 
        and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ is continuous.
   Then there exists a Nash equilibrium $x^*\in{{\mathrm D}}$ of $(F^{(i)})$; if in addition ${\mathsf b}$ is $\eta$-interaction dissipative with $\kappa\ge0$ and the flow of \eqref{eq:SEVI2} is well posed, then $x^*$ is also a steady state, and conversely every steady state is a Nash equilibrium.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The existence of a Nash equilibrium $x^*$ follows directly from Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln}. The steady-state property, and its converse, then follow from Remark~\ref{rem:steady-nash}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:Euclidean_monotonicity}
    Let ${{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}=2.30^{d_i}$, ${{\mathrm X}}=2.30^d$ with $d=\sum_i d_i$, and ${\mathsf d}_{{{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}}$ be the Euclidean norm. If $(F^{(i)})$ are $(\eta,\kappa)$-monotone with respect to linear interpolations according to Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order}, and $F^{(i)}(\cdot,x^{(-i)}) \in C^1(2.30^{d_i};2.30)$ for all $i$, then the following classical definition of monotonicity holds:
    \begin{align*}
       \sum_{i=1}^N \<\nabla_{x^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-\nabla_{y^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}),  x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}> \ge -\lambda \norm{x-y}^2\,.
   \end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
To show this, we first use that $y \mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ is $\kappa$-barycentrically convex, selecting the family linear interpolations for ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2$. The first-order $\kappa$ convexity inequality, comparing $(y,x)$ and $(x,x)$, gives
   \begin{align*}
        \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) \ge \sum_{i=1}^N \bigg(F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})
        \\
       + \nabla_{y^{(i)}} (F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}))\big|_{y=x} (y^{(i)}-x^{(i)}) \bigg) + \frac{\kappa}{2} \norm{x-y}^2\,.
   \end{align*}
   which simplifies to
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) \ge \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{x^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) \cdot  (y^{(i)}-x^{(i)})  + \frac{\kappa}{2} \norm{x-y}^2\,.
   \end{align*}
   Repeating the calculation with test points $(x,y)$ and $(y,y)$ and summing, we have
   \begin{align*}
       &\sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)}) + F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) - F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) \\ 
       & \quad \ge 
        \sum_{i=1}^N \<\nabla_{x^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-\nabla_{y^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}),  y^{(i)}-x^{(i)}> + \kappa \norm{x-y}^2\,.
   \end{align*}
   Now we apply the $\eta$ interaction dissipativity bound to the left-hand side and rearrange to obtain
   \begin{align*}
       \sum_{i=1}^N \<\nabla_{x^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-\nabla_{y^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}),  x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}> \ge (\kappa-\eta) \norm{x-y}^2\,,
   \end{align*}
   which is exactly the first-order game theoretic monotonicity condition with $\lambda=\eta-\kappa$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\label{ex:zeroth_vs_first_order_monotonicity}
    This example illustrates the gap between first order and zeroth order monotonicity. Consider the two-player game in $X^{(1)}=2.30^{d_1}$, $X^{(2)}=2.30^{d_2}$ with energies
    \begin{align*}
    F^{(1)}(z) &= \frac{1}{2} z^{(1)^\top} Q_{1} z^{(1)} + z^{(1)^\top} P z^{(2)}\,, \qquad 
    F^{(2)}(z) = \frac{1}{2} z^{(2)^\top} Q_{2} z^{(2)} 
    \end{align*}
    The convexity parameter is $\kappa=\lambda_{\underline Q}$  (for symmetric $Q_1$, $Q_2$), where  $\lambda_{\underline Q}$ is the smallest eigenvalue among the eigenvalues of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$.
    The first-order monotonicity condition depends on the smallest eigenvalue of $M$, denoted $\lambda_{\underline M}$, where
    \begin{align*}
    \sum_{i=1}^2 \langle \nabla_{z^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(z) - \nabla_{z^{(i)}} F^{(i)}(y), z^{(i)}-y^{(i)} \rangle &= (z-y)^\top M (z-y)\ge \lambda_{\underline M}\norm{z-y}^2\,, \quad M = \begin{bmatrix}
        Q_1 & \frac{1}{2} P \\ \frac{1}{2} P^\top & Q_2 
    \end{bmatrix}\,.
\end{align*}
The interaction dissipativity condition is
\begin{align*}
&{\mathsf b}(y,z)+{\mathsf b}(z,y)\\
    & \ =\sum_{i=1}^2  F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},z^{(-i)})-  F^{(i)}(z^{(i)},z^{(-i)})+
  F^{(i)}(z^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) -F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)})= -(z^{(1)}-y^{(1)})^\top P (z^{(2)}-y^{(2)}) \\
    &\ \le \sigma_{\max}(P)\,\norm{z^{(1)}-y^{(1)}}\,\norm{z^{(2)}-y^{(2)}} \le \tfrac12\sigma_{\max}(P) \norm{z-y}^2\,,
\end{align*}
where $\sigma_{\max}(P)=\norm{P}_{\mathrm{op}}$ is the largest singular value (equivalently, the operator norm) of $P$ and the bound is sharp, so that $\eta = \tfrac12\sigma_{\max}(P)$. According to the first-order monotonicity definition \eqref{eq:Euclidean_monotonicity}, $\lambda=-\lambda_{\underline{M}}$, where $\lambda_{\underline M}$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $M$, whereas according to the zeroth order definition (Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order}), $\lambda=\eta-\kappa=\tfrac12\sigma_{\max}(P)-\lambda_{\underline Q}$. Recall Weyl's inequality: for symmetric matrices $A,B$ one has $\lambda_{\min}(A+B)\ge\lambda_{\min}(A)-\norm{B}_{\mathrm{op}}$. Since $M$ decomposes as $\operatorname{diag}(Q_1,Q_2)$ plus the off-diagonal coupling block $E$ (with $\norm{E}_{\mathrm{op}}=\tfrac12\sigma_{\max}(P)$), it gives $\lambda_{\underline M}\ge \lambda_{\underline Q}-\tfrac12\sigma_{\max}(P)$, so the first-order condition is always at least as tight, and strictly tighter in general.
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
\label{ex:eta-effect}
   This example shows the setting when $\eta>0$, that is, the coupling term causes contractivity to slow down compared to the convexity of each term independently. Let ${{\mathrm X}}^{(1)}={{\mathrm X}}^{(2)}=2.30$, and $a, b\in2.30$, and consider the functionals
    \begin{align*}
        F^{(1)}(x^{(1)},x^{(2)}) = \frac{a}{2}x^{{(1)}^2} + x^{(1)} x^{(2)}\,, \qquad F^{(2)}(x^{(2)},x^{(1)}) = \frac{a}{2}(x^{(2)}-b)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
    The second species is independent of the first species, but the first species evolves based on the second. The first order notion of monotonicity, according to \eqref{eq:Euclidean_monotonicity}, is
    \begin{align*}
        &\< \begin{bmatrix}
            \nabla_{x^{(1)}}F^{(1)}(x^{(1)},x^{(2)}) - \nabla_{y^{(1)}} F^{(1)}(y^{(1)},y^{(2)}) \\
            \nabla_{x^{(2)}}F^{(2)}(x^{(2)},x^{(1)}) - \nabla_{y^{(2)}} F^{(2)}(y^{(2)},y^{(1)})
        \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}
            x^{(1)}  - y^{(1)} \\ x^{(2)} - y^{(2)}
        \end{bmatrix} >\\
        &= 
        a (x^{(1)}-y^{(1)})^2 + (x^{(2)}-y^{(2)})(x^{(1)}-y^{(1)}) + a(x^{(2)}-y^{(2)})^2  \\
        &= \left(a-\frac{1}{2}\right)\norm{x-y}^2 + \frac{1}{2}(x^{(2)}-y^{(2)}+x^{(1)}-y^{(1)})^2 
         \ge \left(a-\frac{1}{2}\right)\norm{x-y}^2\,,
    \end{align*}
    and therefore $\lambda=-(a-1/2)$. Moreover, $y\mapsto b(y,x)= \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})$ is $a$-barycentrically convex with respect to the linear barycentric system in $2.30^2$, and checking monotonicity according to the zeroth-order definition, we have
    \begin{align*}
        &\sum_{i=1,2}  F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},y^{(-i)})-F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},y^{(-i)}) +  F^{(i)}(y^{(i)},x^{(-i)})-F^{(i)}(x^{(i)},x^{(-i)})\\
        & = x^{(1)} y^{(2)}-y^{(1)}y^{(2)} +y^{(1)} x^{(2)} -  x^{(1)} x^{(2)}
        = \frac{1}{2} \norm{x-y}^2 -\frac{1}{2}(x^{(1)}-y^{(1)}+x^{(2)}-y^{(2)})^2 \le \frac{1}{2} \norm{x-y}^2\,,
    \end{align*}
    which satisfies the $\eta$-dissipativity condition in Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order} with $\eta=1/2$. Note that $\kappa=a$ must be large enough for $\lambda<0$ to obtain contraction; this reflects that the strength of the convexity must be large enough to overcome the  effects of the coupling. Additionally, any value of $\lambda\ge -a+1/2$ maintains the first-order monotonicity inequality, in the same way that a $\kappa$-convex function is also $\kappa-\varepsilon$ convex, for any $\varepsilon \ge 0$.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:W2_monotonicity}
    Let ${{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}=\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^{d_i})$, ${\mathsf d}_{{{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}}=\mathscr W_2$, and let each $F^{(i)}$ be smooth enough so that $\nabla_{x^{(i)}} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}](x^{(i)})$ is weakly well-posed. If $(F^{(i)})$ are $(\eta,\kappa)$-monotone with respect to geodesics ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$ according to Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order}, then the monotonicity condition in \cite{conger_monotone_2025} holds,
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{i=1}^N
        \int\< \nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}] (z_i)-\nabla_{v_i} \delta_{\mu^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\mu^{(i)},\mu^{(-i)}] (v_i), z_i-v_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(z_i,v_i)\\ \ge  -\lambda \sum_{i=1}^N \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})\,,
    \end{align*}
    where $\gamma^{(i)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})$ are Wasserstein-2 optimal plans with marginals $\rho^{(i)}$ and $\mu^{(i)}$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Using the $\kappa$-convexity of $y \mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$ along geodesics ${\ensuremath{\mathcal G}}_2$, using $(\mu,\rho)$ and $(\rho,\rho)$ as comparison points in the convexity inequality,
    we have for $(\rho^{(i)}_s)_{s\in[0,1]}$ a geodesic between $\rho^{(i)}$ and $\mu^{(i)}$,
    \begin{align*}
        &\sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}) -F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}) 
        \ge \frac{d}{ds}\left.\sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}\left(\rho^{(i)}_s,\rho^{(-i)}\right) \right|_{s=0} 
        + \frac{\kappa}{2} \mathscr W_2^2(\rho,\mu) 
    \end{align*}
    which can be rewritten, with enough smoothness in $(F^{(i)})$, using the optimal maps $\gamma^{(i)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})$, as
    \begin{align}\label{eq:W2_convexity_inequality}
        &\sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}) -F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}) \notag
        \\
        &\quad \ge
          \sum_{i=1}^N \bigg(  \int\< \nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}](z_i), v_i-z_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(z_i,v_i)  +\frac{\kappa}{2} \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})\bigg)
    \end{align}
    Now using the convexity inequality again with test points $(\rho,\mu)$ and $(\mu,\mu)$ and summing,
        \begin{align*}
         \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}) -F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}) + F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(-i)}) -F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\mu^{(-i)})
         \ge \sum_{i=1}^N \bigg(  \kappa \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})
        \\-  \int\< \nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}] (z_i)-\nabla_{v_i} \delta_{\mu^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\mu^{(i)},\mu^{(-i)}] (v_i), z_i-v_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(z_i,v_i) \bigg) \,.
    \end{align*}
   \sloppy From the $\eta$-dissipativity of ${{{\mathsf b}}(y,x)}$, we upper-bound the left-hand side of the inequality by $\eta \sum_{i=1}^N \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})$ to obtain
    \begin{align*}
      & ( \eta-\kappa) \sum_{i=1}^N \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})
        \\ &\quad \ge \sum_{i=1}^N \bigg(
        -  \int\< \nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}] (z_i)-\nabla_{v_i} \delta_{\mu^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\mu^{(i)},\mu^{(-i)}] (v_i), z_i-v_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(z_i,v_i) \bigg) \,,
    \end{align*}
    and inverting the inequality results in exactly $-\lambda=\kappa-\eta$ monotonicity of $(F^{(i)})$ from \cite{conger_monotone_2025},
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{i=1}^N
        \int\< \nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}] (z_i)-\nabla_{v_i} \delta_{\mu^{(i)}} F^{(i)}[\mu^{(i)},\mu^{(-i)}] (v_i), z_i-v_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(z_i,v_i)\\ \ge  -\lambda \sum_{i=1}^N \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})\,.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:W2GF_satisfies_EVI}
    Consider dynamics given by
    \begin{align}\label{eq:W2_dynamics}
        \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} \rho^{(i)}=\mathrm{div}\left( \rho^{(i)}\nabla_{x^{(i)}}\delta_{\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}(\rho) \right) \quad \text{for all } i\in[1,\dots,N]
    \end{align}
    for functional $F^{(i)}:{{\mathrm D}}\to2.30$.
    Let $(F^{(i)})$ be $(\eta,\kappa)$-monotone according to Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order} with ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_2=\mathcal{G}_2$ given by Wasserstein-2 geodesics. Any (weak, in the sense of distributions) solution to \eqref{eq:W2_dynamics} satisfies the EVI, for all $\mu\in{{\mathrm D}}$ and all $t \ge 0$,
    \begin{align*}
       \frac12 \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} \sum_{i=1}^N\mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)}(t),\mu^{(i)}) + \frac \kappa 2  \sum_{i=1}^N\mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)}(t),\mu^{(i)}) \le \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}(t)) - F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)}(t),\rho^{(-i)}(t)) \,.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Since $\mu\mapsto {{{\mathsf b}}(\mu,\rho(t))}$ is $\kappa$-convex with respect to  geodesics we can use again \eqref{eq:W2_convexity_inequality}
    \begin{align*}
        &\frac \kappa 2 \sum_{i=1}^N \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)}(t),\mu^{(i)}) + \sum_{i=1}^N\int \<\nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)}(t),\rho^{(-i)}(t)](z_i),v_i-z_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(t,z_i,v_i)\\
        &\le \sum_{i=1}^N F^{(i)}(\mu^{(i)},\rho^{(-i)}(t)) - F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)}(t),\rho^{(-i)}(t)) \quad \text{for all } \mu \in{{\mathrm D}}\,,
    \end{align*}
    where $\gamma^{(i)}(t) \in \Gamma_o(\rho^{(i)}(t),\mu^{(i)})$. Identifying 
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{1}{2} \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} \mathscr W_2^2(\rho^{(i)}(t),\mu^{(i)}) = \int \<\nabla_{z_i} \delta_{\rho^{(i)}}F^{(i)}[\rho^{(i)}(t),\rho^{(-i)}(t)](z_i),v_i-z_i> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(t,z_i,v_i)\,,
    \end{align*}
    using \cite[Lemma 8.4.7]{AGS08} allows us to conclude the EVI.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
\label{ex:W2-interactions} 
Let $\hat F^{(1)}:\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\to \mathbb{R}$ and $\hat F^{(2)}:\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d) \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\kappa_1>0$ and $\kappa_2>0$ displacement convex. Consider the setting with a nonlocal interaction kernel $W\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R})$ that is a symmetric function $W(x)=W(-x)$, and energy functionals
\begin{align*}
    F^{(1)}(\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)}) = \hat F^{(1)}(\rho^{(1)}) + \iint W(x_1-x_2) \, \mathrm{d} \rho^{(1)}(x_1) \, \mathrm{d}\rho^{(2)}(x_2)\,, \qquad F^{(2)}(\rho) = \hat F^{(2)}(\rho^{(2)})\,.
\end{align*}
First we check the $\eta$ interaction dissipativity inequality from Definition~\ref{def:monotonicity_zeroth_order}. Only the cross-interaction term coupling the two species appears:
\begin{align*}
&{\mathsf b}(\rho, \mu)+{\mathsf b}(\mu,\rho)\\
    &=-\iint [ W(y_1 - y_2)-W(x_1-y_2) +  W(x_1-x_2)-W(y_1 - x_2)]\, \mathrm{d} \rho^{(1)}(x_1)\, \mathrm{d}\mu^{(1)}(y_1)\, \mathrm{d}\rho^{(2)}(x_2)\, \mathrm{d}\mu^{(2)}(y_2)  \\
    &=\iint  \int_0^1 \int_0^1
    \langle x_1 - y_1, \nabla^2 W(I(s,\tau,x,y)) \cdot (x_2-y_2) \rangle \, \mathrm{d} s \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,  
    \mathrm{d} \gamma^{(1)}(x_1,y_1) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma^{(2)}(x_2,y_2)
\end{align*}
where $I(s,\tau,x,y):=(1-s)x_1+sy_1-(1-\tau)x_2 - \tau y_2$ and $\gamma^{(1)}\in \Gamma_o(\rho^{(1)},\mu^{(1)})$, $\gamma^{(2)}\in \Gamma_o(\rho^{(2)},\mu^{(2)})$. The $\eta$ interaction dissipativity inequality holds if for a.e. $(x_1,y_1)\in\mathop{\rm supp}\nolimits\gamma^{(1)}$, $(x_2,y_2)\in\mathop{\rm supp}\nolimits\gamma^{(2)}$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:Hess-W-bound}
    \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \langle x_1 - y_1, \nabla^2 W(I(s,\tau,x,y)) \cdot (x_2-y_2) \rangle \, \mathrm{d} s \, \mathrm{d} \tau \le \eta \|x-y\|^2\,.
\end{align}
For example, consider the case where $W=W^{(m)}$ is an attractive-repulsive kernel, with $l_a>l_r>0$, $C_r>C_a>0$: 
\begin{align*}
    W^{(m)}(x) = C_r \exp\bigg(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{l_r}\bigg) - C_a \exp\bigg(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{l_a}\bigg)\,.
\end{align*}
This kernel has been studied in a number of applications; see \cite{balague_confinement_2012,craig_convergence_2016} and references therein. The Hessian of $W^{(m)}$ is uniformly bounded in $x$ because
\begin{align*}
    \nabla^2{W^{(m)}}(x) &= 2I_{d}\left( - \frac{C_r}{l_r} \exp(-\|x\|^2/l_r) + \frac{C_a}{l_a} \exp(-\|x\|^2/l_a )\right) 
    \\&\quad 
    + 4x x^\top\left(\frac{C_r}{l_r^2} \exp(-\|x\|^2/l_r) -  \frac{C_a}{l_a^2} \exp(-\|x\|^2/l_a )\right)\,.
\end{align*}
Then, since
\begin{align*}
    \langle x_1-y_1, \nabla^2 W(z)\,(x_2-y_2)\rangle
    \le \|\nabla^2 W\|_{L^\infty}\,|x_1-y_1|\,|x_2-y_2|
    \le \tfrac12\|\nabla^2 W\|_{L^\infty}\,\|x-y\|^2
\end{align*}
for every $z$ (recall $\|x-y\|^2=|x_1-y_1|^2+|x_2-y_2|^2$), the bound \eqref{eq:Hess-W-bound} holds with $\eta:=\tfrac12\|\nabla^2 W\|_{L^\infty}$; integrating this pointwise inequality against $\gamma^{(1)}\times\gamma^{(2)}$ and using the optimality of the plans reproduces the $\eta$-interaction dissipativity. For $W=W^{(m)}$, bounding the two terms of its Hessian separately---the isotropic one by $4\max\{C_r/l_r,C_a/l_a\}=4 C_r/l_r$ (opposite signs and ${\mathrm e}^{-\|x\|^2/l}\le1$), the $4xx^\top$ one via $\|x\|^2{\mathrm e}^{-\|x\|^2/l}\le l\,{\mathrm e}^{-1}$ (as $\sup_{t\ge0}t{\mathrm e}^{-t}={\mathrm e}^{-1}$)---gives
\begin{align*}
    \|\nabla^2 W^{(m)}\|_{L^\infty}\le \Big(4+\tfrac{4}{{\mathrm e}}\Big)\tfrac{C_r}{l_r}
    \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \eta \le 2\Big(1+\tfrac{1}{{\mathrm e}}\Big)\tfrac{C_r}{l_r}\,.
\end{align*}
The coupling also affects the convexity parameter: freezing $\rho^{(2)}$, the map $\rho^{(1)}\mapsto F^{(1)}(\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)})$ carries the potential energy of $W\ast\rho^{(2)}$, whose displacement-convexity modulus is bounded below by $-c_W$, with $c_W:=\sup_z\big(\lambda_{\min}\nabla^2 W(z)\big)_-\le \|\nabla^2 W\|_{L^\infty}$. Hence the joint convexity parameter is $\kappa=\min\{\kappa_1-c_W,\kappa_2\}$ and
\begin{align*}
    \lambda = \eta-\kappa = \tfrac12\|\nabla^2 W\|_{L^\infty}-\min\{\kappa_1-c_W,\kappa_2\}\,,
\end{align*}
which is negative---so that the dynamics contracts---precisely when $\min\{\kappa_1-c_W,\kappa_2\}>\tfrac12\|\nabla^2 W\|_{L^\infty}$, i.e.\ when the convexity of $(\hat F^{(i)})$ dominates the Hessian of the interaction kernel. Here the only interaction between species is generated by the convolution potential $W$, and the $\eta$-interaction dissipativity is thus a Hessian control of $W$. The convexity above is stated along geodesics, which suffices for the monotonicity and the contraction estimate; well-posedness of the associated scheme instead requires convexity along generalized geodesics (Example~\ref{ex:generalized-geo}), since the term $\tfrac{1}{2\tau}\mathscr W_2^2(\cdot,\bar\rho)$ enters the generating bifunction. As the $\hat F^{(i)}$ and $W\ast\rho^{(-i)}$ are internal and potential energies, their geodesic convexity---and hence the parameter $\kappa$ above---transfers to generalized geodesics \cite[Section 9.3]{AGS08}.


Alternatively, one can also proceed via compactness, if $(\hat F^{(i)})$ and $W$ satisfy suitable assumptions. Let us assume for instance that $\hat F^{(i)}$ are proper, lower semicontinuous with respect to $\mathscr W_2$, and have compact sublevels, and $W$ satisfies $L_W:=\|\nabla W\|_{L^\infty}<\infty$ (these assumptions are chosen for convenience; weaker assumptions are possible). Then $V(\rho):=\hat F^{(1)}(\rho^{(1)})+\hat F^{(2)}(\rho^{(2)})$ has compact sublevels on $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\times \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and we can write ${\mathsf b}(\mu,\rho)=V(\mu)-V(\rho)+{\mathsf b}'(\mu,\rho)$ with
\begin{align*}
    {\mathsf b}'(\mu,\rho)&:=\iint W(y_1-x_2){\mathrm d} \mu^{(1)}(y_1){\mathrm d} \rho^{(2)}(x_2) - \iint W(x_1-x_2){\mathrm d} \rho^{(1)}(x_1){\mathrm d} \rho^{(2)}(x_2) \\
    &=\int \Psi_2(x_1) {\mathrm d} (\mu^{(1)}-\rho^{(1)})(x_1)\,,\qquad
    \Psi_2(x_1):=(W\ast \rho^{(2)})(x_1)\\
    &\le L_W \mathscr W_1(\mu^{(1)}, \rho^{(1)})\le  L_W \mathscr W_2(\mu^{(1)}, \rho^{(1)})\,.
\end{align*}
Hence, the Lyapunov decomposition \eqref{eq:lyapunov} from Section~\ref{sec:resolvent} holds with $C_1=L_W$ and $C_2=0$. 
Upper semicontinuity of ${\mathsf b}'(\mu,\rho)$ in $\rho$ is immediate thanks to $W$ being Lipschitz continuous and bounded, so ${\mathsf b}'$ is even continuous under $\mathscr W_2$ convergence. 
In order to apply Theorem~\ref{thm:existence-compact}, additional assumptions on $(\hat F^{(i)})$ and $W$ are needed to guarantee Conditions (1) and (2). Let $\hat F^{(i)}(\rho^{(i)})=\int U_i(x_i){\mathrm d}\rho^{(i)}(x_i)$ for $U_i\in C^2(2.30^d, 2.30)$ with $\nabla^2 U_i \ge \kappa_i I$, and $\kappa:=\min\{\kappa_1-c_W,\kappa_2\}\ge 0$. Then 
Conditions (1) and (2) in Theorem~\ref{thm:existence-compact} hold along generalized Wasserstein-2 geodesics with base point $\bar\mu$ (Example~\ref{ex:generalized-geo}) for any $\tau_o>0$. We conclude that for any $x_0\in{{\mathrm D}}$ there exists a strong solution to \eqref{eq:SEVI2}.
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
\label{ex:L2_W2_monotonicity}
In this example, we study a set of $N$ measures evolving according to a set of velocity fields, which do not necessarily have a gradient flow structure. The flow considered in \cite{wang_local_2026} uses the $\mathscr W_2$ metric but with a notion of monotonicity corresponding to $L^2$ dynamics. To analyze this flow, we first consider dynamics in $\mathscr W_2$ and $L^2$ separately for measures in $\mathscr{P}_2$.
Let ${{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}=\mathscr{P}_2(2.30^{d_i})$, ${{\mathrm D}}\subset \Pi_{i=1}^N {{\mathrm X}}^{(i)}$, and $f^{(i)}:{{\mathrm D}} \to C^1(2.30^{d_i};2.30)$ any potential (not necessarily coming from the first variation of an energy functional).
The $\mathscr W_2$ flow dynamics are given by
\begin{align}\label{eq:team_MFG}
    \dot \rho^{(i)} = \nabla \cdot (\rho^{(i)} \nabla f^{(i)}[\rho]) 
    \quad \text{for all }i\in[1,\dots,N]\,.
\end{align}
The $L^2$ flow dynamics are given by
\begin{align}\label{eq:L2_flow}
    \dot \rho^{(i)} = -f^{(i)}[\rho]
    \,, \quad \int f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i){\mathrm d} v_i = 0 \quad \text{for all }\rho \in {{\mathrm D}}\,, \quad \text{for all }i\in[1,\dots,N]\,.
\end{align}
The work \cite{wang_local_2026} proposes a definition of \textit{linear monotonicity}, given by
\begin{align}\label{eq:linear_monotonicity}
   \sum_{i=1}^N \int \left(f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i)-f^{(i)}[\mu](v_i) \right) {\mathrm d} (\rho^{(i)}-\mu^{(i)})(v_i) \ge 0 \quad \text{for all }\rho, \mu\in{{\mathrm D}}\,.
\end{align}
This notion of monotonicity is closely tied to the $L^2$ metric, as we will see when considering the form of the EVI.
In \cite{conger_monotone_2025} a \textit{displacement monotonicity} definition is given by
\begin{align}\label{eq:displacement_monotonicity}
   \sum_{i=1}^N \int \<\nabla f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i)-\nabla f^{(i)}[\mu](z_i),v_i-z_i > {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(v_i,z_i) \ge 0\,,
\end{align}
where $\gamma^{(i)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})$.
The following $L^2$-bifunction recovers the $L^2$-flow \eqref{eq:L2_flow} with metric $d_{{\mathrm X}}=L^2$:
\begin{align*}
    {\mathsf b}_{L^2}( \mu, \rho) = -\sum_{i=1}^N \int f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i) \,{\mathrm d} (\rho^{(i)}-\mu^{(i)})(v_i)\,.
\end{align*}
Similarly, the following $\mathscr W_2$-bifunction recovers the $\mathscr W_2$-flow \eqref{eq:team_MFG} with metric $d_{{\mathrm X}}=\mathscr W_2$:
\begin{align*}
    {\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}( \mu, \rho) = -\sum_{i=1}^N \int \<\nabla f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i),v_i-z_i>{\mathrm d}\gamma^{(i)}(v_i,z_i) \,,
\end{align*}
where $\gamma^{(i)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})$. In both cases, this choice of bifunction ${\mathsf b}$ recovers interaction dissipativity with $\eta=0$ since linear monotonicity \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity} in $L^2$ (respectively displacement monotonicity \eqref{eq:displacement_monotonicity} in $\mathscr W_2$) implies
$${{{\mathsf b}}(\rho,\mu)} + {{{\mathsf b}}(\mu,\rho)} \le 0\,.$$



Consider now the question of well-posedness for \eqref{eq:team_MFG}-\eqref{eq:L2_flow}. The bifunction 
 ${\mathsf b}_{L^2}$ is affine in $\mu$, hence $0$-barycentrically convexlike along linear interpolations $\mu_t=(1-t)\mu_0+t\mu_1$; along $\mathscr W_2$ generalized geodesics $\mu_t=((1-t)T_0+tT_1)_\#\nu$, however, $\int f\,{\mathrm d}\mu_t=\int f\circ((1-t)T_0+tT_1)\,{\mathrm d}\nu$, so that convexity of $\mu\mapsto{\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ along them amounts to convexity of the potentials $f^{(i)}[\rho]$. Let ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \rho}$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_\rho$ be two families of generalized geodesics (Example~\ref{ex:generalized-geo} and Section~\ref{sec:ex-VMS}) with base points $\bar \rho$ and $ \rho$ respectively. The bifunction $\mu \mapsto {\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}(\mu, \rho)$ is 0-barycentrically convexlike with respect to generalized geodesics ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_\rho$ with basepoint $\rho$, but not necessarily  with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \rho}$. This poses an issue because $\frac{1}{2}\mathscr W_2^2(\cdot,\bar \rho)$ is $1$-barycentrically convexlike with respect to  ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \rho}$, but not with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\rho}$ for any other basepoint $\rho$. Then $\mu \mapsto {\mathsf B}(\tau,\bar \rho;\mu,\rho)={\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}(\mu,\rho)-\frac{1}{2\tau}\mathscr W_2^2(\rho,\bar \rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau}\mathscr W_2^2(\mu,\bar \rho)$ is \textit{not} $1/\tau$ barycentrically convexlike with respect to either ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \rho}$ or ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_\rho$. We will work around this issue later by using  ${\mathsf b}_{L^2}$ rather than  ${\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}$, whilst still fixing the choice of metrix as $\mathscr W_2$. 
Checking the form of the EVIs, we compute the time derivative of the distance function in $\mathscr W_2$ and $L^2$ along solutions to \eqref{eq:team_MFG} and \eqref{eq:L2_flow} respectively,
\begin{align}
     \frac 12 \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} \mathscr W_2^2(\rho(t),\mu) &= -\sum_{i=1}^N\int \<\nabla f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i),v_i-z^{(i)}> {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(v_i,z^{(i)}) \,, \label{eq:W2_EVI} \\
  \frac 12 \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} \sum_{i=1}^N\int\norm{\rho^{(i)}(t,v_i)-\mu^{(i)}(v_i)}^2 {\mathrm d} v_i &= -\sum_{i=1}^N\int f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i)\, {\mathrm d} (\rho^{(i)}-\mu^{(i)})(v_i) \,. \label{eq:L2_EVI}
\end{align}
This shows that solutions to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} with ${\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}$ solve \eqref{eq:team_MFG} and solutions to \eqref{eq:SEVI2} with ${\mathsf b}_{L^2}$ solve \eqref{eq:L2_flow}. However, in \cite{wang_local_2026}, the linear monotonicity condition \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity}, which comes from the $L^2$ geometry, is used with $\mathscr W_2$ dynamics \eqref{eq:team_MFG}, with well-posedness and existence of equilibrium assumed. In particular, \cite{wang_local_2026} considers the EVI
\begin{align}\label{eq:mixed_metric}
   \frac 12 \frac{{\mathrm d}}{{\mathrm d} t} \mathscr W_2^2(\rho(t),\mu) \le {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho(t))  \,.
\end{align}
To relate these dynamics to the $\mathscr W_2$-flow \eqref{eq:W2_EVI}, we derive a bound for the corresponding bifunctions. This will allow us to show well-posedness and existence of an equilibrium for the mixed dynamics \eqref{eq:mixed_metric}, a question that was left open in \cite{wang_local_2026}.
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:bifunction_ineq}
    Let $\nabla^2 f^{(i)}[\rho](z_i) \succeq 0$ for all $\rho\in{{\mathrm D}}$, $z_i\in2.30^{d_i}$, and $i\in[1,\dots,N]$. Then $ {\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}(\mu,\rho)\le {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ for all $\rho,\mu\in{{\mathrm D}}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First, we use that
\begin{align*}
    \int f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i) {\mathrm d} (\rho^{(i)}-\mu^{(i)}) = \int (f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i)-f^{(i)}[\rho](z_i)) {\mathrm d} \gamma^{(i)}(v_i,z_i)
\end{align*}
for $\gamma^{(i)}\in\Gamma_o(\rho^{(i)},\mu^{(i)})$.
Next we use the Taylor expansion 
\begin{align*}
    f^{(i)}[\rho](z_i) &= f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i) + \nabla f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i) \cdot (z_i-v_i) \\
    &+ (z_i-v_i) \cdot \int_0^1 \nabla^2 f^{(i)}[\rho]((1-s)v_i+sz_i)\cdot (z_i-v_i) {\mathrm d} s \\
    &\ge f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i) + \nabla f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i) \cdot (z_i-v_i) 
\end{align*}
using that $\nabla^2 f^{(i)}[\rho](z_i) \succeq 0$.    
\end{proof}
\begin{remark}
    The previous lemma illustrates the relationship between  Wasserstein-2 convexity and linear convexity. Suppose a sufficiently smooth  functional $F:\mathscr{P}_2 \to 2.30$ satisfies displacement convexity:
\begin{align*}
    \text{Hess}_{\mathscr W_2} F[\nu](\Phi,\Phi) &= \int \Phi^\top(z) \nabla^2 \delta_{\nu}F[\nu](z)\cdot \Phi(z) \,{\mathrm d} \nu(z)
    \\
    &\quad
    +\iint \Phi^\top(z) \nabla^2_{z,\hat z } \delta^2_{\nu} F[\nu](z,\hat z) \cdot \Phi(\hat z) \, {\mathrm d} \nu(z){\mathrm d} \nu(\hat z) \ge 0\,,  \quad \text{for all }\Phi\in L^2(\nu)\,.
\end{align*}
\sloppy 
Consider the $\mathscr W_2$-gradient flow of $F$, that is, \eqref{eq:team_MFG} with $N=1$ and $f^{(1)}=\delta_\rho F[\rho]$.
The linear monotonicity condition \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity}  only constrains the second term, $\iint \Phi^\top(z) \nabla^2_{z,\hat z } \delta^2_{\nu} F[\nu](z,\hat z) \cdot \Phi(\hat z) \, {\mathrm d} \nu(z){\mathrm d} \nu(\hat z)\ge 0$ (indeed, this can be derived by choosing $\rho=\nu_t:=\nu+t\sigma$ and $\mu=\nu$ in \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity}, where $\sigma:=-\nabla \cdot(\nu\Phi)$ for $\Phi\in L^2(\nu)$; dividing by $t^2$, letting $t\to0$, and integrating by parts, one obtains the second term above), whereas the additional requirement in Lemma~\ref{lem:bifunction_ineq} provides the other term, $\int \Phi^\top(z) \nabla^2 \delta_{\nu}F[\nu](z)\cdot \Phi(z) \,{\mathrm d} \nu(z) \ge 0$.
\end{remark}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:bifunction_ineq}, $ {\mathsf b}_{\mathscr W_2}(\mu,\rho(t))\le {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho(t))$, and so any solution to \eqref{eq:W2_EVI} solves \eqref{eq:mixed_metric}, and therefore solutions to \eqref{eq:team_MFG} also solve \eqref{eq:mixed_metric}. Conversely, if we can show that \eqref{eq:mixed_metric} has a unique strong solution, then we 
have also shown uniqueness of strong solutions for \eqref{eq:team_MFG}. Here, we will show existence of a unique strong solution to \eqref{eq:mixed_metric} directly via the dual formulation.
    \begin{corollary}[Well-Posedness]\label{cor:wellposednessL2}
        Let linear monotonicity, given by \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity}, hold for all $\mu,\rho\in{{\mathrm D}}$, and $\nabla^2 f^{(i)}[\rho](z_i) \succeq 0$ for all $\rho\in{{\mathrm D}}$, $z_i\in2.30^{d_i}$, and $i\in[1,\dots,N]$. Under \eqref{eq:b-sublevels-bis}-\eqref{eq:conditional-usc} and upper-hemicontinuity of $\rho\mapsto {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ for all $\mu \in {{\mathrm D}}$ with respect to 2-barycentric maps in ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{2,\bar\mu}$, 
        there exists a unique strong solution $\rho(t)$ to \eqref{eq:mixed_metric} starting from $$\rho(0)\in{{\mathrm D}}(\Delta):=\{\rho\in{{\mathrm D}}\,:\,\sum_{i=1}^N\int_{2.30^{d_i}}|\nabla f^{(i)}[\rho](v_i)|^2\,{\mathrm d}\rho^{(i)}(v_i) <\infty \}\,.$$
    \end{corollary}
    \begin{proof}
        Selecting ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \mu}$ to be Wasserstein-2 generalized geodesics, we have that $\mu \mapsto {\mathsf b}_{L^2} (\mu, \rho)$ is $0$-convex with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \mu}$ , since $\nabla^2 f^{(i)}[\rho]\succeq0$, and $\mathscr W_2^2(\cdot,\bar \mu)$ is 1-convex with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}_{\bar \mu}$. The linear monotonicity condition \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity} gives that ${\mathsf b}_{L^2}$ is $0$-interaction dissipative. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:main_existence}, there exists a strong solution to \eqref{eq:mixed_metric}.
    \end{proof}

    \begin{corollary}[Existence of Equilibrium]\label{cor:existenceL2}
        Let $\rho \mapsto {\mathsf b}_{L^2}( \mu, \rho)$ be upper hemicontinuous with respect to a barycentric system 
        ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$  of linear interpolations $\mu_t=(1-t)\mu_0+t\mu_1$ (so that ${{\mathrm D}}$ is assumed to be convex under mixtures) and superlevels $\sigma^+(\mu)=\{\rho \in {{\mathrm D}} \ : \ {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho) \ge 0\}$ be closed in ${{\mathrm D}}$ with a least one compact.
        Then the bifunction ${\mathsf b}_{L^2}$ has a $\rho^*$ such that ${\mathsf b}(\mu,\rho^*) \ge 0$ for all $\mu\in{{\mathrm D}}$. 
    \end{corollary}
    \begin{proof}
        In order to apply Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln}, we need that $\mu \mapsto {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ is jointly barycentrically quasi-convexlike with respect to 
        ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$.  Since $\mu \mapsto {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ is affine along linear interpolations, it is $0$-barycentrically convexlike with respect to ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$, hence also quasi-convexlike, and we apply Theorem~\ref{thm:primal_soln}.
    \end{proof}
    We remark that in order to use the linear monotonicity condition \eqref{eq:linear_monotonicity} to show existence of a \textit{unique} equilibrium point via the dual equilibrium problem, we would need $\mu \mapsto {\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ to be $\kappa>0$ barycentrically convexlike with respect to some family ${\ensuremath{\mathcal B}}$ in order to apply Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium2};  however, this fails along linear interpolations, since $\mu\mapsto{\mathsf b}_{L^2}(\mu,\rho)$ is affine, and along $\mathscr W_2$ generalized geodesics it requires the potentials $f^{(i)}[\rho]$ to be uniformly $\kappa$-convex.
<!-- end example-15 -->

<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
We now introduce the functions
\begin{equation*}
	\ell(t):=t-n\quad \text{if }n< t\le n+1,\quad 
	\ell_\tau(t):=\ell(t/\tau), \quad \ell_\tau(0):=0,
\end{equation*}
and for a discrete solution $X^n_{\tau_1}$ to \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2},
\begin{equation*}
	\zeta_{\tau_1}(s,Y):=(1-\ell_{\tau_1}(s)){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline X_{\tau_1}(s),Y)+
	\ell_{\tau_1}(s){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),Y)
\end{equation*}
Similarly, for another discrete solution $Y^n_{\tau_2}$ to \eqref{eq:D-SEVI2}, we set
\begin{equation*}
	\omega_{\tau_2}(X,t):=(1-\ell_{\tau_2}(t)){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),X)+
	\ell_{\tau_2}(t){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),X).
\end{equation*}
The functions $\zeta_{\tau_1}(s,Y)$ and $\omega_{\tau_2}(X,t)$ are continuous and piecewise linear; hence, they are locally Lipschitz. It immediately follows from  Lemma~\ref{le:simple-but-tricky} that
\begin{equation*}
	\partial_s \zeta_{\tau_1}(s,Y)\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(Y,\overline X_{\tau_1}(s))}\,,\quad
	\partial_t \omega_{\tau_2}(X,t)\le {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))}\,, \quad \text{for a.e. } t,s>0\,.
\end{equation*}
Choosing $Y:=\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)$ in the first inequality and
$X:=\overline X_{\tau_1}(s)$ in the second one, using \eqref{eq:S-lambda1},
and extending $\overline X_{\tau_1}(s)\equiv X^0_{\tau_1}$
for $s<0$, we get, for a.e. $s, t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:discretization_error_estimate}
	\partial_s \zeta_{\tau_1}(s,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))+
	\partial_t \omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),t)\le f(s,t)\,,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
    f(s,t) = \begin{cases}
        {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X^0_{\tau_1},\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))}
	& \quad\text{if }s<0,\\
	 \lambda {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)) & \quad \text{ otherwise}
    \end{cases}\,, \quad t\ge 0 \,.
\end{equation}
We will integrate over the strip $Q_{0,T}^1$ as in \cite{Nochetto-Savare06}:
\begin{align*}
    Q_{0,T}^1 := \big\{ (s,t)\in2.30^2 \ : \ 0\le t \le T, \quad t-1 \le s \le t \big\}\,.
\end{align*}
The integral of \eqref{eq:discretization_error_estimate} over $Q_{0,T}^1$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:discretization_err_integral}
   \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1}  \text{div}_{s,t} \left( \begin{bmatrix}
       \zeta_{\tau_1}(s,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)) \\
	\omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),t)
   \end{bmatrix} \right) \, {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t \le \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1} f(s,t)\, {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t:= a_0\,,
\end{align}
will require five estimates; one from the right hand side, and four over the boundary $\partial Q_{0,T}^1$ from the divergence theorem. In Figure~\ref{fig:strip}, the edges of $Q_{0,T}^1$ are labeled with the corresponding boundary integrals.  Applying the divergence theorem to the lower bound, let 
\begin{align*}
       \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1}  \text{div}_{s,t} \left( \begin{bmatrix}
       \zeta_{\tau_1}(s,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)) \\
	\omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),t)
   \end{bmatrix} \right) \, {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t  =\sum_{i=1}^4 a_i\,, \quad 
   a_1:=\int_{T-1}^T \omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),T)\,{\mathrm d} s\,, \\ 
   a_2:= -\int_{-1}^0 \omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),0)\,{\mathrm d} s \,,  \quad
   a_3:=
   \int_0^T\Big(\zeta_{\tau_1}(t,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))-\omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t),t)\Big)\,{\mathrm d} t\,,\\
   a_4 := 
   \int_0^T\Big(\omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t-1),t)-\zeta_{\tau_1}(t-1,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))
	\Big)\,{\mathrm d} t\,.
\end{align*} 
Therefore \eqref{eq:discretization_err_integral} can be written as
\begin{align}\label{eq:discretization_err_integral_coeffs}
    \sum_{i=1}^4 a_i \le a_0\,.
\end{align}

\begin{figure}
    \centering
    
                                               
                   
                       
                      

                  
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=latex, scale=1.1]

              
  \def5{5}
  \def1{1}

                           
                                                                     
                                                              
                                                
                                                    
  \coordinate (A) at (-1, 0);
  \coordinate (B) at (0, 0);
  \coordinate (C) at (5, 5);
  \coordinate (D) at (5-1, 5);

                   
  \fill[gray!15] (A) -- (B) -- (C) -- (D) -- cycle;

                            
                                  
  \draw[thick] (A) -- (B);
                                      
  \draw[thick] (B) -- (C);
                               
  \draw[thick] (D) -- (C);
                                          
  \draw[thick] (A) -- (D);

                          
  \draw[dashed] (0, 5) -- (5, 5);                     
  \draw[dashed] (5, 0) -- (5, 5);                   

                             
  \draw[->] (-1-0.4, 0) -- (5+0.7, 0) node[below] {$s$};
  \draw[->] (0, -0.3)      -- (0, 5+0.7)  node[left]  {$t$};

               
  \node[left]  at (0, 5) {$t = T$};
  \node[below] at (5, 0) {$s = T$};

                                                    
  \draw[<->] (-1, -0.4) -- (0, -0.4)
    node[midway, below] {$\varepsilon$};

                                                 
  \draw[<->] (5-1, 5+0.4) -- (5, 5+0.4)
    node[midway, above] {$\varepsilon$};

                                          

                                       
  \node[above] at ($0.5*(D)+0.5*(C)+(0,-0.1)$) {$a_1$};

                                          
  \node[below] at ($0.5*(A)+0.5*(B)+(0,0)$) {$a_2$};

                                                                 
  \node[right] at ($(B)!0.22!(C)+(0.15,-0.15)$) {$a_3$};

                                                                
  \node[left]  at ($(A)!0.22!(D)+(-0.15, 0.15)$) {$a_4$};

                                  

                                                                
  \node[left] at ($(A)!0.62!(D)+(-0.1, 0.2)$) {$s = t - \varepsilon$};

                                                           
  \node[right] at ($(B)!0.38!(C)+(0.55,0.25)$) {$t = s$};

                          
                                                                         
  \node at ($(A)!0.5!(C)+(0.0, 0)$) {$Q^{\varepsilon}_{0,T}$};

\end{tikzpicture}
                

    \caption{The strip $Q_{0,T}^1$.}
    \label{fig:strip}
\end{figure}
We compute estimates for $a_1,\dots, a_4$ from below, and for $a_0$ from above, to obtain the Cauchy estimate. We begin with $a_0$.
By Definition~\ref{def:bounded_Delta} with $x\in {{\mathrm D}}(\Delta^{\kappa})$, we have 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:slope_estimate}
        \Delta^{\kappa}(x) := \sup_{y'\in {{\mathrm D}}} \frac{{{{{\mathsf b}^{\kappa}}(y',x)}}_-}{{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(x,y')} \ge  -{{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(y,x)}  \quad \text{for all } y\in{{\mathrm D}}\,.
    \end{align}
Combining this estimate with \eqref{eq:S-lambda1},
we construct the following bound on ${{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X^0_{\tau_1},\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))}$:
\begin{align*}
    {{{\mathsf b}_1^{\kappa}}(X^0_{\tau_1},\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))} \le \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)  + \lambda {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_{\tau_1}^0,\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t))\,.
\end{align*}
Applying this to the definition of $a_0$, and evaluating separately the part of $Q_{0,T}^1$ where $s<0$, we have
\begin{align*}
    a_0 &\le \int_{0}^1 \int_{t-1}^{0} \Delta^{\kappa}(X_{\tau_1}^0) {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t + \lambda \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)) {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t \\
    &=\frac{1^2}2 \Delta^{\kappa}(X_{\tau_1}^0) + \lambda \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t)) {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t \,.
\end{align*}
The integral over the distance term has the upper bound
\begin{align*}
    \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),& \overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t 
    \le  \iint_{Q_{0,T}^1} {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t))  {\mathrm d} s {\mathrm d} t +1 \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t
\end{align*}
Let $n, m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in ((n-1)\tau_1,n\tau_1]$ and $s\in ((m-1)\tau_1,m\tau_1]$. Since each $(s,t)\in Q_{0,T}^1$ satisfies $t-1\le s\le t$, we conclude that $0\le n-m \le 1/\tau_1 + 1$. Using the estimates in Proposition~\ref{le:apriori} and recalling $\tilde\tau:=\big(\frac1\tau-\lambda\big)^{-1}$, we have
\begin{align*}
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t))
    &\le  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),X_{\tau_1}^m)+ {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_{\tau_1}^m,X_{\tau_1}^n)+ {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_{\tau_1}^n,\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t)) =  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_{\tau_1}^m,X_{\tau_1}^n)\\
    &\le \sum_{i=m+1}^{n}  {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X_{\tau_1}^{i-1}, X_{\tau_1}^{i})
    \le \tilde \tau_1 \sum_{i=m+1}^{n}  \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^{i-1})
    \le \tilde \tau_1 (n-m)  c_0 \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)\\
    &\le \tilde \tau_1 (1/\tau_1 + 1)  c_0 \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)\,.
\end{align*}
Combining with the previous estimates, and using that the volume of $Q_{0,T}^1$ is $1 T$, we conclude that
\begin{align}\label{eq:f_upper_bd_Cauchy}
    a_0 
    &\le\frac{1^2}2 \Delta^{\kappa}(X_{\tau_1}^0) + \lambda \tilde \tau_1(1/\tau_1+1)  1 T  c_0 \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)
    + 1 \lambda  \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t \,.
\end{align}
Next, to bound $a_1$ from below, we use the triangle inequality twice to obtain
\begin{align*}
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) &\le {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) + {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s))
    \\ & \le\ell_{\tau_2}(T){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))+ (1-\ell_{\tau_2}(T)) \left( {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s), \underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))\right.\\
    &\left.\quad + {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) \right) + {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s)) \\
    & \le \omega_{\tau_2}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),T)+ {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s)) + {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T),\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) \,.
\end{align*}
Hence,
\begin{align*}
    a_1=\int_{T-1}^T \omega_{\tau_2}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),T) {\mathrm d} s
    \ge 1 {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) - \int_{T-1}^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s)){\mathrm d} s - 1{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T),\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))
\end{align*}
To lower bound the two terms on the right hand side, we note that, again by Proposition~\ref{le:apriori},
\begin{align*}
    \int_{T-1}^T {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(s)) {\mathrm d} s  \le 1 \tilde \tau_1 \left(\frac{1}{\tau_1}+1\right) c_0 \Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0)\,,
\end{align*}
and for $n:= \lceil T/\tau_2\rceil$, we have
\begin{align*}
    {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T),\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) \le {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(Y_{\tau_2}^{n},Y_{\tau_2}^{n-1}\normalcolor)\le \tilde \tau_2 c_0 \Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0\normalcolor)\,.
\end{align*}
Thus, we conclude
\begin{align*}
   a_1\ge  1\left[{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) - c_0(\tilde \tau_1\left(\frac{1}{\tau_1}+1\right)+\tilde \tau_2) \left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right) \right] \,.
\end{align*}
For $a_2$, we get the explicit expression
\begin{equation}
	a_2= -\int_{-1}^0 \omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),0)\,{\mathrm d} s = -\int_{-1}^0 {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline Y_{\tau_2}(0),\overline X_{\tau_1}(0)\normalcolor ) {\mathrm d} s =
	-1 {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})\,.
\end{equation}
Next we will bound $a_3$ and $a_4$. 
We set
\begin{equation}
	\delta_{X,\tau_1}(s):=\sup_{Y\in{{\mathrm D}}} \Big|\zeta_{\tau_1}(s,Y)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(s),Y)\Big|,\quad
	\delta_{Y,{\tau_2}}(t):=\sup_{X\in{{\mathrm D}}} \Big|\omega_{\tau_2}(X,t)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t),X)\Big|
\end{equation}
observing that 
\begin{align*}
    &\ \delta_{Y,\tau_2}(t) = \sup_X \Big|(1-\ell_{\tau_2}(t)){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),X)+
	\ell_{\tau_2}(t){\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),X)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t),X)\Big| \\
    &= \sup_X \Big|(1-\ell_{\tau_2}(t))\big[{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),X)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t),X)\big]\Big|\\
    &=(1-\ell_{\tau_2}(t)) \sup_X \Big|{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),X)-{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t),X)\Big| \le (1-\ell_{\tau_2}(t)) {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))\,,
\end{align*}
and similarly, $\delta_{X,\tau_1}(s)\le (1-\ell_{\tau_1}(s)) {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\underline{X}_{\tau_1}(s),\overline X_{\tau_1}(s))$. Using again Proposition~\ref{le:apriori}, we have
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
    	\delta_{X,\tau_1}(s)\le(1-\ell_{\tau_1}(s)) \tilde \tau_1 c_0 \Delta^{\kappa} (X^0_{\tau_1}),\\
	\delta_{Y,\tau_2}(t)\le (1-\ell_{\tau_2}(t)) \tilde \tau_2 c_0\Delta^{\kappa} (Y^0_{\tau_2})\,.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
Define $h_\tau(t)=\frac t2+\frac \tau2\ell_\tau(t)(1-\ell_\tau(t))$. Then $h_\tau'(t)=1-\ell_\tau(t)$ for a.e. $t$, and $h_\tau(0)=0$. Hence $\int_0^T(1-\ell_\tau(t))=h_\tau(T)$, and so
\begin{align*}
	{\mathrm I}_{X,{\tau_1}} :={}&\int_0^T \delta_{X,\tau_1}(s)\,{\mathrm d} s \le \tilde \tau_1 c_0 h_{\tau_1}(T) \Delta^{\kappa} (X^0_{\tau_1}),\\
	{\mathrm I}_{Y,\tau_2}:=&
	\int_0^T \delta_{Y,{\tau_2}}(s)\,{\mathrm d} s\le 
	\tilde \tau_2 c_0 h_{\tau_2}(T)\Delta^{\kappa} (Y^0_{\tau_2}) \,.
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{align*}
	a_3 &=
    -\int_0^T\Big(\omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t),t)-
	{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))+
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))-
	\zeta_{\tau_1}(t,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))\Big)\,{\mathrm d} t	
	\\&\ge 
	-
    \int_0^T\Big(\delta_{X,{\tau_1}}(t)+
	\delta_{Y,{\tau_2}}(t)\Big)\,{\mathrm d} t=
    -
     \left({\mathrm I}_{X,{\tau_1}}+{\mathrm I}_{Y,{\tau_2}} \right)\,.
\end{align*}
A similar calculation for $a_4$ gives
\begin{align*}
	a_4 &=
	-
    \int_0^T\Big(\zeta_{\tau_1}(t-1,\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))-
	{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t-1),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))+
		{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t-1),\overline Y_{\tau_2}(t))
        -
	\omega_{\tau_2}(\overline X_{\tau_1}(t-1),t)\Big)\,{\mathrm d} t	
	\\&\ge -
	\int_0^T\Big(\delta_{X,{\tau_1}}(t-1)+
	\delta_{Y,{\tau_2}}(t)\Big)\,{\mathrm d} t=
    -
    \left({\mathrm I}_{X,\tau_1}+{\mathrm I}_{Y,{\tau_2}} \right)\,.
\end{align*}
Combining the estimates for the five terms results in
\begin{align*}
&1\left[{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) - c_0\left(\tilde \tau_1 \left(\frac{1}{\tau_1}+1\right)+\tilde \tau_2\right) \left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right) \right] 
-1 {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})
-
2 
\left({\mathrm I}_{X,\tau_1}+{\mathrm I}_{Y,{\tau_2}} \right)\\
&\le
    \frac{1^2}2 \Delta^{\kappa}(X_{\tau_1}^0) + \lambda \tilde \tau_1(1/\tau_1+1)  1 T  c_0 \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)
    + 1 \lambda  \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t \,.
\end{align*}
Rearranging, dividing by $1$, and defining $\tilde\tau:=\max\{\tilde\tau_1, \tilde\tau_2\}$,  gives
\begin{align*}
{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T)) \le &c_0\left(\tilde \tau_1\left(\frac{1}{\tau_1}+1\right)+\tilde \tau_2\right) \left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right) 
+ {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})
+\frac{ 2}{1}\left({\mathrm I}_{X,\tau_1}+{\mathrm I}_{Y,{\tau_2}} \right)\\
&+
    \frac{1}2 \Delta^{\kappa}(X_{\tau_1}^0) + \lambda \tilde \tau_1(1/\tau_1+1)   T  c_0 \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)
    +  \lambda  \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t\\
 \le &c_0\left(\tilde \tau_1\left(\frac{1}{\tau_1}+1\right)+\tilde \tau_2\right) \left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right) 
+ {\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})\\
&+\frac{2}{1}(\tilde \tau_1 +\tilde \tau_2)c_0 (h_{\tau_1}(T)+h_{\tau_2}(T))( \Delta^{\kappa} (X^0_{\tau_1} +\Delta^{\kappa} (Y^0_{\tau_2}))\\
&+
    \frac{1}2 \Delta^{\kappa}(X_{\tau_1}^0) + \lambda \tilde \tau_1(1/\tau_1+1)  T  c_0 \Delta^\kappa(X_{\tau_1}^0)
    +  \lambda  \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t\\
\le
& c_T \tilde \tau \left(2+\frac{(h_{\tau_1}(T)+h_{\tau_2}(T))}{1} +\frac{1}{\tilde \tau} + \frac{1}{\tau_1}\right)
\left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right)
\\&+{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})
+  \lambda  \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t
\end{align*}
for some constant $c_T$ depending on $\tau_o, T, \lambda$ only. 
Optimizing w.r.t.~$1$, we choose $$1=(h_{\tau_1}(T)+h_{\tau_2}(T))^{1/2}\left(\frac{\tilde \tau}{1+\tilde \tau/\tau_1}\right)^{1/2}$$ to obtain
\begin{align*}
{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))
\le{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})+
 a_\tau(T)+  \lambda  \int_0^T{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t) ) {\mathrm d} t\,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{align*}
  a_\tau(T):= 2c_T \sqrt{\tilde\tau} \left[\sqrt{\tilde\tau} +
  \sqrt{\frac{\tau_1 + \tilde \tau}{\tau_1 }(h_{\tau_1}(T)+h_{\tau_2}(T))}
  \right]
\left(\Delta^\kappa (X_{\tau_1}^0) +\Delta^\kappa (Y_{\tau_2}^0)\right)\,.
\end{align*} 
Writing $g(t):={\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(t),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(t))$, the above estimate can be written as 
\begin{align*}
g(T)
\le g(0)+ a_\tau(T)+  \lambda  \int_0^T g(t) {\mathrm d} t\,.
\end{align*}
Applying Gr\"onwall's inequality, we conclude
\begin{align*}
    g(T)\le  e^{\lambda T} g(0) + C_\tau(T)\,,\qquad
    C_\tau(T):= a_\tau(T) +\lambda \int_0^T a_\tau(t) e^{\lambda(T-t)}{\mathrm d} t\,.
\end{align*}
Finally, we investigate the behavior of the upper bound as $\tau_1, \tau_2\to 0$. Notice that $\tilde\tau_i=\mathcal O(\tau_i)$ as $\tau_i\to0$. Since $h_{\tau_1}(T)+h_{\tau_2}(T)\to T$ as $\tau_1, \tau_2\to 0$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \sqrt{\tilde\tau}\left[\sqrt{\tilde\tau} +
  \sqrt{\frac{\tau_1 + \tilde \tau}{\tau_1 }(h_{\tau_1}(t)+h_{\tau_2}(t))}  
  \right] 
  &\sim 
  \sqrt{T \max\{\tau_1,\tau_2\}\left(1+\frac{\max\{\tau_1,\tau_2\}}{\tau_1}\right)} \\
 &\sim
  \begin{cases}
   \sqrt{2T\tau_1}   &\text{ if } \tau_1\ge\tau_2\,,\\
   \sqrt{2T\tau_2^2/\tau_1}   &\text{ if } \tau_1<\tau_2\,.
  \end{cases}
\end{align*}
Hence, as long as $\tau_2^2/\tau_1\to 0$, we have $a_\tau(t)=\mathcal O\left(\max\{\tau_1,\tau_2\}/\sqrt{\tau_1}\right)\to 0$ as $\tau_1, \tau_2\to 0$ uniformly for $t\in [0,T]$. We conclude that $C_\tau(T)\to0$ at the same rate. And so, 
$${\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(\overline{X}_{\tau_1}(T),\overline{Y}_{\tau_2}(T))- e^{\lambda T}{\mathsf d}_{{\mathrm X}}(X^0_{\tau_1},Y^0_{\tau_2})=\mathcal O\left(\max\{\tau_1,\tau_2\}/\sqrt{\tau_1}\right)\to 0$$ 
goes to zero for $\tau_1,\tau_2 \to 0$ with $\tau_2^2/\tau_1\to 0$.
